# Concepts & Domain Model

One vocabulary, defined once. When every team means the same thing by *Workflow*, *Credential*, or *Audit Log*, reviews move faster, handoffs stop leaking, and compliance gaps close before they reach an auditor.

This is the authoritative glossary for sk: each term is defined exactly once, and every other doc uses the meaning given here — not an approximation.

| Group | Covers | Key terms |
|---|---|---|
| [0 — Naming & Acronyms](#group-0-naming--acronyms) | Shared names and expansions | Contextual learning loop, AEAD, DAG, MCP, RBAC |
| [1 — Platform Core](#group-1-platform-core) | Isolation and identity | Tenant, User, API Key, Portal Token |
| [2 — Authoring](#group-2-authoring) | How workflows get built | Conversation, Draft, Skill, Knowledge Source, Discovery |
| [3 — Integration](#group-3-integration) | Reaching external integrations | Connector, Template, Driver, Credential |
| [4 — Execution](#group-4-execution) | What runs, and what it records | Workflow, Step, Execution, Schedule |
| [5 — Governance](#group-5-governance) | Control and proof | Audit Log, RBAC, Before-Request Hook, Self-Healing |
| [6 — Surfaces](#group-6-surfaces) | How callers reach sk | sk CLI, MCP Server, Chat Adapter, Notifications |

Read top to bottom for a full mental model, or jump to a group.

---

## Group 0: Naming & Acronyms

A few names in the codebase differ from the phrasing used in the prose docs, and several acronyms recur across every group. Both are collected here so every reader shares the same vocabulary.

**Contextual learning loop** — the mechanism by which a tenant's authoring context improves over time: every run can surface drift, a drift can produce an operator-reviewed Patch Candidate, a recurring pattern can produce an operator-promoted Skill Candidate, and both feed back into the next authoring run. See [workflows.md](./workflows.md) and the self-healing subsystem.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Run --> Drift --> PC[Patch Candidate] --> SC[Skill Candidate]
  SC --> Author[Better authoring] --> Run
```

**Drift-assisted repair suggestion** — the prose phrasing for the codebase's *self-healing* subsystem (also called *operator-reviewed remediation* in governance contexts). Same concept, different audience.

> **Naming note.** The prose docs say "drift-assisted repair"; the codebase keeps stable technical identifiers (`apps/engine/src/self-healing/`, `rbac/`, `credentials/`, etc.). These names must not be renamed for vocabulary alignment — they are referenced by modules, logs, and tests.

### Acronyms

Collected so every reader has the same expansion at hand.

| Acronym | Expansion | One-line definition |
|---|---|---|
| AEAD | Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data | Encryption that also detects tampering of the ciphertext and the metadata it is bound to. |
| BPMN | Business Process Model and Notation | Classical visual workflow language; cited as a contrast to AI-assisted authoring. |
| DAG | Directed Acyclic Graph | The shape of a Workflow: steps flow forward, never loop back to themselves. |
| DCR | Dynamic Client Registration | OAuth 2.1 mechanism that lets a new external client self-register with the server (RFC 7591). |
| DLP | Data Loss Prevention | Policy layer that recognises sensitive fields (PII, secrets) and blocks them at the boundary. |
| MCP | Model Context Protocol | The standard by which AI clients (IDE assistants, coding agents, chat clients) connect to external integrations (Connectors). |
| OAuth 2.1 | — | The current consolidated OAuth standard (PKCE-by-default, refresh-token rotation, no implicit grant). |
| OIDC | OpenID Connect | Identity layer on top of OAuth 2.x; how sk verifies who a user is. |
| PII | Personally Identifiable Information | Data that identifies a natural person; subject to GDPR / SOC2 controls. |
| PKCE | Proof Key for Code Exchange | OAuth extension that protects the authorization-code flow on public clients. |
| RAG | Retrieval-Augmented Generation | LLM pattern: ground generation in retrieved tenant-specific context (Lewis et al. 2020). |
| RBAC | Role-Based Access Control | Permission model that grants actions through roles rather than per-user grants. |
| ReAct | Reasoning + Acting | Agent pattern that interleaves model reasoning and tool calls (Yao et al. 2023). |
| RLS | Row-Level Security | PostgreSQL feature that enforces tenant boundaries at the database, not the application. |
| RTO/RPO | Recovery Time / Point Objective | Disaster-recovery targets: how fast you recover, and how much data you may lose. |
| SAML | Security Assertion Markup Language | Enterprise SSO standard, alternative to OIDC. |
| SCIM | System for Cross-domain Identity Management | Standard for automated user provisioning and deprovisioning. |
| SSO | Single Sign-On | One login session unlocks multiple applications. |

---

## Group 1: Platform Core

**Tenant** — the top-level isolation unit in sk. All resources — workflows, connectors, credentials, users, skills, conversations, and knowledge sources — belong to exactly one Tenant. Multi-tenancy is structural, not configurable; no shared state crosses tenant boundaries, and every platform operation is scoped to the tenant of the authenticated principal.

**User** — a human principal within a Tenant. A User has a role (admin, member, or end-user) that governs which resources they can see and which actions they are permitted to take. Users authenticate through an Auth Provider (OIDC or API Key) and their identity is linked to their chat-platform accounts when chat integrations are enabled.

**API Key** — a bearer token scoped to a Tenant and a set of permissions. Used for programmatic access, service-to-service integration, and CLI authentication. API Keys carry explicit scopes and can be constrained to specific workflows or connectors. They support overlap-window rotation so access is never interrupted during a key change.

**Portal Token** — a short-lived, scoped credential issued to an end user for single-purpose access. Portal Tokens allow external users to interact with specific workflows without becoming full Tenant members. They are a tighter variant of an API Key, with a shorter default lifetime and a narrower permission surface.

---

## Group 2: Authoring

**Conversation** — the primary authoring session in sk. A User and the AI exchange messages; the AI uses structured authoring actions internally to propose, validate, and assemble a workflow. Conversations are persistent and resumable — a session can be paused and continued without losing context. The Conversation is where Drafts are created, refined, and committed.

**Draft** — a workflow under construction within a Conversation. A Draft exists only in the context of the Conversation until a User explicitly commits it. Committing a Draft creates a versioned, immutable Workflow. Drafts are never executed directly; only committed Workflows run in the execution engine.

**Skill** — a reusable, curated piece of context loaded into the AI during Conversations and other AI-assisted authoring flows such as discovery, diagnosis, and bounded repair. Skills encode best practices, integration patterns, domain-specific knowledge, and known failure modes. They are authored or promoted by operators with explicit human approval. Skills are never auto-generated or auto-promoted from execution history, and committed deterministic workflow execution does not load them.

**Skill Candidate** — a pattern detected from execution history that might improve AI context quality. The platform proposes Skill Candidates automatically when it detects recurring patterns in successful or failed executions. A Skill Candidate becomes a Skill only through explicit operator approval — the platform never promotes one automatically.

**Knowledge Source** — a persistent document store attached to a Tenant or Workflow. Operators upload documents (PDFs, runbooks, compliance policies, architecture diagrams) which are chunked and indexed for semantic search. On interactive upload the AI auto-analyzes the content to generate a short **description** and a set of topical **tags**, so each source is self-describing and routable — the AI can decide which source covers a topic before searching, and searches can be narrowed by tag. The AI searches Knowledge Sources during Conversations, discovery, and repair-oriented authoring flows to ground its proposals in tenant-specific context. Committed workflow execution does not query Knowledge Sources directly.

**Discovery** — a one-shot analysis where the AI examines uploaded files (API specifications, runbooks, architecture diagrams, OpenAPI docs) and proposes Connectors, Skills, and Knowledge Sources inferred from their content. The result is a set of proposals — called Discovery Artifacts — that operators can approve or reject individually. Discovery does not configure anything automatically.

---

## Group 3: Integration

**Connector** — a configured connection to an external integration boundary. A Connector is built from a template, a driver, and credentials. It represents a specific integration instance — for example, a Stripe production account or a GitHub organisation. Connectors are tenant-scoped and versioned.

**Connector Template** — a pre-built blueprint for a well-known service. Templates include the driver type, authentication configuration, documentation ingestion setup, and guided setup instructions. sk ships 55 Connector Templates covering services across payments, CRM, DevOps, data, communication, and cloud infrastructure. Templates are the starting point for creating a Connector; they are not Connectors themselves.

**Driver** — the protocol layer that executes Connector requests. sk has four built-in drivers: HTTP, GraphQL, PostgreSQL, and S3. Each driver handles request construction, response parsing, pagination, and error normalisation for its protocol. Drivers are not pluggable at runtime — the four built-in drivers cover the intended integration surface.

**Credential** — an encrypted secret stored in the platform's credential vault. Credentials include API keys, OAuth2 tokens, connection strings, and similar sensitive values. Connectors reference Credentials by identifier; the raw secret value is never exposed outside the vault. All Credentials are encrypted at rest. OAuth2 Credentials refresh automatically.

---

## Group 4: Execution

**Workflow** — a versioned, directed acyclic graph (DAG) of Steps that produces a deterministic outcome. Workflows are authored through Conversations, approved by a human, and then committed as immutable versions. Each version is a complete snapshot of the workflow at the time of approval. Workflows are tenant-scoped and support a lifecycle of draft, active, and archived.

**Step** — a single unit of work within a Workflow DAG. Step types are: request (call a Connector), transform (reshape data), branch (conditional routing), loop (iterate over a collection), parallel (run Steps concurrently), wait (introduce a delay), wait_for_event (pause until an inbound signal), and call (invoke another Workflow). Each Step declares retry policy, timeout, error handling behaviour, and optional field masking for sensitive data.

**Execution** — a single run of a Workflow. An Execution carries its own state, step-by-step results, logs, and final status. Executions are immutable records — they are never modified after completion. Each Execution records its request source (API, CLI, scheduler, webhook, MCP, or chat) and its environment (dev or prod). Executions are queryable and searchable after the fact.

**Execution Fixture** — a recorded snapshot of a past Workflow execution, capturing the request and response at each Step. Fixtures serve as the dry-run corpus for Self-Healing proposals: before a Patch Candidate is presented to an operator for approval, it is validated against relevant Fixtures to confirm the repair does not break known-good behaviour.

**Schedule** — a cron expression or event trigger attached to a Workflow. The scheduler fires the Workflow at the configured time or in response to an inbound event. Schedules are reconciled at engine boot and on configuration changes. Scheduled fires are recorded in the Audit Log with source `scheduler`.

---

## Group 5: Governance

**Audit Log** — the immutable, append-only record of every state change in the platform. Every entry carries: what changed, who initiated it, from which surface (API, CLI, MCP, chat, scheduler, webhook), and when. The Audit Log cannot be modified or deleted. It is the authoritative record for compliance, debugging, and incident review.

**RBAC** — role-based access control enforced at every platform boundary. Every API route, MCP call, webhook trigger, and execution path checks the caller's role and permissions before proceeding. sk ships five built-in roles: the three user-facing roles (admin, member, enduser) plus the metrics_scraper and portal_token_user system roles. Custom roles and resource-level grants are supported for more granular control. RBAC decisions are recorded in the Audit Log.

**Before-Request Hook** — a sandboxed script that runs before a Connector request executes. Hooks can inspect or modify the outbound request, enforce policy (such as blocking writes during maintenance windows), or abort execution entirely. Hooks run in an isolated sandbox with a strict CPU budget and no access to the host environment. Hook execution is audited. Any error or timeout fails closed and denies the request.

**Self-Healing** — the platform's drift detection and bounded repair system. When a Connector's schema or behaviour changes in a way that causes Step failures, the engine detects the drift, compares the new response against the last known Schema Version, proposes a repair using the AI within a narrow repair loop, and dry-runs the proposed repair against recorded Execution Fixtures. The result is a Patch Candidate presented to an operator for approval. Self-Healing never applies a repair automatically without operator approval.

**Patch Candidate** — a proposed repair generated by the Self-Healing process. Each Patch Candidate carries the proposed change, a classification of safe or unsafe based on the scope and risk of the repair, the Execution Fixtures it was validated against, and a full audit trail. Patch Candidates require explicit operator approval before they are applied to a live Workflow.

---

## Group 6: Surfaces

**sk CLI** — the unified command-line surface and primary human-facing interface for the platform. Built on Ink plus citty commands, it provides a terminal UI that opens a Conversation for end users describing workflow goals, and top-level admin commands for operators managing the platform (`sk connectors`, `sk workflows`, `sk executions`, `sk audit`, and related groups). The sk CLI supports four authentication modes: API Key, OIDC, Portal Token, and headless (stdin pipe for scripted usage). Persona-aware: the surface adapts based on the authenticated user's role.

**MCP Server** — the Model Context Protocol server embedded in the sk engine. It exposes Workflows as callable `wf_<slug>` entries inside the MCP callable surface, Connectors as structured resources, and Skills as curated prompts that can be injected into an AI's context. Any MCP-compatible client — IDE assistants, coding agents, and chat clients alike — can connect to the MCP Server and interact with the platform. All MCP calls are governed by the same RBAC and Audit Log as direct API calls.

**Chat Adapter** — the integration layer for enterprise chat platforms (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Chat). Each adapter normalises platform-specific events — mentions, slash commands, interaction callbacks — into sk's Conversation model, and renders responses back as native platform messages. Approval flows surface as interactive cards with approve and reject buttons. Identity linking connects a chat user's platform identity to their Tenant account.

**Notification Rule** — a tenant-scoped row that selects which engine events fan out to which channel. Carries an event-type pattern, an optional workflow pattern, a severity, an optional `request_source_filter`, and the target `(workspace_id, channel_id)` tuple. Backed by the dispatcher in `apps/engine/src/notifications/service.ts` with a leaky-bucket rate limiter and a three-state circuit breaker. See [docs/operators/notifications.md](../operators/notifications.md).

**Notification Delivery** — the per-attempt outcome of dispatching a Notification Rule against an event. Possible statuses: `sent`, `rate_limited`, `breaker_open`, `failed`, `skipped`. Each row is the audit-grade record of what was (or was not) delivered, mirrored in the audit log via `chat.message.sent`, `chat.message.denied`, or `webhook.outbound.failed`.

**Service Metadata** — the identity envelope every engine code path carries: `{ trace_id, tenant_id, actor_id, actor_email, request_source }`. Constructed at every entry point (HTTP middleware, MCP server, scheduler, CLI bin, conversation tool-chain recursion) and threaded through every log line, audit row, and telemetry event. Defined in `apps/engine/src/observability/service-metadata.ts`. The trace_id is what an operator follows across surfaces during incident triage.

**Result Storage URI** — the pointer in `executions.result_storage_uri` (and per-step rows) that resolves a spilled payload back to its full content. Inline payloads up to `STEP_RESULT_DB_BYTES` (10 KB) live in the row; larger payloads spill to S3 (`s3://<bucket>/<key>`) or the `execution_fixtures` table (`fixture://<uuid>`). A 512-byte text preview always lands inline.

**LLM Judge** — an opt-in scoring layer invoked by the eval runner only when (a) `SUBKIT_EVAL_LLM_JUDGE=1` is set AND (b) the deterministic validator returns `pass=false` with `function_passed=true` (structurally fine, semantically dubious). The judge emits a `passes`/`partial`/`failed` verdict that enriches the report; it never overrides the deterministic gate.

---

## What to Read Next

- [docs/developers/input-surfaces.md](../developers/input-surfaces.md) — How users and systems reach sk: the CLI, REST API, MCP server, chat platforms, webhooks, and scheduled triggers.

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/governance-and-audit.md -->

# Governance & Audit

> **Audience:** Security engineers, compliance reviewers, architects

**Pass the audit on the first pass.** Every interaction in sk is authorised before it runs, recorded in an immutable trail, and stripped of secrets — so "who did what, when, and from where?" is always one query away. Security is the default behaviour by architecture, not by configuration: multi-tenant isolation, a comprehensive audit log, a compliance posture that holds by construction, and secret-hygiene defences at the conversational surface.

Two adjacent concerns have their own admin homes:

- **Access control (RBAC/ABAC), identity, and Before-Request Hooks.** Every API route, MCP call, and workflow trigger is permission-checked before any resource is touched; a sandboxed, fail-closed Before-Request Hook can add dynamic policy on top of static roles. Full model: [RBAC & Roles](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md).
- **The credential vault.** All integration secrets are stored encrypted with AES-256-GCM, referenced by identifier, decrypted only at the moment of use, and never exposed to the AI or to logs. Full model and rotation: [Credentials & Keys](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md).

---

## How every request is governed

A request from any surface passes the same chain before it touches a resource: it is tagged with its source, checked against RBAC/ABAC, run through any tenant Before-Request Hook, then handed to the driver policy chain — and every decision lands in the tenant-scoped audit log.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R[Request<br/>API · MCP · CLI · webhook · scheduler] --> RS[Tag request source]
    RS --> RBAC{RBAC / ABAC check}
    RBAC -->|deny| D1[403 + audit row]
    RBAC -->|allow| HOOK{Before-Request Hook<br/>sandboxed, fail-closed}
    HOOK -->|deny| D2[Blocked + audit row]
    HOOK -->|allow| DRV[Driver policy chain<br/>tool policy · egress · sandbox]
    DRV --> AUD[(Immutable audit log<br/>tenant-scoped)]
```

Secrets never travel through that chain in the clear. A credential is collected through a masked form, encrypted, and stored by reference; the driver decrypts it only at the moment of use, while the LLM and every log surface see a redacted placeholder instead of the value.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    F[Masked form<br/>ask_user_form sensitive] --> ENC[AES-256-GCM encrypt]
    ENC --> V[(Credential vault<br/>referenced by id)]
    V -->|decrypt at moment of use| DRV[Driver request]
    DRV --> EXT[External connector]
    V -.->|secret never exposed| LLM[LLM tool args · transcript]
    V -.->|scrubbed at write| LOG[Logs · audit · debug.log]
```

---

## Multi-Tenancy as a First-Class Concern

sk is multi-tenant from the ground up. Every resource in the platform — workflows, connectors, credentials, users, skills, conversations, audit log entries — belongs to exactly one Tenant. This is not a deployment mode or a configuration setting. It is the data model.

Tenant isolation is enforced at every layer. Database queries always filter by tenant identity. API responses never include cross-tenant data. The audit log is tenant-scoped. A single engine instance can serve multiple organizations with complete isolation between them.

This design means there is no "global" namespace to accidentally share, no configuration flag to toggle isolation on or off, and no way for one tenant's data to appear in another tenant's context. Isolation is structural.

---

## The Audit Trail

Every state change in sk produces an immutable audit log entry. This is not selective logging — it is comprehensive.

The audit log captures: workflow creation, modification, approval, and deletion; connector operations; credential creation, rotation, and revocation; user provisioning and role changes; execution triggers and final results; approval events; skill promotions; patch candidate reviews; and more — over 100 distinct action types across all platform surfaces.

Each entry captures the full context of the event: what action was taken, who took it (user or service account identity), from which surface (API, CLI, MCP, chat, webhook, or scheduler), what changed (a structured diff where applicable), and precisely when. The metadata field on every entry is scrubbed for token-shaped values before persistence — bearer tokens, JWTs, AWS access keys, and any value under a key matching a sensitive name (`password`, `token`, `secret`, `credential`, `*_token`, `authorization`) become `***REDACTED:<kind>***` at write time, regardless of how they reached the audit recorder.

The audit log cannot be modified or deleted. It is the compliance and forensics record for the platform. It is designed to answer the question every audit or incident review requires: "Who did what, when, and from where?"

Audit emissions go through typed recorders under `apps/engine/src/audit/recorders/` — one helper per resource family (connector, workflow, credential, knowledge source, policy). Each recorder requires a non-null `reason` for state-changing rows. Reasons are part of the contract: `auto_persist_on_confirmation` distinguishes harness auto-persist writes from `manual_re_issue` (explicit `save_connector_draft` calls), `force_save_override` marks force-flag overrides of failed probes or previews, `credential_must_use_form` records rejected credential attempts at the draft layer, and `confirm_before_execution` records every tool-policy decision that paused for an operator confirmation.

New audit kinds for the conversational surface include `tool_policy.confirmation_required` (every confirmation gate the policy resolver fires), `connector.draft.credential_rejected` (rejections by the `update_connector_draft` contract), `connector.invoked` (each `call_connector` round-trip), `connector.saved_override` (a save persisted with `force_save: true` despite a failed probe), and `knowledge_source.refreshed` (each discovery cache refresh). The conversational context pipeline also emits `conversation.skill_loaded` — a tenant-scoped row written when a Skill is loaded into a conversation working set under the recency-gated `load_skill` path, with reason `skill_loaded` on first load and `skill_re_promoted` when an already-known Skill is re-promoted (see `apps/engine/src/audit/types.ts` `CONVERSATION_SKILL_LOADED` and `apps/engine/src/audit/recorders/conversation.ts`). It records a state-mutating write: `load_skill` updates the persisted `conversations.loaded_skills` palette — tenant-visible state that survives session resumption — so, like every other tenant-state mutation, it goes through the audit chokepoint. Per-turn recency demotions are derived and intentionally not audited.

Operators can query the audit log by actor, action type, resource, time range, and request source. The `sk audit tail` command provides a real-time stream for operational monitoring. The API exposes the same query surface programmatically.

**Asymmetric coverage on `data.exported` from `POST /v1/extract`.** Binary-format extracts (PDF / DOCX / XLSX / XLS / PPTX) emit an `action = "data.exported"` audit row for both success and parse-failure paths — these formats can carry whole tenant documents (CVs, contracts, financial spreadsheets), so the egress trail is explicit. Text-format extracts (JSON / CSV / YAML / XML / plaintext) deliberately skip the audit row because they are shape-only (the caller is sending data the engine already knows about for schema inference). Operators monitoring `data.exported` for *all* extract calls should be aware of this gradient. The 413 body-cap denial path is audited for every format. See [Observability & Resource Limits](../operators/observability.md#resource-limits-and-operational-safety) for the full operator-controlled metadata surface (`audit_log.metadata.filename`, `audit_log.metadata.error`).

---

## The Compliance Posture

The following properties hold by construction — they are not optional configurations.

**Encryption at rest.** All credentials are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before being written to the database. The encryption key is managed at the engine configuration layer.

**Encryption in transit.** All engine endpoints are served over TLS. The engine does not serve unencrypted HTTP in production configurations.

**API key storage.** Keys are stored as hashes. The comparison during authentication is always against the hash, never against a stored plaintext value. There is no way to recover a key after issuance.

**Webhook signatures.** All inbound webhooks are HMAC-SHA256 signature-verified before any payload is processed; the generic scheme is Standard Webhooks, with vendor adapters for Stripe and GitHub. Requests with missing or invalid signatures are rejected.

**Sandboxing.** Untrusted code — transforms, Before-Request Hooks, and self-healing patch scripts — runs in an isolated QuickJS-WASM sandbox with a strict CPU budget. Sandbox code cannot access the network, the file system, or the database. The sandbox is not a trust boundary that can be configured away; it is where all runtime code execution occurs.

**Egress governance.** Connector requests go through the engine. Clients never call external connector boundaries directly. All egress is logged in the audit log with request source, caller identity, and outcome.

**Request source tracking.** Every platform interaction — API call, MCP invocation, webhook delivery, chat message, CLI command, scheduled trigger — is tagged with its source. "Who initiated this?" is always answerable from the audit log.

---

## Secret Hygiene at the Conversational Surface

The conversational surface introduces additional pressure on secret handling: an LLM may attempt to type a credential into a tool argument, an operator may paste a token into the chat input, or a debug log may capture a verbose elicitation payload. sk applies multiple defences so any one of these doesn't propagate into a persistent surface.

The `update_connector_draft` tool rejects any credential-shaped field in `config` with a structured `credential_must_use_form` envelope. The agent is steered, by both the tool contract and the seed skill content, toward the masked-form path: `ask_user_form(type: password, sensitive: true)` collects the value, the harness auto-persists the connector and credential atomically, and the LLM never sees the secret in any tool argument or transcript.

The HTTP / GraphQL / S3 drivers no longer honour inline credentials from `connector.config`. Probing a draft without a saved credential row returns a structured `credential_required` envelope, which the conversational layer turns into the next ask-form turn. The previous shortcut that lifted `config.token` into the Authorization header has been removed — it made the wrong thing look like progress.

Engine logs, audit metadata, conversation event payloads, and the `~/.sk/debug.log` file pass through a centralized scrubber before write. The scrubber matches known token shapes — DigitalOcean, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Anthropic, Bearer-prefixed bearer tokens, JWTs, AWS access keys — and any value whose key name matches the sensitive-name pattern. Matches become `***REDACTED:<kind>***` at the file-write boundary.

The sk CLI composer detects token-shaped paste in the chat input. When matched, the input is replaced with a one-keystroke confirmation prompt; on confirmation the CLI sends a redirect message that asks the agent to re-prompt through the masked form, instead of forwarding the literal paste to the engine. The detector catches the same regex catalog as the engine scrubber.

Tool policies (`apps/engine/src/conversations/tools/tool-policies.ts`) decide execution mode dynamically per call. Inputs containing token-shaped values or sensitive key names force the policy resolver to `confirm_before_execution`, which inserts an `ask_user_confirm` gate before the tool runs. Every such pause writes a `tool_policy.confirmation_required` audit row with the tool name and the matched sensitive shape — operators can review every policy-gated decision in the audit trail.

The `authenticate_oauth` flow surfaces an authorization URL that the sk CLI auto-launches in the operator's browser. That URL is tenant-controlled input: it is derived from the connector's `oauth.issuer_url` config, which a tenant admin can write. The proportionate control is a scheme clamp — `BrowserUrlSchema` accepts only `http`/`https`, closing `file:`, `javascript:`, and `data:` URLs — so the worst a tenant admin can do is cause the CLI to open an arbitrary http(s) page for an operator who has paused on that connector. This is acceptable because connector-config writes are already an audited, RBAC-gated action: the admin who could set a hostile `issuer_url` is the same admin already trusted to configure the connector's real endpoints, and every such write lands in the audit trail.

---

## Further reading

- [RBAC & Roles](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md) — identity, authentication, RBAC/ABAC, and Before-Request Hooks.
- [Credentials & Keys](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md) — the credential vault, master-key rotation, and release signing.
- [glossary — governance terms](./glossary.md#group-5-governance) — Audit Log, RBAC, Before-Request Hook, Self-Healing, Patch Candidate.

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md -->

# Knowledge & Skills

> **Audience:** Architects and authors who want the model behind the AI's
> organization-specific context.

**Outcome:** authoring grounded in your own conventions — not generic API
docs — so workflows ship faster, with fewer rework cycles and fewer
compliance surprises. The AI proposes against your patterns because your
patterns are in its context.

Two primitives carry that context:

| Primitive | What it is | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Skills** | Dense, operator-authored guidance | Prescriptive rules the AI follows |
| **Knowledge Sources** | Broad organizational documents | Searchable grounding, not rules |

This page covers how the engine assembles them into each authoring turn, how
**Discovery** turns files into proposals, and how the loop compounds. Author
how-tos live in [Custom Skills](../authors/custom-skills.md) and
[Knowledge Sources](../authors/knowledge-sources.md).

---

## Skills: curated context

A Skill is reusable context loaded into the AI during a Conversation and other
AI-assisted flows — discovery, diagnosis, bounded repair. Skills encode your
best practices, integration patterns, security policies, and domain knowledge.
Reference your Stripe connector and the Stripe Skill loads automatically, so
proposals reflect your conventions, not generic API knowledge.

Operators own Skills. Scope each one:

- **Global** — every Conversation.
- **Per-connector** — loaded when that connector is referenced.
- **Per-workflow** — loaded for that workflow.

Skills are never auto-generated or auto-promoted. The engine detects recurring
patterns and surfaces them as Skill Candidates; a candidate becomes an active
Skill only by explicit operator promotion. The engine learns what works; humans
decide what becomes canonical.

---

## Knowledge Sources: enterprise documents

A Knowledge Source is a persistent document store for document-scale context —
runbooks, API specs, compliance frameworks, architecture diagrams. Operators
upload the files; the engine chunks and indexes them for semantic search.
During a Conversation, discovery pass, or repair loop, the AI searches them to
ground its proposals.

Skills prescribe; Knowledge Sources inform. The AI follows Skills as
instructions and searches Knowledge Sources for relevant context without
treating them as rules.

**Committed workflow execution queries neither.** Skills and Knowledge Sources
improve authoring and repair quality; once a workflow is committed, the runtime
path stays deterministic.

---

## Context assembly and trimming

Each authoring turn assembles prompt context in a fixed order. Order matters
twice: it shapes how the model reads context (top is most foundational) and how
the trimmer drops it under budget pressure (top survives longest, bottom goes
first).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph build["Assembly order (top = first written)"]
        direction TB
        B1["1. Base prompt + runtime envelope<br/>(engine · tenant · actor · surface)"]
        B2["2. Auto-loaded Skills<br/>(global → connector → workflow)"]
        B3["3. Explicitly loaded Skills"]
        B4["4. Knowledge Source chunks"]
        B5["5. User memory"]
        B6["6. Connector documentation chunks"]
        B7["7. Prior failures for the current task"]
        B8["8. Authoring-context blocks"]
        B9["9. Current turn history<br/>(user / assistant messages)"]
        B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4 --> B5 --> B6 --> B7 --> B8 --> B9
    end
    Trim{{"Trim order (top = dropped first)"}}
    T1["failures → connector docs → knowledge<br/>→ user memory → authoring context<br/>→ explicit Skills → workflow Skills<br/>→ connector Skills → global Skills"]
    Note["User turns are never trimmed"]
    build --> Trim --> T1
    T1 -. preserved .- Note
```

This order is contract, not implementation detail. Under tight budgets,
operator-curated connector and workflow guidance outlives incidental history —
so a tenant's own conventions are the *last* thing dropped, never the first.

Replay stays bounded: tool results are truncated before re-entering later
turns, compaction markers suppress older replay, and oversized histories
collapse into a deterministic summary plus the recent tail.

---

## Discovery: from files to proposals

Discovery cuts onboarding time for a new integration: instead of hand-configuring
every connector and Skill, it starts from documentation that already exists.

An operator uploads files — API specs, data dictionaries, architecture
diagrams, runbooks — and sk produces structured proposals. Each Discovery
Artifact is a proposed connector, Skill, or Knowledge Source, with a confidence
score and links to the supporting evidence.

Nothing is configured automatically. Proposals are starting points; the
operator approves what to keep.

---

## How the loop compounds

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Run["Run"] --> Drift["Drift detected"]
    Drift --> Patch["Patch Candidate<br/>(operator-reviewed)"]
    Run --> Pattern["Recurring pattern"]
    Pattern --> SkillC["Skill Candidate<br/>(operator-promoted)"]
    Patch --> Author["Better authoring"]
    SkillC --> Author
    Author --> Run
```

Skill Candidates surface production patterns: when connectors or step sequences
recur together and tend to succeed, the engine proposes a new Skill with
confidence scores and links to the supporting executions. Self-healing drift
detection keeps workflows healthy as connected systems change, proposing the
smallest safe fix as a Patch Candidate.

Same shape both times: the engine surfaces proposals, humans decide. The engine
gets smarter over time — but only with human approval at each step.

---

## Further reading

- [Custom Skills](../authors/custom-skills.md) — how to author, scope, and promote Skills.
- [Knowledge Sources](../authors/knowledge-sources.md) — how to upload, tag, and refresh documents.
- [Self-healing](../operators/self-healing.md) — the operational side of the repair loop.
- [glossary — authoring terms](./glossary.md#group-2-authoring) — Conversation, Draft, Skill, Skill Candidate, Knowledge Source, Discovery.

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/overview.md -->

# Architecture Overview

> **Audience:** Anyone forming a first mental model of sk — architects, operators, authors, contributors.

**Ship audited automation in hours, not sprints — and keep every run governed,
versioned, and auditable.** A team describes the outcome in plain language; sk turns it into a
governed, versioned workflow; an operator approves it; the engine runs it
deterministically against the connectors (the SaaS and apps your team already uses).

One contract holds throughout: **AI assists with *authoring*; *execution* is fixed
at approval time and never re-decided at runtime.** Multi-tenancy, RBAC, encrypted
credentials, and an immutable audit trail apply to every entry point.

---

## At a glance

![sk architecture at a glance — outside-the-bridge AI clients cross via the MCP OAuth bridge into the engine; other surfaces enter directly. Tenant Context (Skills · Knowledge · Discovery · Skill/Patch Candidates) is the compounding learning loop.](./overview.png)

*Outside-the-bridge clients (IDE assistants, employee chat) reach governed workflows only through the **MCP OAuth bridge**; other surfaces (Chat adapters, CLI, HTTP REST API, Inbound Webhooks, Scheduler) enter directly. The engine groups into six clusters; the green **Tenant Context** cluster is the compounding loop. Source: [`./overview.drawio`](./overview.drawio).*

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph surfaces["Inbound surfaces"]
        CLI["sk CLI"]
        REST["HTTP REST API"]
        MCP["MCP OAuth bridge<br/>(IDE assistants, employee chat)"]
        Chat["Chat adapters"]
        Hook["Inbound webhooks"]
        Sched["Scheduler"]
    end
    Gate{{"One governance gate<br/>RBAC → Before-Request Hook → audit"}}
    Engine["Engine<br/>(single binary)"]
    PG[("PostgreSQL<br/>queue · scheduler · pub/sub · state")]
    LLM[("LLM provider<br/>(authoring only)")]
    Ctx["Tenant Context<br/>Skills · Knowledge · Discovery<br/>Skill/Patch Candidates"]

    surfaces --> Gate --> Engine
    Engine --> PG
    Engine -. authoring .-> LLM
    Engine <--> Ctx
    Ctx -. improves authoring .-> LLM
```

Every entry point flows through the same governed pipeline. Execution is policy-
and version-bound, auditable, and operator-reviewed for drift-assisted repair.

---

## The governance loop

Authoring and execution are separate trust domains. The model proposes; a human
approves; the engine runs the frozen artefact. Each run can feed the next
authoring — but only through operator promotion, never silently.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Author["Author<br/>(NL → draft)"] --> Review["Review<br/>(human)"]
    Review --> Approve["Approve<br/>(version pinned)"]
    Approve --> Run["Deterministic run<br/>(no LLM)"]
    Run --> Audit["Immutable audit"]
    Audit --> Drift["Drift detection"]
    Drift --> Candidate["Patch / Skill Candidate"]
    Candidate -. operator promotes .-> Author

    Author -. uses .-> LLM[("LLM provider")]
    Candidate -. enriches .-> Ctx["Tenant Context"]
    Ctx -. grounds .-> Author
```

---

## The three things to internalise

1. **Authoring vs. execution are different trust domains.** The LLM proposes; a human approves; the engine runs the approved artefact deterministically. Committed execution never queries Skills, Knowledge, or the model. See [Authoring workflows](../authors/authoring-workflows.md) and [Workflows](./workflows.md).
2. **One dependency.** The engine compiles to a single binary; PostgreSQL is the only stateful dependency. The job queue, cron scheduler, and pub/sub bus all live in Postgres. See [Self-host](../developers/self-host.md).
3. **The compounding loop.** Run → Drift → Patch Candidate → Skill Candidate → better authoring → better run. Every run can improve the tenant's authoring context — but only through operator promotion. See [Knowledge & Skills](./knowledge-and-skills.md) and [Self-healing](../operators/self-healing.md).

---

## Where to go next

- [Glossary](./glossary.md) — every domain term defined exactly once.
- [Connectors & integration](./connectors.md) — Drivers, Templates, Credentials, the vault, OAuth2.
- [Workflows](./workflows.md) — the execution model, step kinds, triggers, versioning, self-healing.
- [Knowledge & Skills](./knowledge-and-skills.md) — how the authoring context compounds.
- [Governance & Audit](./governance-and-audit.md) — multi-tenancy, RBAC, audit, secret hygiene.
- [`AGENTS.md`](../../AGENTS.md) — the canonical repo-wide contributor contract.

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/workflows.md -->

# Workflow Execution

> **Audience:** Engineers integrating the runtime, operators monitoring executions

**Approved workflows run the same way every time — deterministic, immutable, fully audited.** That is what lets an enterprise put revenue operations, compliance reporting, and back-office work on autopilot: every run is permission-checked, recorded, versioned, and replayable. There is no AI in the execution path. AI authors; the engine runs.

This page covers the workflow lifecycle, the execution model, the eight Step kinds, triggers, versioning and rollback, scheduling, self-healing, and the observability surface operators rely on.

---

## Workflow Lifecycle

A workflow moves through three states. Chat authors a **draft**; approval commits it to **active**; retiring or superseding it moves it to **archived**. Promoting a prior version back to active is the rollback path — no redeploy, instant, audited.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> draft: authored in chat
    draft --> draft: refine / re-preview
    draft --> active: approved + committed
    active --> active: new version (immutable snapshot)
    active --> archived: retired / superseded
    archived --> active: promote a prior version (rollback)
    archived --> [*]
```

*Draft → active → archived. Every transition lands in the Audit Log with the actor, the version, and the timestamp.*

---

## The Execution Model

Execution in sk is deterministic. A Workflow is a DAG of Steps; the execution engine walks that DAG in order, following branching and parallel directives exactly as defined. The engine does not re-interpret, adapt, or infer at runtime. There is no AI in the execution path.

There is a single runtime entry point for manual execution: `POST /v1/executions`. Persisted workflows, inline draft definitions, and single-step previews all flow through this same route and the same execution engine. Inline runs complete synchronously by default. Queued background execution is explicit and reserved for persisted workflows, scheduler fires, webhook fan-out, and other detached cases.

All execution surfaces normalize workflow input through the same boundary before dispatch. Conversation `run_workflow`, MCP callable entries, REST workflow-run routes, webhook-bound executions, queue resumes, and scheduler-triggered runs all end up at the same execution contract with the same effective input payload. Surface adapters may differ in how they collect input, but they do not get to define different runtime semantics.

Provider failures on the authoring side do not leak through as generic internal errors anymore. Usage-limit and rate-limit failures are surfaced as typed provider-limited responses, context-window failures are surfaced as context-too-large responses, and temporary provider outages are surfaced as typed provider-unavailable responses. The execution engine remains deterministic; these envelopes only describe authoring-time model failures.

This is a deliberate architectural decision, not a limitation. AI is for authoring — exploring, proposing, and revising. Once a Workflow is approved and committed, the enterprise needs to know it will run the same way every time. Reproducibility and auditability require determinism. The moment execution involves inference, the audit trail becomes "the AI decided" rather than "the workflow ran as specified."

An Execution is an immutable record. It captures the specific Workflow version that ran, who or what triggered it, the inputs and outputs of every Step, timing at every boundary, and the final status. It cannot be modified after it completes. If something goes wrong, the complete record of what happened is preserved exactly as it occurred.

---

## Step Kinds

A Workflow is composed of Steps. sk ships eight Step kinds, grouped by what they do. The discriminator field is `kind`; the schema source of truth is [`apps/engine/src/workflows/types.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/workflows/types.ts) (`StepSchema`). There is no `tool` kind (no docker-based sandbox runner) — this is a data-workflow engine, not a container runtime.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S(["Step (kind)"])
    S --> IO["Data"]
    S --> Logic["Control flow"]
    S --> Time["Time & signals"]

    IO --> request["request<br/>call a connector endpoint"]
    IO --> transform["transform<br/>reshape data (sandboxed JS)"]
    IO --> call["call<br/>invoke another workflow"]

    Logic --> branch["branch<br/>deterministic conditional"]
    Logic --> parallel["parallel<br/>concurrent branches"]
    Logic --> loop["loop<br/>iterate a collection"]

    Time --> wait["wait<br/>fixed delay"]
    Time --> wait_for_event["wait_for_event<br/>HITL signal pause"]
```

| `kind` | Required fields | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `request` | one of `url` / `connector_id` / `sql`; optional `method`, `headers`, `query`, `body`, `pagination`, `graphql`, `sql`, `s3`, `xml`, `expected_statuses`, `expected_row_count`, `idempotency_key`, `outputs`, `side_effects` | Calls a connector endpoint. Routed through the connector's driver (HTTP, GraphQL, Postgres, S3) with the tenant's credentials and the governance layer. Connector tests and request steps share the same request execution core, so authoring-time probes and runtime behaviour stay aligned. |
| `transform` | `expression` (for `javascript`); optional `language` (`javascript` — the default and only expression language — or one of the web-scraper extractors `readability` / `html-to-markdown` / `structured-data`), `input_schema`, `output_schema`, `silence_warnings` | Reshapes data between steps. The expression is a sandboxed JavaScript function body with an explicit `return`: upstream step outputs are at `input.scope.<id>.data`, the workflow input at `input.input`, and (inside a loop body) the current item at `input.scope.$item`. JSONata is not a transform language — it survives only in the one-line slots (`loop.over`, `branch.when`, `output_transform`, `data_selector`, `${scope.x.data}` interpolation). The web-scraper extractors carry no `expression` and read the upstream HTML body. No network access, bounded heap and wall-clock per `SANDBOX_MEMORY_LIMIT_BYTES` / `TRANSFORM_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_MS` (overridable via `sandbox.transform_wall_ms`). |
| `branch` | `when`, `then_steps[]`; optional `else_steps[]` | Deterministic conditional routing. The engine evaluates `when` against scope and dispatches the matching branch — no inference, no fallthrough. |
| `loop` | `body[]`; exactly one of `over` or `data_selector` | Iterates a collection, executing `body` per item. Inside the body the current item is `$item` (JSONata expressions) / `${item.…}` (request placeholder strings), plus the zero-based `$loop_index`. `item_var` is retired: authoring it is rejected (`validateWorkflowDef`); historical stored versions that declared it keep executing unchanged. `data_selector` is the JS expression form (preferred for new loops, surfaces real exceptions); `over` is the legacy path/JSONata form. |
| `parallel` | `branches[][]` | Executes multiple step sequences concurrently and merges their results. The engine fans out, awaits all branches, then continues. |
| `wait` | `duration_ms` (≤ 24 h) | Deliberate delay for polling, rate-limit management, or human-paced flows. |
| `wait_for_event` | `event_name`, `timeout_ms`; optional `match`, `on_timeout` | Signal-driven HITL pause. The runner inserts a `workflow_waits` checkpoint, polls `workflow_signals` at 1 s cadence, and resumes when a matching signal arrives or `timeout_ms` elapses. The runner does NOT implicitly skip downstream steps on timeout — the workflow author MUST follow the wait with an explicit `branch` step that gates the success vs timeout path on `$.steps.<wait_id>.timed_out`. |
| `call` | one of `workflow_id` or `workflow_slug`; optional `input` | Invokes another workflow. Recursion is capped by `MAX_CALL_DEPTH` (5). |

Every step also accepts the shared base fields `id`, `on_error` (`fail` \| `continue`), `data_selector`, and `timeout_ms`.

### Read/write classification and hold-writes previews

Request steps carry an optional `side_effects: "read" | "write"` field. When unset, the driver classifies at dispatch time: HTTP `GET`/`HEAD`/`OPTIONS` = read, other methods = write; GraphQL `query` = read, `mutation`/`subscription` = write; SQL SELECT-only = read, anything else = write; S3 GET/HEAD/LIST = read. Set `"read"` explicitly for a POST that is semantically a search, or `"write"` to force-hold a GET that mutates server state.

The classification drives dry-run previews: a `dry_run_workflow` preview HOLDS WRITES by default. Read steps execute live against the real upstream; write steps (sends, posts, publishes) are fully resolved — URL, headers, the materialized body — but never dispatched; the held request is recorded as the step artifact. The instruction-grounded preview judge reads the held payloads, and a green preview with a passing judge verdict auto-commits the draft. Executing writes for real during a preview requires explicit user confirmation (`execute_writes: true`).

### Wait-for-event timeout pattern

The `wait_for_event` step's `timeout_ms` bounds the per-step wait window. The surrounding `WorkflowDef.timeout_ms` (the workflow envelope) must be ≥ the wait step's bound — the `WorkflowDefSchema` `superRefine` enforces this at save time so a 24 h approval window can't be silently truncated by a 6 h workflow timeout. In practice the envelope should leave headroom for the post-wait merge / abandon transitions; e.g. a 24 h wait inside a 25 h workflow.

Because the runner does not auto-skip downstream steps on timeout, every wait-for-event workflow needs an explicit `branch` step that gates the success vs timeout path. The canonical example is the **`merge-pr-after-approval`** recipe under the GitHub template (`apps/engine/src/connectors/templates.json`): it opens a PR, waits up to 24 h for an external `pr_approved` signal, and routes through a branch step (`when: $boolean($.steps.await_approval.timed_out)`) into either a `merge` request or an `abandon_on_timeout` transform. Cancel-race semantics for human-paused workflows are documented in [`apps/engine/src/conversations/abort.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/conversations/abort.ts) (single-replica caveat, tenant-scoped registry, expected reasons).

---

## Triggers

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Req["request trigger<br/>(default; on-demand)"]
    Hook["webhook trigger<br/>(reverse-bound to<br/>webhooks_inbound row)"]
    Sched["schedule trigger<br/>(cron + tz, reverse-bound<br/>to workflows_schedules row)"]
    Core{{"runExecution()<br/>same contract,<br/>same RBAC, same audit"}}
    Exec[/Execution record/]

    Req --> Core
    Hook --> Core
    Sched --> Core
    Core --> Exec
```

*Three trigger kinds, one execution core. The trigger lands in the immutable Execution and Audit Log alongside the actor identity envelope, so an operator can answer "who/what triggered this and from where" without joining tables.*

`WorkflowDef.trigger` is a discriminated union over `kind`. Omitting the block is equivalent to `{ kind: "request" }`, so every workflow authored before this field existed keeps its behaviour. Setting `webhook` or `schedule` reverse-binds an inbound binding or cron schedule keyed on `(tenant_id, workflow_id)` at save time and removes the binding on delete or version rotate. The schema source of truth is [`apps/engine/src/workflows/types.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/workflows/types.ts) (`RequestTriggerSchema`, `WebhookTriggerSchema`, `ScheduleTriggerSchema`).

The trigger is recorded in every Execution and every Audit Log entry alongside the actor identity envelope.

| `kind` | Fields | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `request` | (none) | Default. Run is initiated on demand by a caller — chat `run_workflow`, MCP, the CLI, or `POST /v1/executions`. Inline runs complete on the request path; `async: true` is honoured only for `source=saved`. |
| `webhook` | `source` (string slug per integration), `events[]` (provider event names; empty means "any"), `verify` (`stripe-signature` \| `github-hmac` \| `none`) | Reverse-bound to a `webhooks_inbound` row. Inbound posts are signature-verified before any processing begins; replay-id deduplication suppresses retried deliveries. Executor lives in `apps/engine/src/webhooks/inbound/service.ts`. |
| `schedule` | `cron` (5-field `m h dom mon dow` or `every:N` shorthand), `tz` (IANA, default `UTC`); optional `business_days_only`, `skip_dates[]` (ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`) | Reverse-bound to a `workflows_schedules` row. The scheduler reconciler validates the cron expression at bind time and uses `tz` so firings land at the operator's local wall-clock time. `business_days_only` skips weekends; `skip_dates` declares holidays / freezes explicitly (no holiday calendar is inferred). Catch-up semantics: a missed firing fires on the next reconciler pass rather than being silently skipped. Executor lives in `apps/engine/src/scheduler/reconciler.ts`. |

All three variants land at the same `runExecution()` core through the same execution contract; only the way the run is initiated differs.

---

## Versioning

Every change to a Workflow creates a new version. A version is a complete snapshot of the workflow's DAG — not a diff, not a patch, but the full definition as it stood at the moment of change. Versions are immutable once created.

At any given time, exactly one version is designated "active." The active version is what runs when the workflow is triggered. Operators can inspect any prior version and promote it to active in a single action.

This is the rollback story for sk. When a change introduces failures, the response is to promote the previous known-good version to active. No code changes are required, no deployment is needed, and the rollback is immediate. The audit log records the promotion decision — who made it, when, and from which version.

---

## Scheduling and Event Architecture

The scheduler uses a durable job queue so that scheduled runs survive engine restarts. A schedule is a commitment: if the engine was unavailable when a run was due, it will fire when availability is restored. The same queue also backs explicitly asynchronous workflow runs, while synchronous API-initiated runs stay inline on the request path.

Execution state changes — a run starting, a step completing, a run finishing — are published as events through a pub/sub system. Subscribers receive these events in real time: the sk CLI can tail a live execution, chat adapters can show progress in a thread, SSE consumers drive external observers, and outbound webhook Subscriptions can notify external connector boundaries.

The platform uses an outbox pattern to ensure that events are never silently lost. Events are written to the database as part of the same transaction as the state change that produced them. Delivery is attempted after the transaction commits, and any undelivered event is retried. The outbox provides a durable event log that survives restarts and partial failures.

Pub/sub channels are **global, not per-tenant**. The `connector.oauth` channel — over which an out-of-band OAuth callback announces `callback_succeeded` / `callback_failed` — carries events for every tenant. A consumer that subscribes to it (e.g. `waitForOAuthCredential` in [`apps/engine/src/credentials/oauth2/wait.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/credentials/oauth2/wait.ts)) is therefore responsible for tenant isolation itself: it MUST drop any event whose `tenant_id` does not match the wait's own `tenant_id` in-handler, before acting on it. There is no channel-level scoping to fall back on.

---

## Self-Healing

Connected boundaries change. The APIs a workflow depends on today may behave differently in six months. Schema fields are renamed, endpoints are moved, error codes change, pagination patterns evolve. Workflows that are not maintained will eventually fail.

sk's self-healing subsystem is designed to catch these failures early and propose repairs before they cause sustained disruption.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Run["Workflow run"]
    Drift["Schema drift detected<br/>(passive — from real responses)"]
    Repair["Repair loop<br/>(LLM proposes patch)"]
    Classify["Classify safe / unsafe"]
    DryRun["Dry-run against<br/>Execution Fixtures"]
    Patch["Patch Candidate<br/>(operator-reviewed)"]
    Approve["Operator approves"]
    NewVer["New workflow version live"]
    Skill["Skill Candidate<br/>(emerges from recurring patterns)"]

    Run --> Drift --> Repair --> Classify --> DryRun --> Patch --> Approve --> NewVer
    Patch -. recurring pattern .-> Skill
    NewVer -. next run .-> Run
```

*No autonomous repair in production. The loop runs through a human gate. The compounding effect — each run improving the next — comes from operator-reviewed drift repair feeding back into authoring.*

The engine monitors active Connectors for schema drift. Drift is detected from execution results — when a Step receives a response that does not match the recorded schema for that endpoint, the engine classifies it as drift and initiates the repair process. Detection is passive: no polling, no scheduled checks, just observation of what actually runs.

When drift is detected, the self-healing loop analyzes the failure, consults the Connector's latest documentation, and proposes the smallest change that would make the Step work again. The proposal is validated by dry-running it against recorded Execution Fixtures — samples of past successful inputs and outputs. This validation step distinguishes a plausible repair from one that would introduce new failures.

The result is a Patch Candidate: a proposed change with a classification of safe or unsafe based on the nature of the repair. Safe Patch Candidates can be applied by an operator with a single approval action. Unsafe ones require manual review of the proposed change.

No Patch Candidate is ever applied automatically. Self-healing is a proposal system, not an autonomous repair system. The platform surfaces the problem and its proposed solution; the human decides whether to apply it.

---

## Synchronous and Queued Execution

`POST /v1/executions` is synchronous by default. The caller receives the full `RunResult` — output, step summaries, connector resolutions, warnings — in the HTTP response body. Draft runs and single-step previews always execute inline regardless of the `async` flag, because they have no persisted workflow context for a queue worker to rehydrate.

Warnings are a first-class runtime state, not a hidden side channel. A run can report
`status: "succeeded"` while still carrying structured `warnings[]`; CLI and MCP clients are
expected to surface that distinction so operators can diagnose partial or suspicious results.

The authoring surfaces are expected to catch the obvious cases before runtime. In particular,
the static verifier rejects the common scope-envelope mistake of writing `$scope.step.field`
instead of `$scope.step.data.field`. Runtime warnings still matter for dynamic cases, but the
baseline contract is to fail fast on structural scope misuse.

Queued (`async: true`) execution is available **only** for `source=saved` runs. In that case the engine inserts the execution row synchronously, enqueues the job on `pg-boss`, and returns `202 Accepted` with `{ execution_id, status: "queued" }`. A worker picks the job up and runs it through the same `runExecution()` core. Scheduler fires, webhook fan-out, and any other detached trigger also land on the queue — but every inline caller gets the run on the request path.

### Following a run live

`GET /v1/executions/:id/stream` is an SSE tail over the execution's outbox events, gated by the resource-scoped `execution:read` permission (following your own run does not require the tenant-wide `audit:read` that `GET /v1/events/stream` carries). The stream replays the run's full event history — `execution.queued` → `execution.started` → per-step `execution.step.started` / `execution.step.finished` frames (with `step_key`, `step_index`, `kind`, `status`, `duration_ms`, and `error_code` on failure) → the terminal `execution.<status>` frame — then tails live and closes right after the terminal frame. `Last-Event-ID` resumes after a dropped connection. `sk workflows run <id> --follow` and `sk executions tail <id>` consume this stream.

Step frames are written transactionally with the `execution_steps` rows, so a follower never observes a step that isn't persisted.

---

## Per-step Request Meta

Every Step in the `RunResult` carries a `request_meta` object with driver-specific fields. For HTTP and GraphQL Request Steps:

- `url` — the final URL actually hit (after path composition and static query merge).
- `method` / `operation` / `operation_name` — HTTP verb or GraphQL operation kind and name.
- `status` — HTTP status code (or HTTP status of the GraphQL endpoint).
- `bytes_in` — response body size in bytes.
- `retry_count` — retries consumed before success or failure (also surfaced at top level).
- `connector` — a sub-object with `connector_id`, `connector_slug`, `driver`, `requested_environment`, `resolved_environment`, `auth_method`, and `base_url`.

`auth_method` is observable at request time, not configured: it distinguishes `oauth2_static` (cached token still fresh) from `oauth2_refreshed` (a stale token was rotated inline before the request went out). Debugging a mysteriously failing credential becomes a lookup in the run result rather than a server-side hunt.

The `RunResult` also rolls the per-step connector info up into `connector_resolutions[]` — one entry per unique connector touched during the run. Operators see at a glance which workflow step landed on which connector, against which environment, with which auth method.

---

## Determinism, Timeouts and Limits

Numeric budgets — step timeouts, recursion limits, payload thresholds,
LLM tool-result truncation, repair attempts — live in
[`apps/engine/src/execution/timeouts.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/execution/timeouts.ts)
so operators have one place to look and reviewers have one place to
gate. The current values:

| Constant | Default | What bites first |
|---|---|---|
| `WORKFLOW_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_MS` | 6 h | Workflow status flips to `timed_out`; in-flight steps abort. |
| `STEP_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_MS` | 1 h | Per-step safety net when the step does not declare its own. |
| `TRANSFORM_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_MS` | 60 s | QuickJS wall-clock and abort signal. |
| `MAX_CALL_DEPTH` | 5 | `call` step refuses to recurse further. |
| `MAX_CALL_RETRIES` | 5 | Transient `request` retries. pg-boss handles backoff. |
| `MAX_PAGINATION_REQUESTS` | 1 000 | Safeguard against missing termination conditions. |
| `MAX_REPAIR_ATTEMPTS` | 2 | Self-healing LLM revision budget per drift signal. |
| `STEP_RESULT_DB_BYTES` | 10 KB | Payload spillover threshold (see below). |
| `STEP_RESULT_PREVIEW_BYTES` | 512 | Inline operator-facing preview when spilled. |
| `LLM_TOOL_RESULT_SUCCESS_BYTES` | 80 KB | Tool-result truncation budget for successful results. |
| `LLM_TOOL_RESULT_ERROR_BYTES` | 50 KB | Same for error results. |
| `SANDBOX_MEMORY_LIMIT_BYTES` | 128 MB | QuickJS heap cap. |
| `SANDBOX_WALL_MS_DEFAULT` | 30 s | Default sandbox wall-clock. |

These constants are not env-overridable except where explicitly noted.
The intent is that an operator should be able to read this table once
and know what the engine will and will not do.

### Result Persistence

Step results are written inline when serialized payload size is
≤ `STEP_RESULT_DB_BYTES`. Larger payloads are spilled to either S3
(when `S3_OFFLOAD_BUCKET` and credentials are set) or the
`execution_fixtures` table, and the original row records a
`storage_uri` of the form `s3://...` or `fixture://<uuid>`. A 512-byte
text preview always lands inline so an operator can see at a glance
what the payload looked like without resolving it.

The `GET /v1/executions/:id` route hydrates from the storage URI when
present; consumers never read the URI directly.

Inside a run, a loop that spills large body payloads keeps its
`iterationResults` array bounded by substituting an `OffloadRef` — a
small in-memory placeholder pointing at the already-spilled
`storage_uri` — in place of each full payload. This is the loop-memory
(OOM) guard: N iterations cost N references, not N resident envelopes.
An `OffloadRef` is an execution-internal, in-memory-only type. It MUST
be fully resolved back to plain JSON before the value crosses any
external surface — the persisted execution result, the REST response,
the MCP `wf_*` tools, or `get_raw_result`. Readers never see the
discriminant; a persisted result that still contains one is a contract
violation. Preview surfaces (loop/parallel step summaries) are exempt
from re-hydration but still carry no discriminant: each `OffloadRef`
collapses to a plain scalar string marker, never a structured object.

### Self-Healing Mode

`RunOptions.self_healing.enabled` lets a caller opt out of the
post-execution drift-detection hook. Default behaviour preserves the
existing path (the tenant policy decides whether to record the
outcome). The eval runner uses the toggle to compare a fixture's
`one_shot` outcome against its `self_healing` outcome — a regression
in either is a gate failure.

## Observability

The execution layer is designed to be fully transparent to operators.

Each Execution emits structured events at every Step boundary. Operators can tail execution logs in real time from the CLI or via SSE streams. Log entries are structured — machine-readable and queryable — not free-form text. Every record carries the same identity envelope (`tenant_id`, `trace_id`, `request_source`, `actor_id`) so an operator can correlate a slow request, an audit row, and a failing step by a single id — see [`apps/engine/src/observability/service-metadata.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/observability/service-metadata.ts).

Prometheus metrics cover the dimensions operators need to monitor platform health: execution duration, Step latency, error rates, retry counts, and queue depth, all scoped per tenant. These metrics are the basis for dashboards, alerts, and capacity planning. Connection pools export their own counters (`pg_pool_*`) so operators can spot saturation before it shows up as step failures. The LLM context-assembly path additionally emits `llm_context_assembled_total{flow,request_source}`, `llm_context_dropped_sections_total{flow,section}`, and a histogram `llm_context_total_tokens` so trimmer pressure surfaces alongside model cost.

The Audit Log records every execution trigger, every Step completion, every error, and every approval decision — with full context for forensic investigation. The audit trail is immutable: it cannot be modified or deleted, and it persists independently of execution records.

---

## Further reading

- [Security & governance](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md) — RBAC, API keys, Before-Request Hooks, Audit Log guarantees, and the policy model that governs every surface in sk.
- [glossary — execution terms](./glossary.md#group-4-execution) — Workflow, Step, Execution, Execution Fixture, Schedule.

# Operators

Run and govern the sk engine day-to-day — register connectors, wire schedules and webhooks, route notifications, watch the run, and apply repairs when an upstream API drifts.

![sk](../_tapes/out/operator-onboard.gif)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[quickstart] --> C[connectors-and-credentials]
    C --> S[scheduling-and-hooks]
    S --> N[notifications]
    S --> O[observability]
    O --> H[self-healing]
    N --> O
```

Start at the quickstart, attach a credential, then put workflows on a schedule or behind a webhook. Notifications and observability tell you when and how a run finished; self-healing turns an upstream break into a ready-to-apply repair.

| Page | What it covers | Link |
|---|---|---|
| Quickstart — Operator | Engine up, admin key minted, first connector registered — three steps to a running engine. | [quickstart.md](quickstart.md) |
| Connectors & Credentials | Register a connector once, attach a credential, and let every workflow reuse it. | [connectors-and-credentials.md](connectors-and-credentials.md) |
| Scheduling & Hooks | Wire scheduled runs that survive restarts and inbound webhooks that trigger workflows. | [scheduling-and-hooks.md](scheduling-and-hooks.md) |
| Notifications | Route run outcomes — succeeded, failed, aborted — to the right people, with per-rule failures logged. | [notifications.md](notifications.md) |
| Observability & Resource Limits | Diagnose a run in minutes with metrics, logs, and traces, bounded so no single workflow runs away. | [observability.md](observability.md) |
| Self-Healing in Operations | Detect upstream API breaks during real execution and apply a validated repair instead of a 3am page. | [self-healing.md](self-healing.md) |
| Runtime Dependencies | The one host dependency outside the single binary — Chromium + playwright for SPA-docs discovery — and how it is provisioned. | [runtime-dependencies.md](runtime-dependencies.md) |

<!-- Source: docs/operators/connectors-and-credentials.md -->

# Connectors & Credentials (operator guide)

**Connect a system once, reuse it everywhere — and the credential is never exposed.**
Operators attach a credential to a connector a single time; every workflow then
references that connector by name. Secrets stay encrypted in the vault, out of
logs, out of LLM context, and out of every response body.

> **Audience:** Operators registering connectors, managing credentials, and
> keeping integrations healthy in production.

This is the operational slice of the connector subsystem: attach and rotate
credentials, test connectivity on demand, invoke an endpoint ad-hoc, and run the
vendor-drift sweep. For the full conceptual model — drivers, templates, the
catalog, schema-version drift — see
[Connectors & Integration](../concepts/connectors.md).

## The onboarding path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Pick template] --> B[Supply credential]
    B --> V[(Credential Vault<br/>encrypted at rest)]
    B --> C[Probe]
    C -->|ok + latency| D[Reference in a workflow]
    C -->|credential_required| B
    V -.referenced by name.-> D
```

| Step | What you do | What the engine does |
|---|---|---|
| Pick template | Match a vendor or URL to a connector template | Pre-fills driver, auth pattern, endpoints |
| Supply credential | `credentials set` once | Encrypts to vault, returns a reference, never the value |
| Probe | `connectors test` | Authenticates, reports status + latency |
| Reference | Name the connector in a workflow step | Applies the saved credential at run time |

![Operator connector onboarding](../_tapes/out/operator-onboard.gif)

---

## Authentication and credential management

sk supports the authentication patterns enterprise systems actually use.

| Pattern | Notes |
|---|---|
| API key | `bearer`, `header`, or `query` placement |
| OAuth2 | Authorisation-code and client-credentials flows |
| Basic auth | Username / password |
| AWS SigV4 | Signed requests |
| Custom header | Arbitrary scheme |

**OAuth2 is fully managed.** Configure the connector once; the engine handles
token refresh, expiry detection, and rotation automatically. No workflow ever
manages token lifecycle.

**Secrets live only in the Credential Vault** — encrypted at rest, never logged,
never exposed outside the engine. Workflows and steps reference credentials by
name, not by value. The full vault model and master-key rotation procedure are in
[Credentials & Keys](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md).

**End-User Credentials** extend this for multi-user scenarios: an individual user
supplies their own credentials, and the platform acts as that user when executing
on their behalf — proper delegation, not credential sharing.

Attach a credential from the CLI:

```bash
sk connectors credentials set <CONNECTOR_ID> --mode bearer --token sk_live_…
#   modes: bearer | header | query | basic | aws_sigv4 | none
sk connectors credentials list <CONNECTOR_ID>
```

## Health and validation

Every connector can be tested independently of any workflow. The engine validates
the connection, authenticates with the configured credentials, and reports the
result plus connection latency. Connector tests and workflow request steps share
the same request-execution path, so a passing test reflects the exact transport a
workflow will use.

```bash
sk connectors test <CONNECTOR_ID>   # re-probe connectivity
```

A draft connector with no saved credential cannot be probed: the probe path
returns a structured `credential_required` envelope rather than silently sending
an unauthenticated request.

## Ad-hoc invocation

Once a connector is persisted, invoke any endpoint against it — for sampling,
pagination validation, or response-shape inspection — without authoring a
workflow. The conversational `call_connector` tool and the matching
`POST /v1/connectors/{id}/call` route apply the saved credential, emit a
`connector.invoked` audit row, and return status, headers, body, latency, and a
truncation flag.

```bash
curl -X POST "$SK_BASE_URL/v1/connectors/$CONNECTOR_ID/call" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "method": "GET", "path": "/v2/droplets", "query": { "per_page": 10 } }'
```

| Driver | `call_connector` |
|---|---|
| HTTP | Supported |
| GraphQL | Supported |
| Postgres / S3 | Returns `driver_not_supported_for_call_connector`, points to workflow authoring |

## Keeping a fleet healthy

Drift is detected from actual execution results, not periodic polling — a
connector that worked last month surfaces drift the moment a real run hits a
changed response shape. That drift feeds the operator-reviewed repair loop in
[Self-healing](./self-healing.md).

To proactively re-verify templates against live vendor APIs, run the vendor-drift
sweep documented in
[Connectors & Integration → Vendor-drift Sweep](../concepts/connectors.md#vendor-drift-sweep).

---

## Further reading

- [Connectors & Integration](../concepts/connectors.md) — the full conceptual model and route surface.
- [Credentials & Keys](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md) — the credential vault and rotation.
- [Self-healing](./self-healing.md) — how connector drift becomes an operator-reviewed Patch Candidate.
