# Notifications

**Operators hear about what matters, not noise.** When a workflow run
ends — succeeded, failed, or aborted — the right people learn about it
in the channel they already watch, with rate limits and circuit
breakers keeping a flapping target from drowning out the signal. Less
log-spelunking, faster incident response, a full audit trail of who
was told what.

sk turns engine outbox events into delivered messages, governed by
tenant-scoped rules, with rate limits, circuit breakers, audit, and
RBAC.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    run([Workflow run ends]) --> ev[events row<br/>execution.status]
    ev --> fan[Outbox fanout]
    fan --> rule{Notification rule<br/>match?}
    rule -->|no| drop([No delivery])
    rule -->|yes| brk{Circuit breaker}
    brk -->|open| skip([record breaker_open])
    brk -->|closed / half-open| rl{Rate limiter}
    rl -->|empty bucket| limited([record rate_limited])
    rl -->|token| ch[Channel adapter]
    ch --> slack[Slack]
    ch --> teams[Teams]
    ch --> gchat[Google Chat]
    ch --> hook[Webhook]
    ch --> rec[(notification_deliveries<br/>+ audit row)]
```

## Surface at a glance

| Concept | Where it lives | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Notification rule | `notification_rules` row | Selects which events go where, with severity + filter |
| Notification channel | `notification_channels` row | Concrete delivery target — Slack workspace+channel, Teams team+channel, Google Chat space, or webhook URL |
| Notification delivery | `notification_deliveries` row | Per-attempt result: `sent`, `rate_limited`, `breaker_open`, `failed`, `skipped` |
| Adapter | `chat/{slack,teams,google_chat}/adapter.ts` + `notifications/channels/webhook.ts` | Talks to the platform |
| Dispatcher | `apps/engine/src/notifications/service.ts` | Matches rules → applies rate limit + breaker → invokes adapter → records audit + delivery row |
| Outbox fanout | `apps/engine/src/webhooks/outbound/fanout.ts` | Drains `events` table → calls `dispatchEvent()` |

## End-to-end flow

| Step | Component | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `execution/state.ts` | Workflow finishes → writes an `events` row, channel `execution.status`, type `execution.<status>` (`succeeded`, `failed`, `aborted`, `timed_out`, …). |
| 2 | `webhooks/outbound/fanout.ts` | Outbox listener forwards the row → fanout looks up active subscriptions (outbound webhooks) AND active notification rules (chat / webhook notifications). |
| 3 | `notifications/service.ts#dispatchEvent` | Per matching rule, runs the dispatch pipeline below. |

For each matching rule, `dispatchEvent`:

1. resolves (or auto-creates) the `notification_channels` row,
2. checks the circuit breaker (`closed` → continue, `open` → record
   `breaker_open` and skip, `half-open` → trial-fire),
3. acquires a token from the leaky-bucket rate limiter (records
   `rate_limited` when the bucket is empty),
4. resolves an adapter via the registry,
5. invokes `adapter.send()` with a structured `ChatDelivery`,
6. records a `notification_deliveries` row + an audit row,
7. updates the breaker state from the outcome (`closed → open` after
   `FAILURE_THRESHOLD` consecutive failures; `half-open → closed` on
   first success).

> The dispatcher always resolves. Per-rule failures are logged and
> recorded, never thrown — a misconfigured rule cannot block other
> deliveries.

## Channels

### Chat (Slack, Teams, Google Chat)

The chat adapters under `apps/engine/src/chat/` ship as full peers —
they verify inbound webhooks, normalize platform events, and post
outbound messages. The notification subsystem reuses the same `send()`
surface to deliver completion signals to the operator's chat
workspace.

### Webhook (`notifications/channels/webhook.ts`)

For tenants that prefer a generic HTTP endpoint over a chat platform.

| Behaviour | Detail |
|---|---|
| Payload | POSTs JSON `{ tenant_id, workspace_id, channel_id, kind, text }` |
| Headers | `content-type: application/json`, `x-subkit-notification: 1`, `x-subkit-attempt: <n>`, optional `x-subkit-secret` shared secret |
| Retry | At most `WEBHOOK_MAX_ATTEMPTS` tries (default 3), exponential backoff capped at `WEBHOOK_BACKOFF_CAP_MS` (30 s) |
| Backpressure | Honours `Retry-After` on `429` / `503` responses |
| Terminal errors | Non-`429` `4xx` treated as terminal — retrying a mis-configured receiver wastes budget |

## Rules

A `notification_rules` row carries:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `event_pattern` | Glob matched against the event type (`execution.*`, `execution.failed`, `*`). |
| `workflow_pattern` | Glob matched against `workflow_id` or `workflow_slug` so a rule can scope to a specific workflow family. |
| `severity` | Drives both the platform-side rendering and the per-rule rate limit. |
| `request_source_filter` | Array of sources the rule should fire for. Default: the dispatcher skips `chat`-sourced runs (the conversation already saw the result) and `mcp` runs (the caller is an LLM, not a human). |
| `target_workspace_id` + `target_channel_id` | Point at the channel row to deliver through. |
| `active` | Soft-disable without deleting. |

## Rate limiting

Per-channel leaky bucket in
`apps/engine/src/notifications/rate-limit.ts`. Tokens regenerate at
`rate_limit_per_minute / 60 000` ms. When the bucket is empty the
dispatcher records `rate_limited` with the resume time and skips
delivery — the rule's downstream consumer is not stalled by the
limiter.

## Circuit breaker

Per-channel three-state breaker in
`apps/engine/src/notifications/circuit-breaker.ts`:

| State | Effect |
|---|---|
| `closed` | Deliveries proceed. Failure count resets on success. |
| `open` | Dispatcher records `breaker_open` and skips. Auto-flips to half-open after `OPEN_DURATION_MS`. |
| `half-open` | One trial delivery is allowed. Success → `closed`; failure → `open`. |

`FAILURE_THRESHOLD` consecutive failures (default 5) opens the breaker.
The breaker is per-channel, not per-rule — a rule that targets a
healthy channel keeps firing even when an unrelated rule's target is
down.

## RBAC

| Permission | Routes / actions |
|---|---|
| `notification:read` | List/get channels, rules, deliveries; `GET` on every notifications endpoint. |
| `notification:write` | Create/update/delete channels and rules; `POST /v1/notifications/rules/:id/test` (because triggering a synthetic event causes a real outbound delivery and a real audit row). |

Every write through the HTTP routes flows through `auditAwait` so the
audit log carries the actor, the resource, and the changed fields.

## HTTP routes

| Method | Path | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/v1/notifications/channels` | |
| `POST` | `/v1/notifications/channels` | |
| `PATCH` | `/v1/notifications/channels/:id` | |
| `DELETE` | `/v1/notifications/channels/:id` | |
| `GET` | `/v1/notifications/rules` | |
| `POST` | `/v1/notifications/rules` | |
| `PATCH` | `/v1/notifications/rules/:id` | |
| `DELETE` | `/v1/notifications/rules/:id` | |
| `POST` | `/v1/notifications/rules/:id/test` | Synthesise a notification event and dispatch it through the rule pipeline. Returns the rule-matching, rate-limit, and channel-dispatch outcome so operators can verify a rule end-to-end without waiting for a real workflow run. Audited as `notification_rule.tested`. |
| `GET` | `/v1/notifications/deliveries?limit=&offset=&status=` | |

All routes are Zod-first (see
`apps/engine/src/http/routes/notifications.ts`) and surface in the
generated OpenAPI document.

## Audit actions

| Action | Trigger |
|---|---|
| `notification_channel.created` / `.updated` / `.deleted` | Channel lifecycle |
| `notification_rule.created` / `.updated` / `.deleted` / `.tested` | Rule lifecycle + test |
| `chat.message.sent` | Delivery `sent` |
| `chat.message.denied` | Delivery `rate_limited` or `breaker_open` |
| `webhook.outbound.failed` | Delivery `failed` |

## Observability

| Signal | Detail |
|---|---|
| Counter `chat_delivery_total{platform,status}` | Partitioned by adapter platform and outcome. |
| Counter `webhook_delivery_total{subscription_id,status}` | For the webhook subscriptions surface (parallel system; see [observability](observability.md)). |
| Structured logs (`notifications/service.ts`) | Carry `tenant_id`, `rule_id`, `channel_id`, `event_type`, `status`. |

## What is intentionally not here

| Not built | Why / where instead |
|---|---|
| Per-user notifications | Recipients are channel-targeted; there is no personal-inbox model. |
| Templating DSL | Message text is built from event metadata. A future template field on rules could land here without changing the dispatch contract. |
| In-app notification surface | No dedicated UI inbox; the deliveries table is the authoritative log. |

## Notification payload pattern — what, why, proposal

Notifications are the first place an operator sees the bounded repair
loop in action. A useful incident message answers four questions in a
single delivery, so the operator can decide without opening logs:

| Question | Carries |
|---|---|
| **What** happened | The failure substance — status, surfaced error, timestamp. |
| **Where** it happened | Workflow slug and version, step id, the external endpoint that drifted. Decisive the moment there is more than one workflow, supplier, or tenant: "the script broke" is not enough. |
| **Why** it happened | The drift the connector or driver actually detected — not just the HTTP status — plus the `patch_candidate` reference when the bounded repair loop has already produced one. |
| **How** to act | The Patch Candidate diff, the deterministic dry-run outcome against recorded fixtures, and the operator actions: **approve**, **reject**, **escalate to human**. |

A concrete delivery body — the same shape across every surface:

```json
{
  "what": {
    "occurred_at": "2026-05-27T14:02:11Z",
    "status": "failed",
    "error": "http_422 — unknown field 'sku_external'"
  },
  "where": {
    "workflow_slug": "sync-suppliers",
    "workflow_version": 4,
    "step_id": "pull-supplier-3",
    "endpoint": "supplier-3/inventory"
  },
  "why": {
    "kind": "schema_drift",
    "diff": { "renamed": [{ "from": "sku_external", "to": "sku" }] },
    "patch_candidate_id": "pc_4711"
  },
  "how": {
    "summary": "Map field 'sku_external' → 'sku' in pull-supplier-3 response shape",
    "dryrun": { "fixtures": 12, "passed": 12, "diverged": 0 },
    "actions": ["approve", "reject", "escalate"]
  }
}
```

One payload contract, every surface:

| Surface | Mode | Renders |
|---|---|---|
| Slack / Teams / Google Chat | Push | Platform-native blocks — four sections as headings, operator actions as buttons. |
| Webhook | Push | The JSON verbatim — the receiving system gets the same four-part answer for its own UI. |
| sk CLI — `sk executions tail` | Pull | Live *what* + *where* + *why* as the run progresses. |
| sk CLI — `sk patch-candidates get <id>` | Pull | The *how*, with `sk patch-candidates approve` / `reject` as the actions. |

The point is not the wire format and not the surface. The point is the
conceptual job: the closed learning loop is only as good as the moment
a human can act on it, and acting requires *what*, *where*, *why*, and
*how* in one place. The alternative — a red workflow plus a "go read
the logs" link — pushes the operator into reconstructing all four
questions from scratch, which is where the compounding loop quietly
stalls into a ticket backlog.

<!-- Source: docs/operators/observability.md -->

# Observability & Resource Limits

> **Audience:** SREs, platform engineers, operators running sk in production

**See every run, catch drift before it costs you.** sk runs unattended: observable
enough to diagnose a problem in minutes, bounded enough that no single workflow,
tenant, or external dependency can degrade the platform for everyone else. The payoff
is operational — fewer incidents, faster root-cause, predictable AI spend.

| You want to | Read |
|---|---|
| Scrape process-wide metrics | [`/metrics` (Prometheus)](#observability) |
| Trace one failing run across surfaces | [Telemetry Surface](#telemetry-surface) — correlate by `trace_id` |
| Answer per-tenant questions over time | [`/v1/stats/*`](#tenant-scoped-runtime-stats-v1stats) |
| Keep a tenant from monopolizing capacity | [Resource Limits](#resource-limits-and-operational-safety) |
| Tune ingestion / knowledge budgets | [Documentation & Knowledge Tunables](#documentation--knowledge-tunables) |

For the leaf-by-leaf tunable reference, see
[`../admins/configuration.md`](../admins/configuration.md) and the generated
[`../admins/settings-reference.md`](../admins/settings-reference.md).

---

## Observability

Four surfaces, one identity envelope. Each answers a different question, and they
chain by `trace_id` so an operator can follow a single request from HTTP edge to
notification.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph emit[Engine emits]
        M[Metrics<br/>/metrics Prometheus]
        L[Structured logs<br/>JSON on stdout]
        T[Execution traces<br/>per-step logs]
        E[SSE event stream<br/>tenant-wide]
    end

    M --> SCRAPE[Prometheus scraper]
    L --> AGG[Datadog / Loki / CloudWatch]
    T --> CLI[sk executions tail]
    E --> DASH[Dashboards / alerting]

    SCRAPE --> STATS[/v1/stats/*<br/>per-tenant, time-bucketed]
    AGG --> STATS
    STATS --> DIGEST[/v1/operator/health-digest<br/>leading-indicator risk]

    M -. trace_id .-> L
    L -. trace_id .-> T
    T -. trace_id .-> E
```

| Surface | Endpoint / command | Scope | Answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Metrics** | `/metrics` | Process-wide, resets on redeploy | Latency by route, execution duration + step counts, error/retry rates, queue depth, token usage, pool stats |
| **Structured logging** | JSON on stdout | Per-event | Query/alert on fields directly — `trace_id`, `tenant_id`, `request_source`, severity |
| **Execution inspection** | `sk executions tail <id>` + API | Per-execution | Per-step logs; failed steps include full error, inputs, raw connector response |
| **Event streaming** | tenant-wide SSE | Per-tenant | Real-time execution events for external dashboards/alerting |

No external metrics system is required for collection — any Prometheus-compatible
scraper works. Logs ship to any standard aggregator without transformation.

**Product analytics (opt-in).** To forward HTTP-response telemetry to an external
product-analytics platform (PostHog, Mixpanel, a custom ingest endpoint), enable
`observability.analytics`. Off by default — no external calls until the operator
opts in. It reuses the existing `request.telemetry` hook in the metrics middleware;
no parallel hook is added.

```yaml
# sk settings set observability.analytics.enabled true
# sk settings set observability.analytics.endpoint '"https://analytics.example.com/capture"'
# sk settings set observability.analytics.api_key '"…"'
# sk settings set observability.analytics.project '"my-project"'
```

| Field | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `observability.analytics.enabled` | `false` | Master switch. No-op when false. |
| `observability.analytics.endpoint` | `""` | Self-hostable ingest URL. Empty = no-op even if enabled. |
| `observability.analytics.api_key` | `""` | Bearer credential (secret). |
| `observability.analytics.project` | `""` | Project/workspace identifier forwarded in each event body. |

Each event carries `method`, `path` (route template, not raw URL), `status_code`,
`duration_ms`, `request_source`, and `tenant_id`. Errors on the analytics call are
caught and logged at debug level — a slow or unavailable endpoint never stalls a
response.

### Telemetry Surface

Every code path an operator may need to debug emits at least one structured event
with a stable `action` field. The full surface:

| Action | Module | When | Key fields |
|---|---|---|---|
| `request.telemetry` | `http` | Every HTTP response (2xx/3xx/4xx) | `method`, `path`, `status_code`, `duration_ms`, `tenant_id`, `trace_id`, `request_source` |
| `request.error` | `http` | 5xx responses | as above + `error` |
| `context.assembled` | `llm` | Every LLM context assembly | `flow`, `model`, `cap_tokens`, `total_tokens`, per-section token counts, `dropped_sections[]` |
| `fallback.triggered` | `llm` | Primary provider error → fallback | `flow`, `primary`, `fallback`, `kind` |
| `tool.loop_detected` | `conversation` | Per-tool loop-breaker fires | `conversation_id`, `tool`, `tool_count` |
| `execution.<status>` | `execution` | Every workflow terminal transition | `execution_id`, `status` |
| `webhook.send_failed` | `notifications` | Webhook adapter exhausted retries | `url`, `last_error` |
| `notification.dispatch_failed` | `notifications` | Per-rule dispatch threw | `rule_id`, `channel_id`, `event_type` |
| `metrics.label_dropped` | `observability` | Metric write used an unknown label | `metric`, `label` (logged once per pair) |
| `metrics.write_failed` | `observability` | Metric write threw | `error` |

**Identity envelope.** Every record above carries `tenant_id` (where applicable),
`trace_id`, and `request_source`. Operators correlate across surfaces
(HTTP → execution → notification) by `trace_id`.

The full Prometheus metric registry is built in
[`apps/engine/src/observability/metrics.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/observability/metrics.ts).
Context and predictive-maintenance metrics:

| Metric | Labels | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| `llm_context_assembled_total` | `flow`, `request_source` | Assemblies per flow |
| `llm_context_dropped_sections_total` | `flow`, `section` | Which sections the trimmer drops per flow |
| `llm_context_total_tokens` | `flow` | Histogram of total prompt tokens per call |
| `db_pool_{total,idle,waiting}_connections` | — | Pool pressure |
| `db_transient_retries_total` | `label` | Cumulative transient retries |
| `db_transient_retry_rate_per_min` | — | **Windowed** retry rate (leading indicator) |
| `dlq_job_count` | `queue` | Dead-letter depth |
| `connector_call_total` | `slug`, `health` | Connector outcomes |
| `llm_call_duration_ms` | `provider`, `model`, `flow` | LLM latency |
| `llm_fallback_invocations_total` | `from`, `to`, `reason` | Fallback frequency |
| `process_memory_rss_high_water_bytes` | — | Memory high-water mark |

These feed the leading-indicator `risk[]` block of `GET /v1/operator/health-digest`.

> **Why the retry rate is windowed.** The `transient_retry` risk signal reads
> `db_transient_retry_rate_per_min` — a windowed rate the 60s memory sampler computes
> (retries since the previous tick ÷ elapsed minutes) against
> `observability.predictive.transient_retry_rate` — **not** the cumulative
> `db_transient_retries_total` ÷ uptime. The window keeps it a leading indicator: a
> one-off Postgres blip decays to 0 within a tick or two instead of latching the warn
> (short uptime) or being averaged into silence (long uptime).

**Risk-signal audit dedup is per-process.** A risk signal crossing into `critical`
(or recovering) writes a single `operator.risk_signal_raised` /
`operator.risk_signal_cleared` audit row on the transition edge, under the **system**
tenant. The edge tracker is in-process, so in an N-replica deployment a standing
critical can produce up to N rows per edge — one per replica that first reads the
digest. Audit volume is small, but SIEM dedup on `(action, resource_id)` should expect
up to N duplicates per incident. A Postgres-side claim (`INSERT … ON CONFLICT` on a
`(kind, window)` table) is the HA hardening if exactly-once attribution becomes a
requirement.

### Tenant-scoped runtime stats (`/v1/stats/*`)

Where `/metrics` is a process-wide Prometheus snapshot that resets on redeploy and is
**not** tenant-scoped, the `/v1/stats/*` surface answers per-tenant operational
questions over time-bucketed history. It aggregates at read time from `executions`,
`audit_log`, and `llm_usage` — no new tables. Every route filters
`tenant_id = principal.tenant_id` as the first predicate and is gated by the single
`stats:read` permission (admins hold it by default; members opt in via a custom role).

| Route | Aggregates over | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /v1/stats/executions` | `executions` | run volume + duration distribution (p50/p95/p99/max) by workflow / status / request_source |
| `GET /v1/stats/connectors` | `audit_log` (`action='connector.invoked'`) | connector-call volume + latency + outcome + status-class (`4xx_auth`/`4xx_rate_limited`/…) |
| `GET /v1/stats/events` | `audit_log` (per `?class=`) | webhook / chat / schedule / self-healing / discovery / policy / external-write event volume |
| `GET /v1/stats/llm` | `llm_usage` | token usage + cache-hit rate + latency by model / flow |

**Bucket grammar.** `bucket` (`minute|hour|day|month|year`), required `from`, optional
`to` (default now) and `tz` (default UTC). Hard window caps reject scans that would
explode (`minute ≤ 24h`, `hour ≤ 31d`, `day ≤ 366d`, …) with
`400 bucket_window_too_large`. Audit-backed routes clamp `from` to the tenant's
audit-retention horizon and surface `truncated_at` on the envelope. Every response
carries three rollups: per-bucket (`groups[].buckets[]`), per-group totals
(`groups[].totals`), and window totals (top-level `totals`).

Two btree indexes back these routes:
`executions (tenant_id, status, started_at)` and `audit_log (tenant_id, action, ts)`.

Operators read this surface from the CLI: `sk stats executions|connectors|events|llm`
(human ASCII table + sparkline by default, `--json` for cron/CI/ETL), and it feeds the
`sk` settings Status heatmap + Usage token bar.

---

## Resource Limits and Operational Safety

sk enforces limits at multiple levels so that no single workflow, tenant, or external
connector dependency can degrade the platform for others. All limits have documented
defaults and are operator-tunable.

| Limit | Protects against |
|---|---|
| Per-execution / per-step timeouts | Runaway workflows consuming resources indefinitely |
| Per-tenant token budgets | Unbounded AI usage costs |
| API rate limits | A single caller monopolizing capacity |
| Connector circuit breakers | Cascading failure from a degraded external boundary — after N consecutive failures the circuit opens and requests fail fast until recovery |
| Queue depth caps | Unbounded work accumulation |

When a circuit breaker trips, the audit log records it and the event stream delivers a
notification. Operators see the failure before users do.

### Documentation & Knowledge Tunables

Documentation ingestion and Knowledge Source budgets are env-configurable so operators
can raise them on hardware that warrants larger corpora. Defaults are conservative and
match the docs in [`../authors/knowledge-sources.md`](../authors/knowledge-sources.md).
Each value falls back to the default when the env var is unset, empty, zero, or
unparseable — there is no half-configured state.

| Env var | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `DOCS_INGESTION_MAX_BYTES_PER_CONNECTOR` | `10485760` (10 MB) | Total ingest budget per connector per run. |
| `DOCS_INGESTION_MAX_BYTES_PER_DOC` | `3145728` (3 MB) | Per-page / per-document hard cap. |
| `DOCS_INGESTION_MAX_LINKS` | `20` | Links followed from `llms.txt` / markdown indices. |
| `DOCS_INGESTION_MAX_SPECS` | `100` | OpenAPI / GraphQL specs per ingest run. |
| `DOCS_INGESTION_MAX_CONCURRENT` | `25` | Concurrent fetches per ingest run. |
| `KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_MAX_BYTES` | `52428800` (50 MB) | Per-source upload cap. |
| `KNOWLEDGE_TENANT_MAX_BYTES` | `524288000` (500 MB) | Per-tenant total knowledge bytes. |
| `KNOWLEDGE_MAX_FILES_PER_MESSAGE` | `10` | Max files attached in a single conversation message. |
| `DOCS_CRAWL_POSITIVE_HIGH` | `api,apis,endpoints,reference,docs` | URL keywords that score `+5` during the playwright fallback crawl. |
| `DOCS_CRAWL_POSITIVE_LOW` | `swagger,openapi` | URL keywords that score `+3`. |
| `DOCS_CRAWL_NEGATIVE` | `pricing,login,signin,signup,/blog/,careers,/locale/,/legal/,/privacy/,/terms/,/contact/` | URL keywords that score `-10`. |

### Binary file parser tunables (compile-time)

The binary office-document parsers (PDF / DOCX / XLSX / PPTX) are guarded by per-format
ceilings that are deliberately **not** env-configurable — the values are
workload-defensive defaults, and an operator who needs to change them should do it in
code with a code review. Their absence from `subkit.config.json` is intentional
(zero-conf principle).

| Constant | Default | Where | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `EXTRACT_BODY_CAP_BYTES` | `104857600` (100 MB) | `http/routes/ai/extract.ts` | Hard request-body cap on `POST /v1/extract` and `POST /v1/ai/extract`. Enforced twice: declared `content-length` and streaming fallback. |
| `TEXT_EXTRACT_PER_FILE_MAX_BYTES` | `1048576` (1 MB) | `llm/core/file-context.ts` | Per-file ceiling on TEXT bytes that reach the LLM context. Applies to the *parsed* output for binary formats. |
| `TEXT_EXTRACT_BINARY_PER_FILE_MAX_BYTES` | `26214400` (25 MB) | `llm/core/file-context.ts` | Per-file ceiling on RAW bytes read for the binary `text_extract` branch. Binaries above this size emit a `[file: <name>] (too large to parse)` placeholder. |
| `TEXT_EXTRACT_PER_TURN_CAP_BYTES` | `4194304` (4 MB) | `llm/core/file-context.ts` | Per-turn cumulative TEXT cap across all files. Subsequent files get a skip placeholder. |
| `PARSER_TIMEOUT_MS.pdf` | `30000` (30 s) | `docs-ingestion/parsers/strategy.ts` | `withParserTimeout` hard kill for PDF. |
| `PARSER_TIMEOUT_MS.docx` | `30000` (30 s) | `docs-ingestion/parsers/strategy.ts` | `withParserTimeout` hard kill for DOCX. |
| `PARSER_TIMEOUT_MS.pptx` | `30000` (30 s) | `docs-ingestion/parsers/strategy.ts` | `withParserTimeout` hard kill for PPTX. |
| `PARSER_TIMEOUT_MS.xlsx` / `.xls` | `60000` (60 s) | `docs-ingestion/parsers/strategy.ts` | Longer budget; SheetJS can hit O(n²) layouts on pathological workbooks. |
| `XLSX_ROW_CAP_PER_SHEET` | `200` | `docs-ingestion/parsers/xlsx.ts` | Per-sheet row cap (mirrors the CSV row cap). |
| `PPTX_SLIDE_CAP` | `2000` | `docs-ingestion/parsers/pptx.ts` | Per-archive slide cap; short-circuits ZIP walk when exceeded. |

When a parser trips its timeout, the request fails with a typed `BinaryParseError`
mapped to HTTP 400 and the structured logger records a
`docs_ingestion.binary_parsers.parse_failed` row. The
`subkit_docs_binary_parse_total{format,result="error"}` counter increments so operators
can chart per-format failure rates.

**Audit-log surface for binary extracts.** Successful and failed binary
`POST /v1/extract` calls emit `audit_log` rows under `action = "data.exported"`. Each
row carries up to ~455 bytes of operator-controlled input inside `metadata`:

- `metadata.filename` — the validated `x-filename` header (≤ 255 chars, no path
  separators or NULs; rejected at the Zod boundary before parse).
- `metadata.error` — the parser's diagnostic (≤ 200 chars, ASCII control characters
  stripped via `audit/sanitize.ts`).

SIEM consumers should expect both fields to be free-form text from the caller's side.
Both pass through `sanitizeForAudit` in `apps/engine/src/audit/sanitize.ts` so a
malformed PDF whose parser message embeds a few bytes of the input can't smuggle
TAB / NUL / CR into the audit row.

**Metric vs audit denominator gradient.** The
`subkit_docs_binary_parse_total{format,result}` counter increments on *every* binary
parse dispatch path — the `/v1/extract` HTTP route, the docs-ingestion file-upload
source, **and** the LLM `text_extract` context-assembly branch. The `audit_log`
`data.exported` rows, by contrast, are written only by the `/v1/extract` route and the
docs-ingestion service (not the LLM context path, which is read-only assembly with no
egress). An operator charting parse errors should therefore expect
`subkit_docs_binary_parse_total{result="error"}` to be a strict superset of `audit_log`
`data.exported` rows with `result="error"` — the metric is the broader denominator.
Reconcile by parsing surface, not 1:1.

---

- [Self-healing in operations](./self-healing.md) — how the engine detects connector drift and proposes operator-reviewed Patch Candidates.
- [Configuration](../admins/configuration.md) — the operator-facing settings surface, with the generated [settings reference](../admins/settings-reference.md).
- [Notifications](./notifications.md) — routing engine events to Slack / Teams / Google Chat / webhooks.

<!-- Source: docs/operators/quickstart.md -->

# Quickstart — Operator

**Outcome: a governed, audited automation engine your whole team can use — live in production in 15 minutes.** Every workflow run is permission-checked, recorded, and replayable, so you ship automation without trading away control.

Three steps get you there: engine up → admin key minted → first connector registered.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Engine up<br/>Docker, :3000] --> B[Admin key<br/>sk init]
    B --> C[First connector<br/>sk connectors create]
    C --> D[Operational<br/>workflows, audit, metrics]
```

![sk REPL](../_tapes/out/operator-onboard.gif)

> **Brand new to sk?** The [zero-to-running quickstart](../developers/self-host.md) walks a complete beginner from the Docker image through a first connector, workflow, and knowledge article.

> **Just kicking the tires?** The local-dev path (postgres-only compose + `bun run dev`) is in [docs/developers/quickstart.md](../developers/quickstart.md). This page stands up a production engine with the all-in-one Docker image.

## 1. Install the `sk` CLI

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mikebild/subkit/main/scripts/install.sh | bash
```

See [docs/developers/input-surfaces.md](../developers/input-surfaces.md) for Windows and manual platform installs. The install script may place a `subkit` compatibility alias on disk; the canonical command surface is `sk`.

## 2. Run the engine (Docker)

sk ships an all-in-one image (`mikebild/subkit`) that bundles the engine + PostgreSQL:

```bash
docker run -d --name subkit -p 3000:3000 -v subkit-data:/data mikebild/subkit:latest
```

On first boot it initializes Postgres, persists a `MASTER_KEY`, runs migrations, and serves the API on `:3000`. The `subkit-data` volume holds all state. Verify:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:3000/v1/health | jq
```

Full guide (external-DB mode, TLS-fronting, persistence, resource limits): [docs/developers/self-host.md](../developers/self-host.md).

## 3. Create the first tenant + admin key

A fresh engine has no tenants. It prints a one-time bootstrap token to the logs:

```bash
docker logs subkit 2>&1 | grep 'sk init --token'
```

Complete setup with `sk init` — creates the tenant, mints the admin key, and wires the LLM provider in one shot (the bundled CLI runs inside the container):

```bash
docker exec subkit sk init --token <token> \
  --admin-email you@example.com \
  --tenant-name "My Org" \
  --llm-provider anthropic \
  --llm-api-key sk-ant-…
```

To get a full admin key you can paste into a `sk` CLI on your host (tenant slug is the kebab-cased name, e.g. `My Org` → `my-org`):

```bash
docker exec subkit engine --issue-admin-key --tenant my-org   # printed once
sk login --engine-url http://localhost:3000 --api-key wf_live_…
```

## 4. Register your first connector

```bash
sk connectors create \
  --template stripe \
  --name stripe-prod
```

Pick from 55 connector templates — see [docs/concepts/connectors.md](../concepts/connectors.md) for how templates, drivers, and credentials work together.

## 5. You're operational

- `sk workflows list` — see what's defined.
- `sk executions list` — watch executions.
- `sk audit tail` — confirm every state change is recorded.
- `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" http://localhost:3000/metrics` — Prometheus scrape target.
- `sk settings configure` — interactive form for every runtime config leaf (database, LLM provider, observability, etc.). See [`subkit.config.example.json`](../../subkit.config.example.json) at the repo root for the full schema with defaults.

## How `curl /install | bash` works against your engine

The engine serves install artifacts at `/install/sk-:platform-:arch`, `/install/agent-:platform-:arch`, and `/install/sha256sums`. Anyone who can reach your engine URL can install the CLI:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://my-engine.example.com/install | bash
```

The script probes `${ENGINE_URL}/install/sk-${os}-${arch}` first; on `200` it streams from there with `x-subkit-sha256` verification against `${ENGINE_URL}/install/sha256sums`. On `404` (the case for systemd-deployed engines that don't bundle CLI binaries on the host), the script falls back to the matching GitHub Release. Either way `~/.subkit/bin/sk` matches the engine's running version exactly — no version drift.

## Next steps

- [docs/concepts/connectors.md](../concepts/connectors.md) — connector management, credentials, and OAuth2.
- [docs/admins/rbac-and-roles.md](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md) — RBAC, identity setup (OIDC/SSO), API key rotation, and Before-Request Hooks.
- [docs/operators/observability.md](./observability.md) — observability, resource limits, self-healing, and backup strategy.

<!-- Source: docs/operators/runtime-dependencies.md -->

# Runtime Dependencies

> **Audience:** SREs, platform engineers, operators running sk in production

**Outcome: discovery works against every documentation site, including JavaScript-rendered SPAs.** The engine ships as a single self-contained binary, but one last-resort capability — rendering an SPA documentation site to discover a connector — needs a real browser on the host. This page documents that dependency, why it exists, and how it is provisioned so the strategy runs in production instead of silently self-skipping.

## What needs a host dependency

The engine is a `bun build --compile` single binary: no Node, no runtime install, no container spawning. Everything it needs is inside the binary — with **one** exception.

| Dependency | Used by | Required? | If absent |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chromium + the `playwright` package** | The SPA-docs connector-discovery strategy (`connectors/discovery/playwright-crawl.ts`) | Optional | The strategy self-skips with a clean `strategy_skipped`; the engine boots and serves normally — only documentation sites that need a rendered DOM become undiscoverable |

Nothing else in the engine reaches outside the binary. Postgres and Caddy are separate services, not engine dependencies.

## Why a browser, and why on disk

Connector discovery tries cheap strategies first (OpenAPI specs, GraphQL introspection, static HTML). When a documentation site renders entirely client-side — an SPA that ships no machine-readable spec and no server-rendered HTML — the only way to read it is to render it. The last-resort strategy launches **headless Chromium** via [Playwright](https://playwright.dev), renders the page, and extracts a docs corpus.

Because the engine is compiled, a bare `import("playwright")` resolves against the embedded virtual filesystem (`bunfs`) and fails — playwright is intentionally **not** bundled into the binary. So the runtime loads playwright from an **on-disk** install via an absolute path, and launches a Chromium build that was downloaded to a fixed location.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Discovery request] --> B{Cheaper strategies<br/>OpenAPI / GraphQL / HTML}
    B -->|spec found| Z[Connector discovered]
    B -->|all fail| C{Chromium + playwright<br/>present on host?}
    C -->|yes| D[Render SPA → docs corpus]
    C -->|no| E[strategy_skipped<br/>clean, no error]
    D --> Z
```

## How the engine finds it

Two environment variables wire the binary to the on-disk install. The production systemd unit sets both:

| Variable | Points at | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `SK_PLAYWRIGHT_ENTRY` | The absolute path to the playwright package **entry file** (e.g. `…/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs`) | The runtime dynamic import reads this. Bare `playwright` is kept only as the dev fallback when running via `bun run` — it cannot resolve inside the compiled binary. |
| `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` | The directory holding the downloaded Chromium build | Module resolution alone is not enough — `chromium.launch()` still needs the browser binary present. |

If `SK_PLAYWRIGHT_ENTRY` is unset or wrong, discovery falls back to the bare specifier, which cannot resolve in the binary, and the strategy self-skips. There is no crash and no wasted run-and-fail — the availability probe is cached.

## Provisioning in production

The droplet provisioning lives in the **subkit-deploy** repo, not here. The one-time `bootstrap.sh` run:

1. Installs the `playwright` package into a fixed directory (`/opt/subkit/playwright`).
2. Downloads the matching Chromium build with `playwright install --with-deps chromium` into a fixed browsers directory (`/opt/subkit/ms-playwright`), pulling the OS libraries headless Chromium needs.
3. The `subkit-engine.service` systemd unit sets `SK_PLAYWRIGHT_ENTRY` and `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` to those paths.

The installed playwright version must stay in lockstep with the `playwright` dependency range in the engine's `package.json` — the package and the Chromium download must come from the same version so the browser revision matches the launcher. Re-running `bootstrap.sh` reinstalls the pinned version in place (idempotent).

> Operators on a host **without** Chromium (local dev, a minimal box, a container image that omits the browser) need do nothing: discovery simply self-skips the SPA-docs strategy and every cheaper strategy still runs. Install the dependency only when you need to discover SPA-only documentation sites.

## Verifying

After a deploy, a discovery run against an SPA documentation site with no cheaper spec should run `playwright-crawl` and return a corpus — `journalctl -u subkit-engine` shows no `playwright_failed`. On a host without the dependency the same run logs `strategy_skipped` instead of a thrown error. See [observability.md](observability.md) for reading discovery outcomes in the run timeline, and [self-healing.md](self-healing.md) for how discovery feeds repair.

<!-- Source: docs/operators/scheduling-and-hooks.md -->

# Scheduling & Hooks (operator guide)

> **Audience:** Operators wiring scheduled runs, webhook triggers, and
> Before-Request Hooks.

**Outcome:** automation that fires on time or on event — verified at the door.
Scheduled runs survive restarts and fire when due; inbound webhooks are
signature-verified and replay-deduplicated before any work happens; and a
Before-Request Hook adds dynamic policy in front of every connector call. One
execution contract, one RBAC check, one audit trail — only the trigger differs.

| Lever | What it buys you |
|---|---|
| **Schedule** | Time-driven runs that are a durable commitment, not a best-effort timer. |
| **Webhook** | Event-driven runs gated by signature verification and replay dedup. |
| **Before-Request Hook** | Per-request policy that static roles cannot express, fail-closed. |

The execution model these sit on top of is in
[Workflows](../concepts/workflows.md); the access-control model the hook
extends is in [RBAC & Roles](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    cron[["Cron schedule<br/>(workflows_schedules)"]] --> rec{Reconciler<br/>due?}
    rec -->|fires| core
    hook[["Inbound webhook<br/>(webhooks_inbound)"]] --> verify{Signature<br/>valid?}
    verify -->|no| drop[Reject]
    verify -->|yes| dedup{Replay-id<br/>seen?}
    dedup -->|yes| drop
    dedup -->|no| core
    req[On-demand<br/>chat / MCP / CLI / API] --> core[["runExecution()<br/>RBAC + audit"]]
    core --> wf[Workflow run]
```

---

## Triggers

`WorkflowDef.trigger` is a discriminated union over `kind`. Omitting the block is
equivalent to `{ kind: "request" }`. All three variants land at the same
`runExecution()` core through the same execution contract, the same RBAC, and the
same audit — only the way the run is initiated differs.

| `kind` | Fields | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `request` | (none) | Default. Run is initiated on demand — chat `run_workflow`, MCP, the CLI, or `POST /v1/executions`. Inline runs complete on the request path; `async: true` is honoured only for `source=saved`. |
| `webhook` | `source` (slug), `events[]` (provider event names; empty = any), `verify` (`stripe-signature` \| `github-hmac` \| `none`) | Reverse-bound to a `webhooks_inbound` row. Inbound posts are signature-verified before any processing; replay-id deduplication suppresses retried deliveries. |
| `schedule` | `cron` (5-field `m h dom mon dow` or `every:N`), `tz` (IANA, default `UTC`); optional `business_days_only`, `skip_dates[]` | Reverse-bound to a `workflows_schedules` row. The reconciler validates the cron at bind time and fires at the operator's local wall-clock time. `business_days_only` skips weekends; `skip_dates` declares holidays/freezes explicitly. A missed firing fires on the next reconciler pass rather than being silently skipped. |

Setting `webhook` or `schedule` reverse-binds the inbound binding or cron schedule
keyed on `(tenant_id, workflow_id)` at save time and removes the binding on delete
or version rotate. The trigger is recorded in every Execution and Audit Log entry
alongside the actor identity envelope.

### Webhook verification & replay dedup

Inbound deliveries are checked **before** any workflow logic runs. Verification
proves the payload came from the declared provider; replay dedup proves it is not
a retried copy of a delivery already accepted.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Provider
    participant E as sk engine
    participant W as Workflow
    P->>E: POST /v1/hooks/{source}<br/>(payload + signature + replay-id)
    E->>E: Verify signature<br/>(stripe-signature / github-hmac)
    alt signature invalid
        E-->>P: 401 reject (no run)
    else signature valid
        E->>E: Look up replay-id
        alt replay-id already seen
            E-->>P: 200 accepted (deduped, no run)
        else first delivery
            E->>E: Match events[] filter
            E->>W: runExecution() — RBAC + audit
            W-->>E: result
            E-->>P: 200 accepted
        end
    end
```

| Stage | Guarantee |
|---|---|
| Signature verify | Forged or tampered payloads are rejected before processing (`verify: none` opts out — only for trusted-network sources). |
| Replay dedup | Provider retries of an already-accepted delivery are suppressed; the workflow runs at most once per replay-id. |
| Event filter | `events[]` narrows which provider event names trigger a run; empty matches any. |

## Scheduling durability

The scheduler uses a durable job queue so scheduled runs survive engine restarts.
A schedule is a commitment: if the engine was unavailable when a run was due, it
fires when availability is restored. The same queue backs explicitly asynchronous
workflow runs, while synchronous API-initiated runs stay inline on the request
path.

Execution state changes are published through a pub/sub system backed by an outbox
pattern — events are written in the same transaction as the state change that
produced them, so they are never silently lost. Subscribers (CLI live-tail, chat
progress, SSE consumers, outbound webhooks) receive them in real time.

| Property | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Restart survival | Due-but-unfired runs fire when the engine returns; nothing is silently dropped. |
| Missed firing | Fires on the next reconciler pass, not skipped. |
| Outbox events | Written in the same transaction as the state change — never lost. |

## Before-Request Hooks

A Before-Request Hook is a sandboxed script that runs **before a connector request
executes**. It receives the full request context — caller identity, target
connector, operation type, request parameters — and can enforce policy that static
roles cannot express: block writes during a maintenance window, require approval
for specific production connectors, enforce data-residency constraints, or log
requests matching a pattern.

Hooks run in an isolated QuickJS-WASM sandbox with a strict CPU budget. They
cannot access the network, the file system, or the database. An error or timeout
fails **closed**: the request is denied. Every hook execution is recorded in the
audit log.

**Evaluation order:** RBAC is evaluated first. If the caller has no permission, the
request is denied before the hook is consulted. If RBAC passes, the hook runs; if
it aborts, the request is denied with the hook's reason. Only if both pass does the
request proceed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    req[Connector request] --> rbac{RBAC<br/>permitted?}
    rbac -->|no| deny[Denied]
    rbac -->|yes| hook{Hook<br/>aborts?}
    hook -->|sk.deny / error / timeout| deny
    hook -->|passes| egress[Connector egress]
```

A hook is plain sandboxed JavaScript and can use the frozen `sk` standard library
(`sk.deny("reason")`, `sk.http.isMutating(method)`, `sk.get(...)`) — see
[Custom Skills → the sk-Stdlib](../authors/custom-skills.md). The authorization
model the hook layers onto is in [RBAC & Roles](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md).

| Guard | Effect |
|---|---|
| Sandbox | No network, file system, or database access; strict CPU budget. |
| Fail-closed | Error or timeout denies the request. |
| Audit | Every hook execution is recorded. |

---

## Further reading

- [Workflows](../concepts/workflows.md) — the execution model, triggers, versioning, and self-healing.
- [RBAC & Roles](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md) — the access-control model Before-Request Hooks extend.
- [Notifications](./notifications.md) — routing the events these triggers emit.

<!-- Source: docs/operators/self-healing.md -->

# Self-Healing in Operations

> **Audience:** SREs, platform engineers, operators running sk in production

**Outcome: workflows survive upstream API changes without silent failure.** When an external API renames a field, moves an endpoint, or adds a required parameter, the engine detects the break during real execution and hands the operator a validated, ready-to-apply repair — instead of a 3am pager and a from-scratch diagnosis.

## Why it matters

External APIs evolve constantly. Without detection, a workflow that worked yesterday fails today — silently or noisily — and the operator owns the cleanup. Self-healing turns that open-ended incident into a single review-and-apply decision.

| Without self-healing | With self-healing |
|---|---|
| Drift surfaces as a mystery failure | Drift surfaces as a structured diff |
| Operator reverse-engineers the change | Engine classifies the change as safe / unsafe |
| Fix is hand-written and untested | Fix is dry-run against recorded history |
| Separate health-check jobs needed | Detected during real work, when it matters |

## The bounded repair loop

Drift is caught during normal execution — no separate health check, no manual test run. The operator stays in control: nothing is applied without a decision.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Workflow execution] --> B{Step result<br/>as expected?}
    B -->|Yes| Z[Recorded run]
    B -->|No| C[Drift detected]
    C --> D[Patch Candidate<br/>structured diff]
    D --> E[Dry-run against<br/>recorded history]
    E --> F[Classify<br/>safe / unsafe]
    F --> G[Operator review]
    G -->|Approve| H[Apply repair]
    G -->|Reject| I[Discard / escalate]
    H --> A
```

## Stages

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Execution** | A connector step runs as part of a real workflow. |
| **Drift detect** | The engine spots a discrepancy in the response shape, status, or contract. |
| **Patch Candidate** | A proposed repair is generated with a structured diff of exactly what changed. |
| **Dry-run** | The candidate is validated against recorded execution history before it is offered. |
| **Classify** | The repair is marked safe or unsafe based on the scope of the change. |
| **Operator review** | The operator approves or rejects — one action, not a manual rebuild. |
| **Apply** | On approval, the repair updates the connector and the loop closes. |

## Operator guarantees

- **No silent failure.** Drift becomes a visible, structured signal.
- **No auto-apply.** The operator always decides; sk only proposes.
- **Validated before offered.** Every Patch Candidate is dry-run against real history.
- **Caught early.** Leading-indicator risk signals flag a degrading connector boundary before it fails wholesale — see [Observability](./observability.md).

---

## Further reading

- [Observability & resource limits](./observability.md) — the metrics and risk signals that flag drift early.
- [Workflows](../concepts/workflows.md) — the execution model and the self-healing repair loop (Run → Drift → Patch Candidate → Skill Candidate) in full.

# Authors

Build and run workflows by chatting with `sk` — describe the outcome in plain
language, approve what the AI proposes, and ship a governed, versioned workflow.

![sk](../_tapes/out/repl-author.gif)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[quickstart.md<br/>authenticate · first conversation] --> R[repl-tour.md<br/>the sk REPL · approve-to-commit]
    R --> A[authoring-workflows.md<br/>the AI authoring loop]
    A --> RC[recipes.md<br/>reusable recipes]
    A --> CS[custom-skills.md<br/>encode your conventions]
    A --> KS[knowledge-sources.md<br/>ground proposals in your docs]
    R --> SL[slash-commands.md<br/>REPL command reference]
    R --> SE[settings.md<br/>sk config reference]
```

| Doc | What it covers |
|---|---|
| [quickstart.md](quickstart.md) | Get authenticated and open your first authoring conversation in about 5 minutes. |
| [repl-tour.md](repl-tour.md) | Author connectors and workflows by conversation in the `sk` REPL — the approve-to-commit loop, slash commands, headless `-p`. |

# AI-Assisted Authoring

**Describe the outcome. Get a governed, audited, versioned workflow in minutes — not a build project that runs for weeks.**

Traditional workflow tools put construction on the builder: know the connector, learn the config syntax, draw it on a blank canvas. You ship what developers can build, not what the business needs. sk inverts that — the author states intent in plain language, the AI does the structural work, and a human signs off before anything runs.

| Business outcome | How sk delivers it |
|---|---|
| **Time** — first workflow in minutes | One `author_workflow` pass generates the complete definition, grounded in real endpoint evidence |
| **Compliance** — audit-ready by construction | Nothing reaches the engine without an explicit human approval; every step is reviewable |
| **Risk** — no raw secrets in the loop | Credentials are referenced by name through the Credential Vault, never seen during authoring |
| **Determinism** — production is AI-free | Once committed, the engine runs the workflow with zero AI involvement |

![sk REPL authoring — prompt to governed workflow](../_tapes/out/repl-author.gif)

> **Reading time:** ~18 min · **Audience:** engineers integrating with sk's authoring, operators curating Skills & Knowledge

---

## The Conversation Model

A Conversation is the primary authoring interface. The user describes a goal; the AI replies with a structured proposal — a Draft workflow that can be inspected, modified, and approved — never free-form code or autonomous decisions.

| Property | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Persistent** | Survives reloads, reconnects, multi-day sessions |
| **Resumable** | Start Monday, return Wednesday, pick up exactly where you left off — context, draft state, pending questions recalled |
| **Structured** | The AI operates over a fixed palette of authoring actions; its reasoning is a visible sequence of explicit moves, not opaque text |

The primary entry is `author_workflow` — one call that takes the user's goal verbatim, grounds generation in recorded endpoint samples and ingested docs, emits the complete evaluated draft, and returns structured `recorded_eval` findings. Around it sit grounding actions (probe a connector, search docs), the hold-writes preview, and repair actions that each apply one specific finding.

Operators and scripted clients that already know the target definition use the same model through the direct workflow and execution surface — skipping the conversational loop and working directly with definitions plus `POST /v1/executions` for preview and execution.

### One turn, end to end

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor U as User
    participant C as Conversation (sk)
    participant G as Grounding tools
    participant E as Engine
    participant J as Judge
    U->>C: Describe the outcome (plain language)
    C->>G: probe_connector / search_docs / search_knowledge
    G-->>C: recorded endpoint samples + docs
    C->>E: author_workflow (one pass)
    E-->>C: complete draft + recorded_eval findings
    C->>E: dry_run_workflow (writes held)
    E-->>C: reads run live, writes resolved but not dispatched
    C->>J: evaluate artifacts vs stashed goal
    J-->>C: verdict (pass / findings)
    C->>U: preview draft for approval
    U->>C: approve
    C->>E: commit (versioned workflow)
    E-->>U: runnable, governed workflow
```

---

## The Authoring State Machine

The engine maintains an explicit state machine per conversation and uses it to decide which actions are visible, which moves are blocked, and what the next valid move is. The model does not infer progress from transcript history.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ConnectorDraft
    ConnectorDraft --> ConnectorInspected: inspect
    ConnectorInspected --> ConnectorValidated: validate
    ConnectorValidated --> ConnectorProbed: probe
    ConnectorProbed --> ConnectorPersisted: green probe (auto)
    ConnectorPersisted --> WorkflowDraft: author_workflow (one-shot generate + evaluate)
    WorkflowDraft --> WorkflowPreviewed: dry_run_workflow (writes held)
    WorkflowPreviewed --> WorkflowJudged: instruction-grounded judge reads artifacts incl. held payloads
    WorkflowJudged --> WorkflowPersisted: green preview + judge pass (auto-commit)
    WorkflowJudged --> WorkflowRepair: judge / recorded_eval findings
    WorkflowPreviewed --> WorkflowRepair: preview failure
    WorkflowRepair --> WorkflowPreviewed: edit_workflow_patch / update_param, then preview again
    WorkflowPersisted --> WorkflowExecuted: run
    WorkflowExecuted --> Diagnosis: warnings / failure
    Diagnosis --> WorkflowRepair: repair draft
    WorkflowExecuted --> [*]: success
```

**Verification is persistence.** Probe persists the connector inline; a green, judged dry-run commits the workflow inline. There is no separate "save" step on the happy path. Dry-runs hold writes — read steps execute live, write steps are fully resolved (URL, headers, materialized body) but never dispatched, and the held request is recorded as the artifact the judge evaluates. Any draft mutation invalidates downstream checkpoints automatically.

**Stage gate.** `propose_step` and `update_param` are repair-stage tools. While the draft is in its initial stage — no recorded preview, no recorded-eval/judge findings — they refuse with `authoring_stage_violation` and name the exact next valid actions (`author_workflow`, `build_workflow`, `dry_run_workflow`, `edit_workflow_patch`), none of which is ever gated. The moment a preview or findings exist, both unlock unconditionally. Initial authoring is ONE `author_workflow` call, not a micro-iterated step-by-step build.

The state is persisted in the conversation draft summary:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `mode` | `connector`, `workflow`, `execution`, or `diagnosis` |
| `stage` | concrete state, e.g. `connector_probed`, `workflow_previewed` |
| `lifecycle_state` | active target is `draft_only` or `persisted` |
| `blocked_by` | exact missing checkpoints/fields blocking the next durable action |
| `next_required_action` | next state-advancing action to take or have the user approve |
| `checkpoints[]` | freshness for `inspect`, `validate`, `probe`, `preview`, `persist`, `execute`, `diagnose` |

The current stage, active target, and checkpoint freshness are part of the runtime contract, not prompt advice. The same grounding rule applies to explanatory follow-ups: when a user asks why something was named or configured a certain way, the assistant answers from recorded state, audit history, ingested docs, or a fresh grounding call — or says plainly that the reason is not recorded. It does not speculate.

### New draft versus saved workflow

A conversation can stay bound to a saved workflow after rename, commit, and execution so follow-up runs and repairs stay grounded. That binding is intentional but not sticky against explicit new-workflow intent.

When the user says they want to create a new workflow after inspecting or running an existing one, the engine clears the saved-workflow binding before the next authoring move. The next `author_workflow` or `build_workflow` call targets a fresh draft, not an in-place update. Updating a saved workflow remains an explicit path: keep the bound target and commit back into it.

---

## The Human-in-the-Loop Approval Gate

The most important architectural decision in sk: **nothing reaches the execution engine without an explicit human approval.**

When the AI finishes a Draft, it pauses the authoring loop and presents it for review. The operator sees every step, connector reference, parameter, and branching condition — and can push back, ask for changes, iterate. On approval, the Draft is committed as a new versioned Workflow; the Conversation transitions to active and the workflow is ready to run.

This is the governance model, not a UX convenience. It is the structural answer to "How do we know the AI did the right thing?" — because a human checked and signed off before anything ran.

The gate sits on top of hard quality gates:

| Gate | Rule |
|---|---|
| Connector save | Blocked until `inspect`, `validate`, `probe` checkpoints are fresh |
| Workflow commit | Blocked until `inspect`, `validate`, `preview` checkpoints are fresh |
| Workflow run | Always targets a persisted version, never an ambiguous draft |
| Connector persistence | A green `probe_connector_draft` calls `saveConnectorAtomic` inline (audit reason `auto_persist_on_green_probe`), returns `auto_saved: true` |
| Workflow persistence | A green, judged `dry_run_workflow` calls `commitWorkflowAtomic` inline (audit reason `auto_persist_on_green_dry_run`), returns `auto_committed: true` |
| Force overrides | `force_save: true` (after a failed probe) and `force_commit: true` (after a failed dry-run) go through the explicit `ask_user_confirm` carrier so the deviation is auditable |

Approval is the final human sign-off after the state machine has already established that the draft is internally coherent — not a substitute for missing technical checks.

---

## Probe Before Save, Preview Before Commit

The clean authoring experience treats intermediate verification as first-class product steps, not optional debugging.

**Connectors:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Start or update the connector draft |
| 2 | Inspect the current draft |
| 3 | Validate required fields and config shape |
| 4 | Probe the real upstream boundary — a green probe persists inline; envelope carries `auto_saved: true` |

**Workflows:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | **Ground** — `list_connectors`, `probe_connector` for any never-called connector (records the real response shape), `search_docs` / `search_knowledge` when the endpoint surface is unclear |
| 2 | **`author_workflow`** (one call) — generates the COMPLETE definition (steps, transforms, input/output schema, trigger), evaluates it against recorded evidence with bounded auto-repair, stashes it as the draft; read the `recorded_eval` findings |
| 3 | **`dry_run_workflow`** — hold-writes preview: reads run live; writes resolved (URL, headers, materialized body) but never dispatched, recorded as held request artifacts |
| 4 | **Judge** — instruction-grounded judge evaluates the artifacts (held payloads included) against the stashed goal; green preview + judge pass auto-commits (`auto_committed: true`) |
| 5 | **Repair on findings** — apply specific findings via `edit_workflow_patch` (structural) or `update_param` (single field), iterate a transform with `dry_run_transform`, then preview again |
| 6 | **Run** the persisted workflow |

No separate "save"/"commit" on the happy path — the verification step is the persistence step. Executing write steps for real during a preview is the rare exception, behind explicit user confirmation (`execute_writes: true`); externally visible destinations (recipient addresses, channels, webhook URLs) must always come from the user, never fabricated placeholders.

The engine tracks checkpoints as fresh or stale. Any draft mutation invalidates later checkpoints — editing after a successful preview makes the preview stale, so the workflow must be previewed again before commit. The assistant does not "think" a connector is ready; it reads that from checkpoint state. The draft summary carries the concrete next suggested tool, so prompt assembly, confirmations, and surface-specific evaluations all reason from the same contract.

### CLI parity

The `sk` CLI mirrors the conversational gates, so operators get the same guarantees from a script or pipeline:

| Conversation tool | sk CLI subcommand |
|---|---|
| `validate_draft` | `sk workflows validate <file.json>` |
| `dry_run_workflow` / `dry_run_step` | `sk workflows preview <file.json>` (alias: `dry-run`) |
| `save_workflow_draft` | `sk workflows create <file.json>` |
| `validate_connector_draft` (shape check) | — (use the conversational loop for structural checks) |
| `probe_connector_draft` / `test` | `sk connectors probe <id>` (alias of `test`) |
| `inspect_connector_draft` | `sk connectors inspect <id>` (alias of `get`) |

`sk workflows create` runs `validate` + `preview` as a pre-flight by default. `sk connectors create` runs a driver probe after the create returns. Both accept `--skip-checks` as an explicit escape hatch — it surfaces a stderr warning and is reserved for callers that already validated elsewhere. The same `inspect → validate → preview/probe → commit/save` state machine gates the persisted write on both surfaces.

### Warnings feed the next turn

When a dry-run (`dry_run_workflow`, `dry_run_step`) produces structured warnings — unresolved identifiers, rate-limit signals, pagination edges — they attach to the draft's `latest_preview` and feed automatically into the next turn's `prior_failures` block. The assistant sees them as structured context without the user quoting them back. `sk workflows run` mirrors this by printing a `WARN step=<key> code=<code> msg=<text>` line per warning on stderr while keeping the JSON payload on stdout unchanged.

### Submit/abort retry loop

Every structured LLM flow — `generate`, `extract`, `repair`, `discover` — goes through the same tool loop in `AiSdkModel.generateObject`. The model must call `submit` (return the final structured object) or `abort` (give up with a reason). Unknown tool calls trigger another iteration with the result appended so the model can self-correct. The loop is hard-capped at `MAX_TOOL_LOOP_ATTEMPTS = 8`; callers can tighten it per-flow via `maxAttempts`.

### Prompt caching

Stable context (skills, ingested docs, knowledge chunks) is marked with an Anthropic ephemeral `cache_control: { type: "ephemeral", ttl: "1h" }` breakpoint. Volatile context (user memory, prior failures, the current turn's messages) refreshes every call. The `llm.cache.hit_rate` metric (`llm_cache_hit_tokens_total` / `llm_prompt_tokens_total`) tracks reuse of stable blocks within the 1-hour window; the mock provider simulates the same accounting so tests can assert on cache behaviour.

### Tools for context

The assembler pre-loads Skills + docs + Knowledge chunks before every turn. On-demand retrieval uses four conversation tools, in precedence order:

| Order | Tool | Use |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `search_knowledge` | semantic search over tenant Knowledge Sources |
| 2 | `search_docs` | ranked search over a connector's ingested docs (OpenAPI/GraphQL/HTML/Markdown); hits carry a `match_type` (endpoint / auth / schema / text). Use when `search_knowledge` is empty and the answer is connector-specific |
| 3 | `fetch_connector_docs` | full doc overview for a connector |
| 4 | `web_search` | Anthropic-native server-side web search (billed per search; Claude models only). On by default; advisory escalation in `policies/web-search-escalation.ts`; gated per tenant by `llm.web_search` (toggle via /settings) |

### Self-healing retry

When drift is detected, the repair flow proposes a patch, classifies it, and dry-runs it against the most recent `execution_fixtures` row. If either gate rejects, the loop re-prompts the LLM with the structured rejection folded into `prior_failures`, up to `MAX_REPAIR_ATTEMPTS = 2` total. The final patch candidate carries a `metadata.rejection_chain` array recording every prior rejection, so reviewers see what was tried. Rate-limit-class drift (HTTP 429 / 503 with a template `rate_limits` hint) produces a distinct `kind: "rate_limited"` candidate — same retry loop, but the patch only adjusts backoff metadata.

---

## Diagnosis Is Part of Authoring

Execution is not the end of the loop. When a persisted workflow runs and produces warnings or a suspicious result, the conversation enters diagnosis mode instead of generic retry.

Diagnosis keeps the latest execution and its causal context attached to the draft summary:

| Field | Captures |
|---|---|
| `latest_execution` | exact persisted workflow id and version that ran |
| `diagnosis_available` | the latest run should be inspected before editing |
| `latest_diagnosis` | structured reason, warning sources, step-level summaries from the diagnosis pass |

This matters most for expression-heavy workflows. A run can technically succeed while carrying warnings such as unresolved identifiers in scope paths. The static verifier checks the step-id segment of a reference: a reference to a non-existent step — writing `$scope.wrong_step.data` when no `wrong_step` exists — is blocked before commit. It does not catch field-path mistakes on an existing step: writing `$scope.step.field` instead of `$scope.step.data.field` passes the static check and surfaces only as a runtime unresolved-identifier warning. For those, the right recovery is not "run it again" but "diagnose, repair the draft, preview again, commit again, then run again." Diagnosis is a first-class authoring phase, not an operator-only debugging escape hatch.

---

## Stage-Aware Prompting And Tool Narrowing

The loop constrains both prompt guidance and the visible authoring surface by mode and stage:

| Mode | Prompt focus | Visible surface |
|---|---|---|
| connector | Stay inside connector work until the connector is persisted | Connector actions |
| workflow | Inspection, validation, preview, commit | Workflow actions; commit only when checkpoints permit |
| execution / diagnosis | The latest persisted run and its repair path | Run + diagnosis actions |

Premature actions — connector save, workflow commit, diagnosis — only become visible when the relevant stage and checkpoint state permit them, rather than always-visible with runtime rejection. Prompt guidance, action visibility, and runtime gates all read from the same state model, which is why the flow stays consistent across turns.

---

## Multi-AI Provider

sk is not tied to a single AI model. It supports Claude (Anthropic), OpenAI GPT models, and Google Gemini. Providers are interchangeable — swapping models requires no changes to connectors, workflows, or skills.

| Property | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Routing | Best available provider by operator config and task type |
| Budgets | Token budgets enforced per tenant and per Conversation; operators set a monthly ceiling, consumption surfaces in the audit log |
| Runtime | The provider is an authoring-layer detail; a committed workflow runs with no AI involvement, regardless of which model authored it |

### OpenAI-compatible endpoints

The `openai` provider also drives any **OpenAI-compatible** endpoint — a self-hosted open-weight model, an internal gateway, or a third-party API speaking the OpenAI wire format. Point the slot at the endpoint:

```
llm.provider                  = openai
llm.providers.openai.base_url = https://llm.internal.example/v1   # your endpoint
llm.providers.openai.api_key  = <key>                             # sent as a Bearer token
llm.providers.openai.model    = <model-id>
llm.summarize_provider        = openai                            # optional
llm.summarize_model           = <fast-model-id>                   # optional
```

Two behaviours switch on automatically whenever `base_url` is non-empty, because a custom host typically implements only a subset of the OpenAI surface:

- **Transport.** Requests use `POST <base_url>/chat/completions` (Chat Completions), not the OpenAI Responses API.
- **Attachments.** The Files API upload path and audio/video inputs are disabled; files fall back to inline content or extracted text. Inline images and small documents still work.

Leaving `base_url` empty keeps the slot on real OpenAI with full Responses API and Files API behaviour. Structured-output authoring works on any tool-calling endpoint — it runs through a provider-agnostic tool loop rather than OpenAI-specific JSON-schema response formats.

> **Known limitation.** The attachment downgrade is a conservative default: it assumes an arbitrary custom endpoint serves text and inline images only. Some OpenAI-compatible servers (e.g. vLLM, SGLang) do serve vision/audio and a real Files API — there is currently no per-endpoint opt-back-in, so those richer capabilities aren't used on a custom `base_url`. A per-endpoint capability override is a tracked follow-up.

---

## Skills: Curated Context

The AI is only as useful as its context. Without organization-specific context it proposes generic workflows — not one that follows your GDPR handling policy, uses your Salesforce field mappings, or respects your API versioning conventions.

A Skill is a curated, reusable piece of context loaded into the AI's window during a Conversation and other AI-assisted flows (discovery, diagnosis, bounded repair). Skills encode best practices, integration patterns, security policies, and domain knowledge specific to your organization. When the AI proposes a workflow involving your Stripe connector, the Stripe Skill loads automatically — and the proposals reflect your conventions, not just generic Stripe API knowledge.

| Aspect | Rule |
|---|---|
| Ownership | Operators create and manage Skills |
| Scope | Global (all Conversations), per-Connector (loaded when referenced), or per-Workflow |
| Promotion | Not auto-generated, not auto-promoted; the platform surfaces Skill Candidates from execution history, a human promotes |

The platform learns from what works; humans decide what becomes canonical guidance.

---

## Knowledge Sources: Enterprise Documents

Skills are concise and curated. For document-scale context — runbooks, API specifications, compliance frameworks, architecture diagrams — sk provides Knowledge Sources.

A Knowledge Source is a persistent document store. Operators upload PDFs, runbooks, API specs, compliance documents, and diagrams; the platform chunks and indexes them for semantic search. During a Conversation, discovery pass, or diagnosis/repair loop, the AI searches them to ground its proposals. A workflow that correctly follows your GDPR compliance runbook is possible because the runbook is a searchable Knowledge Source.

When a document is uploaded interactively — from chat, an attached file, or `sk knowledge-sources create` — the AI auto-analyzes it to generate a short description and topical tags, making each source self-describing: the AI can list sources and decide which covers a topic before searching, and a search can be narrowed to a tag. The description is generated only when none was supplied; tags are a deduped set that re-analysis replaces wholesale. Auto-analysis is best-effort — if it fails (e.g. the model budget is exhausted) the upload still succeeds without enrichment. Re-run it anytime (`sk knowledge-sources analyze <id>`, or the `analyze_knowledge_source` tool in chat). Bulk paths — crawled pages, scheduled refreshes — stay mechanical and are not auto-analyzed.

Knowledge Sources have configurable refresh strategies — manual, scheduled, or webhook-triggered — and can be scoped to a tenant (global) or to specific workflows.

| | Skills | Knowledge Sources |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Dense, operator-authored guidance | Broader organizational artifacts |
| Treatment | Specific instructions the AI should follow | Searched for context, not prescriptive rules |

Committed workflow execution does not query Skills or Knowledge Sources. Those systems improve authoring and repair quality; the runtime path stays deterministic once a workflow is committed.

## Context Assembly And Trimming

For each AI-assisted turn, the engine assembles prompt context in a fixed order. Order matters twice — it shapes how the model sees context (top is most foundational) and how the trimmer drops it under pressure (top survives longest, bottom goes first):

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph build["Assembly order (top = first written)"]
        direction TB
        B1["1. Base prompt + runtime envelope<br/>(engine · tenant · actor · surface)"]
        B2["2. Auto-loaded Skills<br/>(global → connector → workflow)"]
        B3["3. Explicitly loaded Skills"]
        B4["4. Knowledge Source chunks"]
        B5["5. Connector documentation chunks"]
        B6["6. Prior failures for the current task"]
        B7["7. User memory + authoring-context blocks"]
        B8["8. Current turn history<br/>(user / assistant messages)"]
        B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4 --> B5 --> B6 --> B7 --> B8
    end
    Trim{{"Trim order (top = dropped first)"}}
    T1["failures → connector docs → knowledge<br/>→ user memory → authoring context<br/>→ explicit Skills → workflow Skills<br/>→ connector Skills → global Skills"]
    Note["User turns are never trimmed"]
    build --> Trim --> T1
    T1 -. preserved .- Note
```

This order is part of the contract. Operator-curated connector and workflow guidance survives longer than incidental historical context under tight budgets — so the AI's deep grounding in a tenant's own conventions is the *last* thing dropped, not the first.

Conversation replay is bounded: tool results are truncated before re-feeding into later turns, explicit compaction markers suppress older replay, and oversized histories collapse into a deterministic summary plus the recent tail. The model keeps the current task context without dragging every historical tool payload back through the window.

---

## The Connector Catalog

When a user names an external boundary — "pull from our Salesforce instance" or "post to Slack" — the AI needs connector-specific knowledge. Generic HTTP knowledge is not enough.

| Source | What it gives the AI |
|---|---|
| Connector Templates | A catalog covering common enterprise services — driver type, auth config, doc references, setup guidance. The AI understands the target API, not just the idea of it |
| Documentation Ingestion | OpenAPI specs, GraphQL schemas, and HTML docs are indexed and become context for that connector — specific endpoints, parameters, error codes |
| Credential Vault | Users never handle raw secrets; the AI proposes "use your Stripe connector" without seeing the key. Credentials are referenced by name, never by value |

---

## Discovery: From Files to Proposals

Discovery accelerates onboarding new systems. Rather than manually configuring every connector and skill, it starts from documentation that already exists.

An operator uploads files — API specs, data dictionaries, architecture diagrams, runbooks — and sk analyzes them into structured proposals. Each Discovery Artifact is a proposed Connector, Skill, or Knowledge Source, with a confidence score and links to the specific evidence in the uploaded files. The operator reviews each proposal and decides what to approve.

Nothing is automatically configured — the proposals are starting points, not decisions. Discovery is built for the scenarios enterprises actually hit: a new vendor relationship, an acquired company's systems, a newly discovered internal API. The goal is documentation into a working starting point in minutes rather than weeks, while keeping every configuration decision in human hands.

---

## How Authoring Improves Over Time

sk's authoring layer is not static — it improves as the platform accumulates execution history and operator feedback.

| Mechanism | Trigger | Output | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Skill Candidates** | Connectors / step sequences used together frequently and succeeding | A proposed Skill with confidence scores and links to supporting executions | Operator promotes or rejects |
| **Self-healing drift detection** | A connector's behavior diverges from what the workflow expects (endpoints move, fields shift, new error codes) | A Patch Candidate — the smallest safe change the AI can propose | Operator reviews before anything is applied |

The pattern is identical: the platform surfaces improvement proposals, humans make the decisions. The platform gets smarter over time, but only with human approval at each step.

---

## The sk-Stdlib In The Sandbox

Operator-authored JavaScript — transform steps with `language: "javascript"`, before-request hooks — runs inside a QuickJS-WASM sandbox with zero host globals. To keep that code concise, uniform, and reviewable, every context ships a curated `sk` global: a frozen, versioned, deterministic standard library.

The surface is intentionally small — the patterns that showed up repeatedly in real tenant code: HTTP-method classification, null-safe property access, allow/deny builders, common array reshapers, type guards.

| Instead of | Authors write |
|---|---|
| Maintaining a POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE list by hand | `sk.http.isMutating(method)` |
| Hand-coding `{ allow: false, reason }` | `sk.deny("reason")` |
| Chained null checks | `sk.get(input, "request.method", "")` |

Nothing in the stdlib touches the host — no `Date.now`, no `Math.random`, no I/O — so dry-runs stay reproducible and self-healing stays deterministic. The stdlib is versioned with semantic versioning: additive changes are minor bumps; signature or semantic changes are major bumps paired with a migration proposal. When the engine's stdlib version drifts past the major recorded on a persisted workflow, self-healing surfaces a Patch Candidate so operators can review the migration before anything runs.

The conversational layer is aware of the stdlib and proposes `sk.*` forms by default. Operators can still write raw comparisons in edge cases, but the stdlib form is the norm — it shortens review and keeps policy uniform across tenants.

- [glossary — authoring terms](../concepts/glossary.md#group-2-authoring) — Conversation, Draft, Skill, Skill Candidate, Knowledge Source, Discovery.
