# Custom Skills

> **Audience:** Authors and operators encoding organization-specific guidance for
> the AI.

**Outcome:** sk encodes your conventions once, then applies them on every
Conversation, discovery, and repair — so authored workflows ship faster, pass
review sooner, and stay policy-uniform across tenants. With approval, it gets
smarter over time.

A Skill is a curated, reusable piece of context loaded into the AI's context
window during a Conversation and other AI-assisted authoring flows (discovery,
diagnosis, bounded repair). Skills encode best practices, integration patterns,
security policies, and the domain knowledge that makes the AI propose *your*
conventions, not generic ones. For how Skills sit alongside Knowledge Sources and
how the engine assembles them into each turn, see
[Knowledge & Skills](../concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md).

## How a Skill reaches the AI

Three sources feed Skills; activation rules decide which load; the engine then
assembles the active set into the turn.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Sources
        M[Manual<br/>create_skill / CLI]
        T[Template<br/>seeded conventions]
        C[Skill Candidate<br/>promoted by operator]
    end

    subgraph Activation
        G[Global scope]
        CN[Connector scope]
        WF[Workflow scope]
    end

    M --> G
    T --> CN
    C --> WF
    M --> CN
    M --> WF

    G --> A[Active skill set]
    CN -->|Connector referenced| A
    WF -->|Authoring / repairing workflow| A

    A --> L[Context load<br/>into the turn]
    L --> AI([AI proposes your conventions])
```

| Source | Origin | Becomes active when |
|---|---|---|
| **Manual** | `create_skill` / `update_skill` in chat, or `sk skills create` | Its scope matches the turn |
| **Template** | Seeded conventions shipped with the platform | Its scope matches the turn |
| **Candidate** | Detected from execution history, **promoted by an operator** | Its scope matches the turn |

---

## Authoring and scoping a Skill

Operators create and manage Skills. They can be scoped:

| Scope | Loads when |
|---|---|
| **globally** | Available in all Conversations |
| **per-Connector** | That Connector is referenced (the Stripe Skill loads when the AI touches your Stripe connector) |
| **per-Workflow** | Authoring or repairing that workflow |

In chat you can author a Skill conversationally (`create_skill` / `update_skill`),
or manage them from the CLI:

```bash
sk skills list
sk skills create --file ./stripe-skill.json
```

The `--file` argument is a SkillDef JSON, not markdown. The SkillDef body carries
the `scope`, `connector_id`, and `title` — there are no separate `--title` or
`--scope` flags.

A Skill is dense, prescriptive guidance the AI should follow — keep each one tight and single-purpose. Broader, document-scale context belongs in a [Knowledge Source](./knowledge-sources.md) instead.

| Use a Skill when | Use a [Knowledge Source](./knowledge-sources.md) when |
|---|---|
| Guidance is prescriptive — "always do X" | Context is reference material to draw from |
| It fits in a tight, single-purpose page | It is document-scale |
| You want it followed, not just consulted | You want it available for lookup |

## Skill Candidates: learning from what works

Skills are not auto-generated and not auto-promoted. The platform detects recurring patterns from execution history — Connectors or step sequences that are used together frequently and tend to succeed — and surfaces them as **Skill Candidates** for operator review. Each candidate carries a confidence tier (low / medium / high) and links to the executions that support it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    E[Execution history] --> D{Recurring,<br/>successful pattern?}
    D -->|no| E
    D -->|yes| SC[Skill Candidate<br/>confidence tier + supporting executions]
    SC --> R{Operator review}
    R -->|reject| X[Discarded]
    R -->|promote| AS[Active Skill]
    AS --> CTX[Loaded into future turns]
    CTX --> E
```

A candidate becomes an active Skill only through explicit operator promotion:

```bash
sk skill-candidates list
sk skill-candidates approve <id>
```

sk learns from what works, but humans decide what becomes canonical guidance.

## The sk-Stdlib the AI proposes

JavaScript that authors write — transform steps with `language: "javascript"`, before-request hooks — runs inside a QuickJS-WASM sandbox with zero host globals. Every sandbox context ships a frozen, versioned, deterministic `sk` standard library (HTTP-method classification, null-safe access, allow/deny builders, array reshapers, type guards). The conversational authoring layer is aware of the stdlib and proposes `sk.*` forms by default — `sk.http.isMutating(method)`, `sk.deny("reason")`, `sk.get(input, "request.method", "")` — which shortens code review and keeps policy uniform across tenants. Nothing in the stdlib touches the host, so dry-runs and self-healing stay reproducible.

---

## Further reading

- [Knowledge & Skills](../concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md) — the conceptual model, context-assembly order, and the compounding loop.
- [Knowledge Sources](./knowledge-sources.md) — the broad-context counterpart.
- [AI-assisted authoring](./authoring-workflows.md) — how Conversations load and use Skills.

<!-- Source: docs/authors/knowledge-sources.md -->

# Knowledge Sources

> **Audience:** Authors and operators grounding the AI in their own documents.

**Outcome:** workflows follow *your* runbooks and compliance docs, not generic
knowledge. A workflow that correctly honors your GDPR retention rule exists
because the runbook is a Knowledge Source the AI searched while authoring — so
compliance ships by construction, not by review after the fact.

A Knowledge Source is a persistent, indexed document store the AI can search
while authoring, discovering, or repairing workflows. For the conceptual model —
and how Knowledge Sources differ from Skills — see
[Knowledge & Skills](../concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md).

## How grounding works

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    src[Your docs<br/>runbooks, policies, specs] --> ingest[Ingest<br/>upload, crawl, scheduled refresh]
    ingest --> chunk[Chunk<br/>split into searchable passages]
    chunk --> embed[Embed and index<br/>vectors + tags]
    embed --> search[Hybrid search<br/>semantic + tag filter]
    search --> ground[Grounds authoring<br/>follows your rules, not generic knowledge]
    ground --> wf[Authored / repaired workflow]
```

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| Ingest | Upload, crawl, or scheduled refresh pulls the document in. |
| Chunk | The text is split into searchable passages. |
| Embed + index | Passages become vectors; tags and descriptions are attached. |
| Hybrid search | Queries rank by semantic relevance, narrowed by tag. |
| Ground | Matched passages enter the authoring context so the workflow follows your rules. |

---

## Adding a source

In the REPL, say *"add this file as a knowledge source tagged weather, runbook"*.
The scriptable form:

```bash
sk knowledge-sources create --file ./runbook.md \
  --title "Weather Runbook" --tags "weather,runbook,open-meteo"
sk knowledge-sources list
sk knowledge-sources search "open-meteo"   # semantic search; ranks by relevance
```

| Flag | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `--tags` | Authoritative — no AI auto-tagging when you supply them. |
| `--description` | Authoritative when supplied. |
| (omit both) | The engine generates tags and a description. |

## Auto-analysis and self-description

When a document is uploaded interactively — from chat, an attached file, or
`sk knowledge-sources create` — the AI auto-analyzes its content to generate a
short description and a set of topical tags. This makes each source
self-describing: the AI can list sources and decide which one covers a topic
before searching, and a search can be narrowed to sources carrying a given tag.

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Description | Generated only when none was supplied. |
| Tags | A deduped set; re-analysis replaces them wholesale. |
| Failure mode | Best-effort — if it fails (e.g. model budget exhausted) the upload still succeeds, just without enrichment. |
| Re-run | `sk knowledge-sources analyze <id>`, or the `analyze_knowledge_source` tool in chat. |
| Bulk paths | Crawled pages and scheduled refreshes stay mechanical — not auto-analyzed. |

## Refresh strategies and scope

Knowledge Sources have configurable refresh strategies, so the AI always works
from current documentation. When a runbook is updated, the source refreshes and
the next workflow follows the new rule.

| Axis | Options |
|---|---|
| Refresh | Manual or scheduled. |
| Scope | Tenant-wide (available globally) or pinned to specific workflows. |

## Budgets

Per-source and per-tenant byte caps, per-message file counts, and ingestion
concurrency are operator-tunable. Defaults are conservative; raise them on
hardware that warrants larger corpora. The full tunable table lives in
[Observability & Resource Limits → Documentation & Knowledge Tunables](../operators/observability.md#documentation--knowledge-tunables).

---

## Further reading

- [Knowledge & Skills](../concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md) — the conceptual model and context-assembly order.
- [Custom Skills](./custom-skills.md) — the dense, prescriptive counterpart to Knowledge Sources.
- [AI-assisted authoring](./authoring-workflows.md) — how Conversations draw on Knowledge Sources.

<!-- Source: docs/authors/quickstart.md -->

# Quickstart — Authors

Turn a plain-language request into a governed, audited, runnable workflow — in about 5 minutes, no code. You describe the outcome; sk builds the connector, drafts the workflow, and holds the writes until you approve.

![sk REPL](../_tapes/out/repl-author.gif)

## Your first conversation

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor You
    participant sk
    You->>sk: Describe the outcome in plain language
    sk-->>You: Proposes a workflow (connector + steps)
    You->>sk: /preview
    sk-->>You: Dry-run result, no writes
    You->>sk: /approve
    sk-->>You: Commits a versioned workflow
    You->>sk: Run it
    sk-->>You: Audited execution + result
```

Every step is permission-checked and recorded. Nothing writes to a real system until you approve.

## Connect

Your operator has given you **one** of the following. Pick the matching path.

- **Engine URL + API key** — you operate a tenant directly → Path A.
- **Portal-token link** — you are a scoped end-user → Path B.
- **Slack / Teams / Google Chat** where the sk bot is installed → Path C.
- **An MCP client** (Claude Desktop, Cursor, …) → Path D.

> **Want to run your own engine first?** [Self-host quickstart](../developers/self-host.md) takes you from the Docker image to a first connector and workflow.

## Path A — CLI with API key

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mikebild/subkit/main/scripts/install.sh | bash
sk login --engine-url <URL> --api-key <wf_live_…>
sk                         # opens the TUI, picks up your session
```

## Path B — CLI with portal token

Portal tokens are time-limited and pre-scoped. Click the link your operator sent; it provisions a session for `sk` automatically.

```bash
sk login --portal-token <token>      # token is time-limited and pre-scoped; reusable until it expires or is revoked
sk
```

## Path C — Chat (Slack / Teams / Google Chat)

Nothing to install. In the workspace your operator set up:

- **Slack.** `@sk run <workflow>` or just `@sk …` to start a conversation.
- **Teams.** Same pattern — `@sk …` in a channel or DM.
- **Google Chat.** Invite the bot to a space; mention it.

See [input surfaces](../developers/input-surfaces.md) for how each chat adapter works.

## Path D — MCP client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.)

Add the engine as a streamable-HTTP MCP server:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sk": {
      "url": "https://<engine-host>/mcp",
      "transport": "streamable-http",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <key>" }
    }
  }
}
```

Your client discovers workflows, prompts, and resources automatically. See [input surfaces](../developers/input-surfaces.md) for MCP details.

## Troubleshooting

Any failed request prints `{code}: {message} [trace=…]`. Send the `trace_id` to your operator — they correlate it with `sk diagnostics errors --trace-id <trace_id>`.

## Next steps

- [input surfaces](../developers/input-surfaces.md) — every surface: CLI, REST, MCP, chat, webhooks, schedules.
- [authoring workflows](./authoring-workflows.md) — what Conversations can do: proposing workflows, Skills, Knowledge Sources, Discovery, and the approval gate.
- [REPL tour](./repl-tour.md) — the authoring state machine and slash commands end to end.

<!-- Source: docs/authors/recipes.md -->

# Recipe authoring

**Common automations start from a vetted blueprint, not a blank page.** A
recipe is a pre-authored workflow attached to a connector template. The LLM
clones one via `start_workflow_from_recipe(template_slug, recipe_slug)`
instead of synthesizing a workflow from scratch — collapsing a multi-turn
debugging spiral into a 30-second authoring loop.

This guide is the authoring contract: schema, conventions, quality gate, and
promotion checklist.

## How a recipe becomes a workflow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  intent["User intent<br/>plain language"] --> match["Recipe match<br/>intent_keywords rank"]
  match --> param["Parameterize<br/>sample_input + connector binding"]
  param --> wf["Runnable workflow<br/>cloned draft"]
```

| Stage | What happens | Author's lever |
|---|---|---|
| Intent | Operator describes an outcome in plain language. | — |
| Match | The LLM ranks the prompt against each recipe's keywords. | `intent_keywords` |
| Parameterize | The clone tool binds connectors and seeds the first dry-run. | `required_connectors`, `sample_input` |
| Workflow | A runnable draft lands, ready to preview, run, and commit. | `workflow` def |

## Where recipes live

Every recipe ships inline on its connector template.

| Concern | Location |
|---|---|
| Catalog | `apps/engine/src/connectors/templates.json` |
| Schema | `apps/engine/src/connectors/templates.ts` (`ConnectorRecipeSchema`) |
| Lint | `scripts/lint-recipes.ts` |

Recipes are read-only at runtime. Tenant-scoped per-recipe overrides are
planned via a `connector_recipes` table; today every operator sees the same
shipped catalog.

## Schema

| Field | Required | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `slug` | yes | — | unique within the template; lowercase-kebab |
| `title` | yes | — | human-readable; verb-led when there is an action |
| `description` | yes | — | one-paragraph summary; the LLM reads this in `inspect_recipe` |
| `intent_keywords[]` | yes | `[]` | 3-7 phrases the LLM ranks user prompts against |
| `derived_from_skill` | no | `null` | pointer to `template-skills.json` slug for skill-schema gating |
| `category` | yes | `"other"` | mirrors the connector category enum (`crm`, `payments`, `database`, etc.) |
| `tags[]` | no | `[]` | shape labels (`"webhook"`, `"daily-digest"`, `"notification"`) |
| `difficulty` | no | `"intermediate"` | `beginner` / `intermediate` / `advanced` |
| `estimated_setup_minutes` | no | `5` | time-to-first-save after cloning |
| `prerequisites[]` | no | `[]` | external setup the operator must have ready |
| `sample_input` | no | `null` | canonical JSON satisfying `workflow.input_schema` |
| `expected_output_preview` | no | `null` | redacted output example for `inspect_recipe` |
| `required_connectors[]` | no | `[]` | multi-connector binding (see below) |
| `version` | no | `"1.0.0"` | semver; bump on shape changes |
| `author` | no | `"subkit-builtin"` | provenance |
| `last_validated_at` | no | `null` | ISO date when last dry-run against vendor sandbox |
| `deprecated` | no | `null` | `{ since, replacement_slug }` when superseded |
| `workflow` | yes | — | full workflow validated through `WorkflowDefSchema` |

## Conventions

### `intent_keywords`

The lint script (`scripts/lint-recipes.ts`) enforces:

- **Length 3-7.** Fewer than 3 means the LLM has nothing to rank
  against; more than 7 inflates per-turn tokens for marginal lift.
- **Lowercased.** Matched lowercase against the user prompt.
- **No single-word duplicate of a title word.** "List GitHub issues" +
  keyword `"issues"` adds zero ranking signal — replace with `"list
  issues"` or `"open issues"`.

Good keywords describe the operator's *phrasing*, not the recipe's
mechanics: `"recent customers"`, `"who paid me last month"`. Bad
keywords describe the workflow shape: `"GET /v1/customers"`.

### `tags`

Free-form labels for ranking and pack assembly. Common tags:

- Trigger shape: `"webhook"`, `"schedule"`, `"request"`.
- Pattern: `"daily-digest"`, `"approval"`, `"sync"`, `"backfill"`,
  `"reverse-etl"`.
- Vertical: `"revops"`, `"customer-success"`, `"finance"`, `"devops"`,
  `"security"`.

Tags ARE matched by the recipe-pack endpoints (`GET
/v1/recipe-packs/{vertical}`); be deliberate.

### `sample_input`

When the recipe has an `input_schema` with required fields, lint enforces
that `sample_input` covers every required key. Keep the values realistic
(don't use `"foo"` / `"bar"`) — the LLM uses `sample_input` to populate
the cloned draft's first dry-run.

### `expected_output_preview`

Redact PII / secrets. Operators see this in `inspect_recipe` to confirm
a recipe matches intent before paying for `start_workflow_from_recipe`.

### Multi-connector recipes (`required_connectors`)

Recipes that span more than one connector declare each placeholder up
front:

```json
"required_connectors": [
  { "placeholder": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001", "template": "stripe" },
  { "placeholder": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002", "template": "slack" }
]
```

Inside `workflow.steps[*].connector_id`, use the placeholder UUID
matching the template the step targets.
`start_workflow_from_recipe` walks `required_connectors`, asks the
operator for one connector binding per placeholder, then deep-clones
the workflow with each placeholder rebound to a saved connector id.

Lint enforces that every declared placeholder appears at least once in
the workflow's steps.

### Single-connector recipes (the legacy path)

The legacy `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` placeholder still
works when `required_connectors` is empty — the clone tool's single
`connector_id` arg rebinds it. Use this for SQL / Postgres recipes
that cannot express the connector via a `base_url` placeholder.

## Walkthrough — request/response recipe (Stripe `create-customer`)

```json
{
  "slug": "create-customer",
  "title": "Create a Stripe customer",
  "description": "Create a customer with email + optional metadata. Returns the new customer id.",
  "intent_keywords": ["create customer", "new customer", "add stripe customer"],
  "derived_from_skill": "stripe-basics",
  "category": "payments",
  "tags": ["create"],
  "difficulty": "beginner",
  "estimated_setup_minutes": 3,
  "prerequisites": ["Stripe API key with `write` scope"],
  "sample_input": { "email": "billing@acme.test", "metadata": { "tier": "pro" } },
  "expected_output_preview": { "id": "cus_***", "email": "billing@acme.test" },
  "required_connectors": [],
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": "subkit-builtin",
  "last_validated_at": null,
  "deprecated": null,
  "workflow": {
    "name": "stripe-create-customer",
    "input_schema": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["email"],
      "properties": {
        "email": { "type": "string" },
        "metadata": { "type": "object" }
      }
    },
    "steps": [
      {
        "kind": "request",
        "id": "create",
        "method": "POST",
        "url": "${connector.stripe.base_url}/customers",
        "headers": { "content-type": "application/json" },
        "body": {
          "email": "${input.email}",
          "metadata": "${input.metadata}"
        },
        "idempotency_key": "${input.email}"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

## The `trigger` block

`workflow.trigger` is a discriminated union over `kind`. Omitting it is
equivalent to `{ "kind": "request" }`.

| `kind` | On save | Self-contained |
|---|---|---|
| `request` | nothing extra | runs on demand |
| `webhook` | reverse-binds an inbound binding | no webhook-registration step |
| `schedule` | reverse-binds a cron schedule | no `sk schedule create` |

`webhook` and `schedule` bindings are removed on delete or version rotate, so
the recipe stays self-contained.

The schema source of truth is
[`apps/engine/src/workflows/types.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/workflows/types.ts)
(`RequestTriggerSchema`, `WebhookTriggerSchema`, `ScheduleTriggerSchema`);
runtime semantics are documented in
[`docs/concepts/workflows.md`](../concepts/workflows.md#triggers).

When you author a webhook or schedule recipe, tag it with
`"trigger:webhook"` or `"trigger:schedule"` so the recipe-pack endpoints
can group it correctly.

## Walkthrough — webhook-triggered recipe (Stripe `charge.failed` → Slack)

This is the shipped `stripe.on-charge-failed-notify-slack` recipe (from
`apps/engine/src/connectors/templates.json`). It reverse-binds an inbound
binding on save: when Stripe posts `charge.failed` to the workflow's
inbound URL, the engine verifies the Stripe signature, extracts the
failed-charge fields, and posts a redacted alert into the operator's
Slack channel.

```json
{
  "slug": "on-charge-failed-notify-slack",
  "title": "On Stripe charge.failed, post a Slack alert",
  "description": "Webhook-triggered: when Stripe fires `charge.failed` against the workflow's inbound URL, this recipe verifies the Stripe signature, extracts the failed-charge fields (id, amount, currency, decline reason, customer email), and posts a redacted alert into the operator's chosen Slack channel. Demonstrates the workflow `trigger: { kind: 'webhook' }` block end-to-end.",
  "intent_keywords": [
    "charge failed slack",
    "stripe failure alert",
    "notify slack on failed charge",
    "stripe webhook alert"
  ],
  "derived_from_skill": "stripe-basics",
  "category": "payments",
  "tags": ["webhook", "trigger", "alerting", "demonstration"],
  "difficulty": "advanced",
  "estimated_setup_minutes": 12,
  "prerequisites": [
    "Stripe webhook endpoint signing secret (whsec_...) configured on the bound webhook row",
    "Slack bot token connector with chat:write scope",
    "Slack channel id where the alert should land"
  ],
  "required_connectors": [
    { "placeholder": "7d046f2e-9c40-4b8a-aa14-ff3eb87b5046", "template": "slack" }
  ],
  "workflow": {
    "name": "stripe-on-charge-failed-notify-slack",
    "description": "Triggered by an inbound Stripe `charge.failed` webhook; posts a redacted alert into the operator's Slack channel.",
    "trigger": {
      "kind": "webhook",
      "source": "stripe",
      "events": ["charge.failed"],
      "verify": "stripe-signature"
    },
    "input_schema": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["body", "alert_channel"],
      "properties": {
        "body": { "type": "object", "required": ["data", "type"] },
        "alert_channel": {
          "type": "string",
          "description": "Slack channel id (e.g. C0123ALERT) where the alert should be posted."
        }
      }
    },
    "steps": [
      {
        "kind": "transform",
        "id": "extract",
        "language": "javascript",
        "expression": "const o = input.input.body.data.object; return { charge_id: o.id, amount: o.amount, currency: o.currency, failure_code: o.failure_code, failure_message: o.failure_message, email: o.billing_details.email };"
      },
      {
        "kind": "request",
        "id": "post",
        "method": "POST",
        "connector_id": "7d046f2e-9c40-4b8a-aa14-ff3eb87b5046",
        "url": "${connector.slack.base_url}/chat.postMessage",
        "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json; charset=utf-8" },
        "body": {
          "channel": "${input.alert_channel}",
          "text": "[stripe] charge.failed — ${scope.extract.data.currency} ${scope.extract.data.amount} — ${scope.extract.data.failure_code} — ${scope.extract.data.email} — ${scope.extract.data.charge_id}"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Notes for authors:

- `verify: "stripe-signature"` requires the inbound binding to carry the
  `whsec_...` signing secret. The driver rejects unsigned or
  signature-mismatched posts before any step runs.
- `events: ["charge.failed"]` filters at the inbound driver, so noisy
  events never reach `runExecution()`. Use `[]` only when the workflow
  legitimately needs every event from `source`.
- The `input_schema` documents what the engine guarantees the workflow
  scope holds at step time — `body` is the verified Stripe payload and
  `alert_channel` is the per-tenant Slack channel id supplied at bind
  time.

## Walkthrough — schedule-triggered recipe (daily charges digest)

This is the shipped `stripe.daily-charges-digest` recipe. Saving it
upserts a `workflows_schedules` row keyed on `(tenant_id, workflow_id)`;
the scheduler reconciler wakes the workflow up at 08:00 Europe/Berlin on
business days and skips the listed German bank holidays for 2026. No
external cron, no `sk run` loop.

```json
{
  "slug": "daily-charges-digest",
  "title": "Daily charges digest (08:00 Europe/Berlin, business days only)",
  "description": "Pull yesterday's charges every business day at 08:00 Europe/Berlin and summarise total volume + count by currency. Skips weekends and the dates listed in `skip_dates` (German bank holidays seeded for 2026). Wired through the schedule trigger so the workflow wakes itself up — no external cron, no `sk run` loop.",
  "intent_keywords": [
    "daily charges digest",
    "scheduled charges report",
    "yesterday charges",
    "daily revenue summary"
  ],
  "derived_from_skill": "stripe-basics",
  "category": "payments",
  "tags": ["scheduled", "trigger:schedule", "digest"],
  "difficulty": "intermediate",
  "estimated_setup_minutes": 8,
  "prerequisites": [
    "Stripe connector with read access to /v1/charges",
    "Schedule trigger requires the engine's scheduler reconciler to be running"
  ],
  "required_connectors": [],
  "workflow": {
    "name": "stripe-daily-charges-digest",
    "description": "Pull yesterday's charges and summarise by currency. Wakes itself up at 08:00 Europe/Berlin every business day.",
    "trigger": {
      "kind": "schedule",
      "cron": "0 8 * * *",
      "tz": "Europe/Berlin",
      "business_days_only": true,
      "skip_dates": [
        "2026-01-01",
        "2026-04-03",
        "2026-04-06",
        "2026-05-01",
        "2026-05-14",
        "2026-05-25",
        "2026-10-03",
        "2026-12-25",
        "2026-12-26"
      ]
    },
    "steps": [
      {
        "kind": "request",
        "id": "list",
        "method": "GET",
        "url": "${connector.stripe.base_url}/charges",
        "query": { "limit": 100 },
        "pagination": {
          "strategy": "cursor",
          "cursor_request_param": "starting_after",
          "cursor_response_path": "data[last].id",
          "page_size": 100
        }
      },
      {
        "kind": "transform",
        "id": "summary",
        "language": "javascript",
        "expression": "const charges = input.scope.list.data.body.data; const byCurrency = {}; for (const c of charges) { const g = (byCurrency[c.currency] ??= { count: 0, amount_total: 0 }); g.count += 1; g.amount_total += c.amount; } return { count: charges.length, by_currency: byCurrency };"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Notes for authors:

- `cron` is the standard 5-field expression (`m h dom mon dow`); the
  reconciler also accepts the engine's `every:N` shorthand for sub-minute
  cadences.
- `tz` must be a valid IANA timezone — the reconciler hands it to
  pg-boss so the firing lands at the operator's local wall-clock time
  instead of UTC.
- `business_days_only` skips weekends. Holiday calendars are NOT
  inferred — declare every freeze date explicitly via `skip_dates`. The
  reconciler compares each entry against the trigger's `tz` so a date
  here means "this calendar day in the workflow's timezone".
- A schedule recipe typically has `sample_input: null` because the
  scheduler itself supplies no payload — the workflow reads its inputs
  from the connectors it queries.

## Walkthrough — auth-chain recipe (mint then use)

This is the shipped `firebase.signin-email-password-then-firestore-read`
recipe. It demonstrates the canonical *mint then use* shape for any
non-OAuth2 username/password JWT flow — Firebase Auth REST, Cognito
InitiateAuth (when not handled by the connector's OAuth2 grant),
generic POST `/login` endpoints, etc. Two patterns are load-bearing:
**redacted secret outputs** and **dot-path scope substitution** in
downstream headers.

```json
{
  "slug": "signin-email-password-then-firestore-read",
  "workflow": {
    "name": "firebase-signin-email-password-then-firestore-read",
    "steps": [
      {
        "kind": "request",
        "id": "signin",
        "method": "POST",
        "url": "https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com/v1/accounts:signInWithPassword",
        "query": { "key": "${input.api_key}" },
        "body": {
          "email": "${input.email}",
          "password": "${input.password}",
          "returnSecureToken": true
        },
        "outputs": {
          "idToken": { "secret": true },
          "refreshToken": { "secret": true }
        }
      },
      {
        "kind": "request",
        "id": "read_document",
        "method": "GET",
        "url": "https://firestore.googleapis.com/v1/projects/${input.project_id}/databases/(default)/documents/${input.collection}/${input.document_id}",
        "headers": {
          "Authorization": "Bearer ${scope.signin.idToken}"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Notes for authors:

- **`outputs.<path>.secret = true`** marks the field for redaction in
  audit log, step preview, and offload — but the raw value stays in the
  in-memory scope so downstream steps can still substitute it. Reach for
  this on every minted token (`idToken`, `access_token`,
  `AuthenticationResult.IdToken`, `AssumeRoleResult.Credentials.SessionToken`).
- **`${scope.<step_id>.<dot.path>}`** is dot-notation, NOT JSON-pointer.
  Nested paths work transparently:
  `${scope.signin.idToken}` (top-level) and
  `${scope.assume.AssumeRoleResult.Credentials.AccessKeyId}` (nested) both
  resolve via repeated property lookup.
- The first step has no `connector_id` substitution because the auth API
  lives at a fixed URL distinct from the protected resource. Use the
  hard-coded URL in step 1 and `${connector.<slug>.base_url}` (or another
  hard-coded URL) in step 2.
- When the protected resource API is reachable via a connector with an
  existing auth mode (`oauth2` Authorization Code, `oauth2` Password
  Grant, `aws_sigv4`, `bearer`, etc.), prefer that mode over a hand-wired
  two-step chain — the connector's `refreshIfStale()` handles minting
  transparently and the workflow stays single-step. Use this two-step
  pattern only when no built-in auth mode fits the provider's flow.

## Quality gate

Every recipe-touching PR runs:

```sh
bun run lint:recipes        # recipe lint
bun run test:unit           # includes apps/engine/src/connectors/recipes.test.ts
bun run verify:ai           # includes recipe-discovery validator
```

`lint-recipes` enforces:

- `category` is set and a member of `RecipeCategoryEnum`.
- `intent_keywords` is 3-7, lowercase, no title-word duplicates.
- `sample_input` covers `input_schema.required` when both are set.
- `required_connectors` placeholders all appear in `workflow.steps`.
- Per-primitive coverage of `WorkflowDefSchema` step kinds (catches
  regressions when a previously-demonstrated primitive drops to zero
  recipes).

## Promotion checklist

Before opening a PR:

1. Recipe loads through `loadBuiltinTemplates()` without throwing.
2. `bun run lint:recipes` is green.
3. `intent_keywords` reflects how the operator would phrase the
   request, not the workflow's mechanics.
4. `sample_input` is realistic (no `"foo"` / `"bar"` placeholders).
5. If the recipe was dry-run against a vendor sandbox, set
   `last_validated_at` to today's ISO date.
6. If you are deprecating an existing recipe, set `deprecated` rather
   than deleting the slug — operators may have cloned drafts that
   reference it.
7. PR description names the operator pain the recipe solves. The
   recipe must beat any industry equivalent on validation,
   prerequisites clarity, or step efficiency — not just match.

## Related

- `docs/concepts/connectors.md` — connector templates (parent surface).
- `apps/engine/src/connectors/AGENTS.md` — connector subsystem rules.
- `scripts/lint-recipes.ts` — quality lint source.

# Using the `sk` REPL — authoring by conversation

**Go from idea to a governed, versioned workflow in minutes** — no JSON, no
glue code. Describe the outcome in plain language; the AI proposes a connector
or workflow, previews a real result, and only commits when you approve. Every
saved artifact is permission-checked, audited, and replayable.

![sk REPL](../_tapes/out/repl-author.gif)

This guide assumes you are already authenticated (see
[zero-to-running](../developers/self-host.md), Steps 1–2). Everything below also works
inside the container as `docker exec -it subkit sk …`.

---

## The authoring state machine

One conversation, one gate. The AI iterates on a draft as long as you want;
**approval is the only path to a saved, runnable workflow.**

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Describing
    Describing --> Proposing: AI has enough to draft
    Proposing --> Previewing: dry-run the draft
    Previewing --> Proposing: revise (reject / "change X")
    Previewing --> Committed: /approve
    Committed --> Running: sk workflows run
    Committed --> [*]
    Running --> [*]

    note right of Proposing
        AI proposes — nothing is
        saved or executed yet
    end note
    note right of Committed
        Versioned resource:
        audited, permission-checked,
        replayable
    end note
```

---

## Start a conversation

```bash
sk                      # opens the interactive REPL
sk "current weather in Berlin"   # opens the REPL with a first message
sk -c                   # continue your most recent conversation
sk -r <conversation-id> # resume a specific one
```

You type in natural language. The AI replies, and — when it has enough — it
**proposes** a connector or workflow as a structured draft. Nothing is saved or
executed until you approve.

---

## The authoring loop (what actually happens)

```
You    ▸ get the current temperature in Berlin
AI     ▸ I'll use the open-meteo connector (keyless). Here's the workflow I propose:
         1. request  GET /v1/forecast?latitude=52.52&longitude=13.41&current=temperature_2m
         2. transform extract { city, time, temperature_c }
         (shows the draft + a dry-run preview result: 21.4 °C)
         Approve to save this as a workflow?
You    ▸ /approve
AI     ▸ Saved workflow "berlin-current-temperature" (v1). Run it with: sk workflows run berlin-current-temperature
```

Key properties:

- **AI proposes, you approve.** The AI never commits a workflow or runs it in
  production on its own — approval is the governance gate.
- **Preview before save.** The proposal includes a dry-run so you see a real
  result before committing.
- **Iterate in place.** Reject or just say what to change (“also return
  windspeed”, “use Munich instead”) and the AI revises the draft.

---

## Slash commands

Type `/` for the live menu. The shipped commands:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/approve` | Approve the AI's current proposal (commit the draft). |
| `/reject` | Reject the proposal (optionally with a reason); the AI revises. |
| `/preview` | Dry-run the current workflow draft now (`/preview show` for the last result). |
| `/probe` | Test the current connector draft now (`/probe show` for the last result). |
| `/draft` · `/connector` · `/workflow` | Inspect the current authoring state. |
| `/templates` | Browse connector templates suggested for the draft. |
| `/onboard` | Guided wizard: pick a template, enter credentials, probe, save. |
| `/versions` · `/restore <n>` | List committed workflow versions / roll back to one. |
| `/skills` · `/knowledge` | List reusable Skills / knowledge sources in scope. |
| `/clear` (`/new`) · `/compact` · `/resume` | New conversation · shrink history · reattach. |
| `/setup` · `/status` · `/cost` · `/usage` | Readiness · session+persona · budget · token usage. |
| `/config` | Open the searchable Config tab (every engine setting). |
| `/settings` (`/preferences`) | Open the 5-tab settings palette (Status / Config / Usage / Skills / Knowledge). |
| `/model` · `/tenant` · `/login` · `/logout` | Switch model · switch/list tenants · auth. |
| `/attach` · `/upload` · `/files` | Attach a file to the message · upload · list files. |
| `/yolo` | Lift the destructive-action confirm gate for a few turns (typed `yes`). |
| `/help` · `/exit` (`/quit`) | Cheat sheet · leave the REPL. |

## Mentions & attachments

- `@file:<id>` — attach a previously uploaded file to the message.
- `@skill:<name>` — pull a specific Skill into context.
- Attach files when launching headless: `sk -p "build a connector from this" --attach ./openapi.json`.

---

## Example conversations to try

```
create a connector for the open-meteo forecast API (https://api.open-meteo.com), no auth
```
```
make a workflow that returns tomorrow's high and low for a city I pass as input
```
```
add a knowledge article from ./runbook.md tagged ops,weather
```
```
run berlin-current-temperature and show me the result
```

After `/approve`, the artifact is a normal, versioned resource — manage it with
the non-conversational commands (`sk workflows …`, `sk connectors …`,
`sk executions …`) or from your own machine over the API.

---

## Headless = the same loop, scripted

For CI or one-liners, `-p` runs one prompt non-interactively through the **same**
authoring engine (no TTY, no slash commands — the AI completes autonomously up to
`--max-turns`):

```bash
sk -p "create a workflow that returns the current temperature in Berlin using the open-meteo connector" \
   --output text --max-turns 40
sk -p "list my workflows" --output json
```

`--output {text|json|stream-json}` controls the shape; non-zero exit codes signal
failure so scripts can branch reliably.

<!-- generated by scripts/gen-sk-settings-doc.ts — do not edit by hand -->

# sk settings

Settings for the `sk` CLI itself — separate from the engine's runtime
settings (see [settings-reference](../admins/settings-reference.md)).
Open the in-REPL palette with `/settings`.

## Files

`sk` reads two files under `~/.sk`, plus per-project overlays:

| file | purpose |
| ---- | ------- |
| `~/.sk/settings.json` | User settings (the `SkSettings` shape below). |
| `~/.sk/config.json` | Multi-profile auth/connection config (the `SkConfig` shape below). |
| `<repo>/.sk/settings.json` | Project settings, walked upward from the cwd. |
| `<cwd>/.sk/settings.local.json` | Local, git-ignored overrides (highest precedence). |

Settings merge later-wins in that order. `config.json` is written with
`0600` permissions because it holds the API key.

## Settings (`~/.sk/settings.json`)

| field | type | default | description |
| ----- | ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| `model` | string | — | Default model id for new conversations. |
| `defaultTenant` | string | — | Tenant id used when no `--tenant` / profile tenant is set. |
| `additionalDirectories` | string[] | — | Extra directories the session may read files from. |
| `mcpServers` | Record<string, { url?, command?, args? }> | — | External MCP servers to surface inside the session. |
| `includeMemoryFile` | boolean | `true` | Inject `SK.md` into each session. |
| `maxInlineMentionBytes` | number | `262144` | Max bytes inlined when an `@mention` expands a file. |
| `headless.maxTurns` | number | — | Cap on model/tool steps for one `sk -p` headless turn. |
| `headless.maxBudgetTokens` | number | — | Token budget ceiling for a headless turn. |
| `nextCommandPreviewEnabled` | boolean | `true` | Show the engine's next-message ghost-text preview after each turn. |

### Status line (`statusLine`)

Provide `command` to drive the line from a shell hook, or `format` for a
local template. The boolean/`refreshMs` fields tune the built-in line.

| field | type | default | description |
| ----- | ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| `statusLine.command` | string | — | Shell command run per refresh; receives `StatusLineInput` JSON on stdin, its stdout becomes the line. |
| `statusLine.format` | string | — | Local template rendered when `command` is absent (placeholders below). |
| `statusLine.showCost` | boolean | `false` | Show cost in the default line. |
| `statusLine.showTokens` | boolean | `true` | Show token counters in the default line. |
| `statusLine.showPersona` | boolean | `true` | Show the resolved persona in the default line. |
| `statusLine.refreshMs` | number | `500` | Minimum milliseconds between status-line rebuilds. |

#### `statusLine.format` placeholders

Unknown placeholders expand to an empty string.

| placeholder | meaning |
| ----------- | ------- |
| `{persona}` | Resolved persona (admin / operator / member / enduser / portal). |
| `{tenant}` | Active tenant id. |
| `{model}` | Model id for the active conversation. |
| `{engine_url}` | Engine base URL. |
| `{session_id}` | Active conversation id. |
| `{turn_tokens}` | Tokens spent on the most recent turn. |
| `{remaining_tokens}` | Tokens left in the budget. |
| `{cwd}` | Current working directory. |
| `{git_branch}` | Current git branch. |

## Profiles (`~/.sk/config.json`)

`SkConfig` holds an `active_profile` (default `"default"`) and a
`profiles` map. Each `Profile` carries:

| field | type | default | description |
| ----- | ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| `engine_url` | string | `"http://localhost:3000"` | Engine base URL for this profile. |
| `api_key` | string | — | Bearer API key (omitted when signed out). |
| `active_tenant_id` | string \| null | `null` | Tenant selected for this profile. |
| `persona_hint` | enum("admin","operator","member","enduser","portal") | — | Cached persona for status-line rendering; re-probed via RBAC on startup. |
| `portal_locked` | boolean | — | True for profiles authenticated via a portal token. |
| `notification_inbox_cursor` | number | — | Highest notification-inbox row id this profile has paged. |

Profile resolution precedence (later loses): CLI flags
(`--engine-url`, `--api-key`, `--tenant`, `--profile`) → env
(`SUBKIT_ENGINE_URL`, `SUBKIT_API_KEY`, `SUBKIT_TENANT`,
`SUBKIT_PROFILE` / `SK_PROFILE`) → on-disk profile fields → defaults.

# Slash commands

Slash commands run from the `sk` REPL. Type `/` to open the fuzzy
picker, or `/help` for the persona-filtered cheat sheet. A command
with a `requires` permission is hidden from any persona that cannot
invoke it — the engine still enforces the permission on every call,
so this column is the UX gate, not the security boundary.

## Session

| command | aliases | requires | description |
| ------- | ------- | -------- | ----------- |
| `/approvals` | — | `conversation:read` | Show approval history for the active conversation |
| `/approve` | — | `conversation:approve` | Approve a pending request_human_approval |
| `/clear` | `/new` | `conversation:write` | Start a new conversation |
| `/compact` | — | `conversation:write` | Compact the message history |
| `/connector` | — | `conversation:read` | Inspect the current connector draft |
| `/draft` | — | `conversation:read` | Inspect the current connector/workflow authoring state |
| `/fork` | — | `conversation:write` | Fork the current session into a new conversation |
| `/model` | — | `conversation:write` | Switch the conversation's model |
| `/onboard` | `/install` | `connector:write` | Launch an interactive onboarding wizard — pick a template, enter credentials, probe, save |
| `/policy` | — | `conversation:write` | List tool execution-mode badges, or pin a per-tool override. `/policy` lists; `/policy <tool> <auto\|ask\|review>` sets; `/policy <tool> reset` clears. |
| `/preview` | — | `conversation:write` | Bare `/preview` runs now; `/preview show` inspects the last result; `/preview run` is the explicit action form |
| `/probe` | — | `conversation:write` | Bare `/probe` runs now; `/probe show` inspects the last result; `/probe run` is the explicit action form |
| `/reject` | — | `conversation:approve` | Reject a pending approval (with optional reason) |
| `/rename` | — | `conversation:write` | Rename the current session — `/rename <new-title>` |

| `/workflow` | — | `conversation:read` | Inspect the current workflow draft |
| `/yolo` | — | `conversation:write` | Arm yolo mode — lifts the destructive-action confirmation gate (typed `yes` confirmation; auto-disarms after 10 turns / 10 min). `/yolo off` disarms now. |

# Developers

**Integrate, extend, and self-host sk — without forking security per surface.** Everything here gets you from a clone to a running engine, a green quality gate, and a workflow reachable from the CLI, REST, MCP, or your own infra.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[quickstart.md] --> SH[self-host.md]
    SH --> IS[input-surfaces.md]
    IS --> TP[tool-palette.md]
    IS --> CLI[cli-reference.md]
    TP --> EP[evidence-process.md]
```

Start with **quickstart** for a green gate locally, then **self-host** to stand up your own engine. **input-surfaces** maps the doors in (CLI, REST, MCP), with **cli-reference** and **tool-palette** as the per-surface detail. **evidence-process** is the bar for changing LLM-driven paths.

| Page | What it covers | Link |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quickstart — Developer | Clone to a passing test suite and a live engine in ~10 minutes. | [quickstart.md](quickstart.md) |
| Quickstart — Zero to Running | Self-host the engine in your own infra with PostgreSQL, no SaaS lock-in. | [self-host.md](self-host.md) |
| Input Surfaces | The doors into the engine — CLI, REST, MCP, webhooks — over one RBAC and Audit model. | [input-surfaces.md](input-surfaces.md) |
| sk CLI reference | Non-interactive `sk` commands for scripting and CI. | [cli-reference.md](cli-reference.md) |
| Tool palette and dispatch | Every LLM action as a named, governed, audited tool. | [tool-palette.md](tool-palette.md) |
| Evidence process | Verifying a behavioral / LLM-path change with proof, not guesses. | [evidence-process.md](evidence-process.md) |
