# sk CLI reference

Non-interactive commands for the `sk` CLI. Running bare `sk` opens the
interactive REPL; every command below is scriptable and prints to
stdout. Pass `--help` to any command (e.g. `sk workflows --help`) for
its flags and subcommand usage.

The `requires` column is the persona-aware *visibility* gate used for
`--help` filtering — the engine independently enforces permissions on
every API call.

| command | requires | description | subcommands |
| ------- | -------- | ----------- | ----------- |
| `sk apikeys` | `api_key:read` | Manage API keys | `create`, `list`, `revoke`, `rotate` |
| `sk attach` | `file:write` | Upload a file and link it to a conversation (shortcut) | — |
| `sk audit` | `audit:read` | Query the append-only audit log | `export`, `query`, `show`, `tail` |
| `sk auth` | `connector:write` | Start a reauthentication flow for a connector (OAuth2 authorize URL) | — |
| `sk connector-templates` | `connector:read` | Manage connector templates | `create`, `delete`, `list`, `recipe`, `recipe-pack`, `recipes`, `search`, `set-oauth` |
| `sk connectors` | `connector:read` | Manage connectors | `create`, `delete`, `docs-delete`, `docs-ingest`, `docs-list`, `docs-search`, `get`, `inspect`, `list`, `patch`, `probe`, `test` |
| `sk credentials` | `credential:read` | Manage connector credentials | `delete`, `list`, `rotate`, `set` |
| `sk diagnostics` | `audit:read` | Engine diagnostics: errors, LLM status, setup validation | `errors`, `llm`, `setup` |
| `sk discovery` | `discovery:read` | Manage discovery runs and artifacts | `approve`, `artifacts`, `create`, `get`, `list`, `reject` |
| `sk doctor` | — | Diagnose engine connectivity, authentication, and setup. Exits 0 (ok or warn) or 2 (blocked). | — |
| `sk events` | `audit:read` | Query audit events | `get`, `list` |
| `sk executions` | `execution:read` | Manage workflow executions | `abort`, `get`, `list`, `rerun`, `result`, `steps`, `tail` |
| `sk extract` | `conversation:write` | Extract structured data from a file (LLM for text, native parsers for binary) | — |
| `sk files` | `file:read` | Manage files (upload, download, link, …) | `delete`, `download`, `get`, `link`, `list`, `stats`, `upload` |
| `sk health` | — | Runtime posture: liveness, token budget, failing runs, risk signals, schema drift, and process runtime. Use `sk doctor` for connectivity/setup. | — |
| `sk hooks` | `inbound_hook:read` | Manage inbound webhook bindings | `create`, `delete`, `get`, `list` |
| `sk init` | — | Complete first-run engine bootstrap (consumes the token printed at engine boot) | — |
| `sk install` | `connector:write` | Guided setup for enterprise integrations | `github`, `google-workspace`, `hubspot`, `jira`, `salesforce`, `slack`, `teams` |
| `sk invites` | `identity:read` | Manage user-provisioning invites | `list`, `revoke` |
| `sk join` | — | Redeem an invite to provision your personal API key (no login required) | — |
| `sk knowledge-sources` | `knowledge:read` | Manage knowledge sources | `analyze`, `create`, `delete`, `get`, `list`, `patch`, `search` |
| `sk login` | — | Authenticate against a subkit engine | — |
| `sk logout` | — | Drop the active profile | — |
| `sk logs` | `audit:read` | Tail the engine's runtime log ring. --follow streams via SSE; --since accepts 5m / 2h / 1d / ISO-8601. | — |
| `sk ls` | — | List cached conversation sessions for the active profile | — |
| `sk mcp` | — | Run a stdio MCP server proxied to the engine | — |
| `sk mcp-servers` | `mcp_server:manage` | Manage external MCP servers | `add`, `authorize`, `disable`, `enable`, `get`, `inspect`, `list`, `remove`, `set-credential` |
| `sk notifications` | `notification:read` | Manage notification channels, rules, deliveries, and the inbox | `channels`, `deliveries`, `inbox`, `rules` |
| `sk patch-candidates` | `workflow:read` | Manage patch candidates | `approve`, `get`, `list`, `reject` |
| `sk portal-tokens` | `portal_token:read` | Manage portal tokens | `create`, `list`, `revoke` |
| `sk profile` | — | Manage named profiles (environments) | `add`, `delete`, `list`, `show`, `use` |
| `sk rbac` | `rbac:read` | Manage RBAC roles, permissions, grants, groups, and hooks | `can`, `grants`, `groups`, `permissions`, `request-hooks`, `roles`, `users`, `whatcan` |
| `sk rename` | — | Assign or change a short alias for a session (used by `sk -r <alias>`) | — |
| `sk review` | `workflow:read` | Aggregated approval digest: pending patch candidates, proposed skill candidates, and recent failed executions. | — |
| `sk rm` | — | Drop a session from the local cache (the server-side conversation row is preserved) | — |
| `sk schedules` | `workflow:read` | Scheduled workflow runs | `list` |
| `sk self-healing` | `workflow:write` | Trigger and review proactive drift scans (admin) | `list`, `scan`, `show` |
| `sk sessions` | — | Manage locally-cached conversation sessions | `ls`, `rename`, `rm`, `search`, `show` |
| `sk settings` | `settings:read` | List, read, write, or interactively configure engine settings (secrets always masked) | `configure`, `get`, `list`, `set` |
| `sk show` | — | Show cached metadata for a session by id or alias | — |
| `sk skill-candidates` | `skill:read` | Manage skill candidates | `approve`, `get`, `list`, `reject` |
| `sk skills` | `skill:read` | Manage skills | `activate`, `archive`, `create`, `delete`, `edit`, `get`, `history`, `list`, `patch`, `restore` |
| `sk stats` | `stats:read` | Tenant-scoped runtime statistics (needs stats:read) | `connectors`, `events`, `executions`, `llm` |
| `sk status` | — | Print the active profile + engine reachability | — |
| `sk subscriptions` | `subscription:read` | Manage event subscriptions | `create`, `delete`, `deliveries`, `get`, `list`, `patch`, `replay` |
| `sk system-accounts` | `identity:read` | Manage system accounts | `create`, `delete`, `list` |
| `sk tenants` | — | List tenants you belong to or switch the active one | — |
| `sk update` | — | Update sk CLI to the latest version | — |
| `sk users` | `identity:read` | Manage identity users | `create`, `delete`, `get`, `invite`, `list`, `patch` |
| `sk workflows` | `workflow:read` | Manage workflows | `create`, `delete`, `dry-run`, `get`, `history`, `invoke-snippet`, `list`, `preview`, `restore`, `run`, `validate` |

<!-- Source: docs/developers/evidence-process.md -->

# Evidence process — verifying a behavioral / LLM-path change

**Outcome:** changes to LLM-driven paths ship proven, not guessed. Every claim
that a metric moved is backed by a test or benchmark run — so reviewers spend
their time on the diagnosis, not on re-verifying the author's intuition.

This is the discipline behind the format-aware-judge work, where it caught a
confident wrong self-diagnosis mid-flight (see [Worked example](#worked-example-format-aware-judge)).

> **Rule:** evidence MUST be confirmed by real tests. Never state that a metric
> moved unless a test or the benchmark shows it. Separate "logic verified by a
> unit test" from "end-to-end outcome verified by the benchmark", and report
> both states honestly.

## The loop

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[State the thesis<br/>one falsifiable sentence] --> B[Instrument first<br/>structured logger lines]
    B --> C[Two-tier tests<br/>unit + live benchmark]
    C --> D[Read logs &amp; raw output<br/>not the intent]
    D --> E{Unit-verified<br/>moved e2e?}
    E -->|yes| F[Ship]
    E -->|diverges| G[Diagnose the gap<br/>artifact / stochastic / real defect]
    G --> H{Which one?}
    H -->|measurement artifact| B
    H -->|stochastic| C
    H -->|real defect| C
```

| Step | What you do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1. State the thesis | One falsifiable sentence, e.g. *"the grounding rule makes single-shot `author_workflow` emit a markdown table as the final output"*. | Vague theses can't be refuted. |
| 2. Instrument first | Add structured `logger` lines at every decision point *before* you trust the change — a greppable `action` name plus the deciding fields. They stay in the code so the failure class is findable later. | The log is the ground truth you read in step 4. |
| 3. Two-tier tests | Deterministic unit tests for the *logic*; live benchmark for the *end-to-end metric*. Both real. | Unit = the load-bearing "verified"; benchmark = the honest outcome. |
| 4. Read logs &amp; raw output | Grep the engine log for your instrumented actions; inspect the *actual* tool output, not what the code "should" produce. | The raw output is ground truth for "is the final output really a markdown table?". |
| 5. A/B a thesis | Run the same scenario on two git states and compare — no env feature-flag. | Variants are two git states, not a runtime toggle. |
| 6. Distinguish verified vs not | Treat a unit-verified-vs-e2e divergence as a *finding*, not noise. | Honesty about what is and isn't proven. |
| 7. Diagnose before fixing | Name the cause of the gap before touching code. | Stops speculative code added to chase a number. |

### Instrumentation — example actions

These greppable actions are the instrumentation left behind by the
format-aware-judge path:

| Action | Fields |
|---|---|
| `authoring_pipeline.output_format_grounded` | `{ named_format }` |
| `preview_judge.format_check` | `{ named_format, matched, failed_checks }` |
| `preview_judge.format_mismatch` | emitted on a `passes→partial` downgrade |
| `oauth2.refresh_skipped_needs_reauth` | the F1 short-circuit |

### The two tiers

| Tier | Tests | Verifies | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deterministic unit (no LLM) | Mock the LLM seam (`getMockProvider().generateOverrides.<flow>`), feed hand-built inputs, assert the decision. | The *logic* — the load-bearing "verified". | `apps/engine/src/conversations/tests/preview-judge.test.ts`, `output-format.test.ts` |
| Live benchmark (real LLM) | Boot the engine on the working tree, drive a real authoring conversation, score the targets, analyze the log. | The *end-to-end metric*. | `benchmarks/authoring/` |

### What to read (step 4)

| Artifact | Contents |
|---|---|
| `benchmarks/authoring/out/new.engine.log` | The structured log — grep your instrumented actions here. |
| `benchmarks/authoring/out/new.report.results.json` | The **raw per-scenario tool outputs** — the model's actual `dry_run_workflow` result. Ground truth for the final output. |

### A/B a thesis (step 5)

Run the same scenario on two code states and compare. The variants are two git
states — never an env feature-flag.

**Committed path** (works in any clone) — the eval driver takes a `--baseline`:

```
bun run eval:live --engine-url <A> --api-key <k> --scenario <slug> --out a.json
bun run eval:live --engine-url <B> --api-key <k> --scenario <slug> --out b.json --baseline a.json
```

It prints per-metric OLD-vs-NEW changes (regressions flagged).

**Local convenience wrapper** (`benchmarks/authoring/`, gitignored review
scaffolding — reconstruct from its README) boots two throwaway engines + DBs
around the above:

```
BENCH_OLD_REF=HEAD BENCH_SCENARIOS=weather-ranking-table ./run.sh delta
```

OLD runs in an isolated git **worktree** (`BENCH_OLD_REF`, default `HEAD^`), NEW
on the working tree. NEVER `git stash` to switch states on a shared checkout —
the wrapper uses a worktree for exactly this reason.

### Diagnosing a divergence (step 7)

When unit-verified logic doesn't move the e2e number, name the cause — don't
bolt on speculative code to chase a number (benchmarks are review scaffolding;
permanent regressions go in unit tests).

| Cause | Signal | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Measurement artifact | The test and the code read different corpora/fields. | Fix the *benchmark*, not the product. |
| Stochastic generation | The LLM is probabilistic; one run is weak evidence. | Run several trials. |
| Real defect the test didn't cover | The metric is correctly red. | Widen the test. |

## Worked example (format-aware judge)

The first conclusion was: *"the benchmark's `content_pass=false` is a measurement
artifact — the judge logged `format_check matched:true`, so generation IS
producing markdown."* The evidence loop refuted it.

| Step | Finding |
|---|---|
| Dump raw results (`run.sh` step 4) | The actual `dry_run_workflow` output was **6.5 KB, zero pipes, zero separator row** — the final output the caller receives genuinely is NOT a markdown table. |
| Re-read the verdict | So `content_pass=false` was *correct*. |
| Locate the real defect | Generation rendered markdown in an intermediate step (which the judge's `step_artifacts` view saw → `matched:true`), but a later `output_transform` discarded it. The final output isn't markdown, and the judge — evaluating step artifacts — was blind to the final-output transform. |

The log + raw-output inspection turned a confident wrong answer into the right
diagnosis. That is the entire point of the process.

## Files

**Committed (available in any clone):**

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `apps/engine/eval/live-authoring.ts` | The eval driver (`bun run eval:live`); writes the scored report + the sibling `*.results.json` raw dump, and A/B-compares with `--baseline`. |
| `apps/engine/eval/live-report.ts` | `LIVE_SCENARIOS` + scoring + content checks. |

**Local-only (gitignored review scaffolding — reconstruct from the README, do
not expect it in a fresh clone):**

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `benchmarks/authoring/run.sh` | `bench` (current tree) \| `delta` (A/B vs ref); boots throwaway engine(s) + DB around `eval:live`. |
| `benchmarks/authoring/analyze-log.mjs` | Log verdict (CLEAN / REVIEW / ISSUES). |

<!-- Source: docs/developers/input-surfaces.md -->

# Input Surfaces

> **Reading time:** ~12 min
> **Audience:** Engineers integrating with sk, operators configuring surfaces

**Meet your team where they already work — without re-implementing access control per channel.** A developer lives in a terminal. An analyst lives in Slack. A CI pipeline needs a machine-readable API. An AI coding assistant wants to call a workflow directly. sk gives each of them a native door, and every door opens onto the *same* governed engine: one RBAC model, one Audit Log, one identity envelope (`tenant_id`, `actor_id`, `request_source`, `trace_id`). Adopting sk never forces a tooling migration, and security never forks per surface.

## Surfaces at a glance

| Surface | Reach it via | Best for | Auth |
|---|---|---|---|
| **sk CLI** | `sk` in a terminal | Human authoring + operator admin | API key · OIDC · portal token · headless |
| **REST API** | `/v1/*` + OpenAPI | Programmatic + CI | API key |
| **MCP server** | Streamable HTTP + stdio | AI clients / coding agents | OAuth 2.1 or API key |
| **Chat** | Slack · Teams · Google Chat | In-thread authoring + approvals | Linked platform identity |
| **Webhooks** | Signed inbound URLs | Connector-boundary events | Standard Webhooks signature |
| **Schedules** | Cron triggers | Time-based runs | RBAC on the trigger |

## One gate, many doors

Every inbound surface funnels through a single governance gate before it ever reaches the engine. The gate is the same callable, the audit row is the same shape, and the identity envelope is populated at every entry.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CLI["sk CLI<br/>Ink + citty"]
    REST["REST API<br/>/v1/* + OpenAPI"]
    MCP["MCP Server<br/>Streamable HTTP + stdio"]
    Chat["Chat<br/>Slack · Teams · Google"]
    Hook["Webhooks<br/>inbound + outbound"]
    Cron["Schedules<br/>cron + catch-up"]
    Gate{{"Governance gate<br/>can(actor, action, resource) + audit on every call"}}
    Engine[/"sk engine"/]

    CLI --> Gate
    REST --> Gate
    MCP --> Gate
    Chat --> Gate
    Hook --> Gate
    Cron --> Gate
    Gate --> Engine
```

For system-wide context — where external AI clients cross the MCP OAuth bridge and other surfaces enter directly — see the architecture overview:

![sk architecture overview — every inbound surface routes to the same engine; external AI clients cross the MCP OAuth bridge; other surfaces enter directly.](../concepts/overview.png)

*Source: [`overview.drawio`](../concepts/overview.drawio).*

---

## The sk CLI (Conversations + Admin Commands)

The sk CLI is the primary human-facing authoring tool and the canonical operator CLI — one Ink-based binary that opens a Conversation on launch and also exposes admin command groups such as `sk connectors`, `sk workflows`, `sk executions`, and `sk audit`. The surface adapts to the authenticated user's role; there is no separate operator-only CLI.

**Who uses it.**

| Role | What they do |
|---|---|
| End users | Describe workflow goals in natural language, work the AI-assisted authoring loop. |
| Operators | Manage Connectors, review Skill Candidates and Patch Candidates, query the Audit Log, inspect executions, administer the platform. |

**Authentication.** Four modes, all resolving to the same identity and RBAC model:

| Mode | For |
|---|---|
| API Key | Developers and CI |
| OIDC | SSO-enabled organizations |
| Portal Token | Scoped external-user flows |
| Headless (stdin) | Scripted / automated usage with no TTY |

**In-conversation actions.** Users drive the AI authoring loop with slash commands — `/approve` to commit a Draft, `/reject` to discard a proposal, `/draft` to inspect the current draft snapshot, `/context` to inspect the current authoring state, and others — without leaving the terminal. Connector onboarding runs through `/install`, an alias of `/onboard`.

**Slash-command reference.** The canonical, always-current list of every conversational and admin slash command — names, aliases, and one-line descriptions — is the generated reference at [`slash-commands.md`](../authors/slash-commands.md). It is regenerated from the registry in `apps/sk/src/slash.ts`, so it never drifts from what the CLI actually accepts.

**State visibility.** The CLI does not infer progress from transcript text. It renders the engine's authoring summary directly — current mode, stage, active target, checkpoint freshness, blockers, next required action, latest execution, latest diagnosis — which is what makes resume, repair, and handoff predictable across long-running sessions.

**Guided progression.** The guided CLI flow follows the same state machine as the engine:

| Transition | Gated by |
|---|---|
| Connector save | Fresh inspect / validate / probe checkpoints |
| Workflow commit | Fresh inspect / validate / preview checkpoints |
| Execution run | The persisted workflow version tracked in the conversation state |

The normal guided flow does not expose conversational force bypasses for these transitions.

**Resource references.** Inside a Conversation, users mention platform resources directly with `@connector` and `@skill` syntax, grounding AI proposals in the specific Connectors and Skills the tenant has configured.

**Headless mode.** When stdin is not a TTY, the sk CLI runs without interactive prompts — enabling scripted workflows, CI pipeline integration, and automated testing where no human is at the terminal.

**Outbound network from CLI startup.** The welcome banner can pull a one-line "what's new" headline from a remote JSON endpoint on REPL start, but the **default posture is opt-in**. With `SK_WHATS_NEW_URL` unset, no network call fires and the resolver renders the bundled `CHANGELOG.md` head. Operators who want the upstream feed set `SK_WHATS_NEW_URL=<url>` (recommended: `https://updates.subkit.dev/whats-new.json`); the fetch is async, 3-second timeout, 24-hour on-disk cache at `~/.sk/whats-new-cache.json`, identifies itself with a `User-Agent: sk-cli/<version>` header, and the JSON payload is Zod-validated (`{ headline: string }`, strict — unknown keys reject) before any string reaches the banner. The request carries no auth and no tenant identifier. The opt-out sentinels (`""`, `"disabled"`, `"off"`, `"0"`) remain compatible with operators who inherited a populated default and want to disable explicitly. All headline strings (cache, remote, CHANGELOG) pass through `sanitizeHeadline` which strips ANSI escapes and control bytes and truncates to 80 chars before render. After three consecutive remote-fetch failures (including Zod parse failures) the resolver opens a 7-day circuit breaker: subsequent REPL boots skip the network call entirely until the breaker re-arms or a future success resets it.

---

## The REST API (OpenAPI)

The REST API is the full programmatic interface to sk and the canonical interface that every other surface — including the CLI and MCP server — ultimately uses. Every capability available through any other surface is available here.

| Concern | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Coverage** | CRUD for all resources: Workflows, Connectors, Executions, Credentials, Skills, Skill Candidates, Knowledge Sources, Conversations, Schedules, Webhooks, Audit Log entries, and more. Every state change flows through the API layer, so RBAC and the Audit Log apply uniformly. |
| **Runtime entry** | One execution entry point at `POST /v1/executions`. Persisted workflows, inline draft definitions, and single-step previews all run through that same contract. Inline runs complete synchronously by default; queued background execution is explicit. |
| **Schema-first** | Request/response shapes are Zod schemas; the OpenAPI 3.1 spec is generated from them, never hand-written — so the spec is always accurate and generated clients always match the implementation. |
| **Conversation state** | Conversation responses expose the authoring state machine directly — `authoring_mode`, `authoring_stage`, active target metadata, checkpoint statuses, stale checkpoints, `next_required_action`, persisted resources, latest execution / diagnosis references. Clients never reconstruct progress from free-form text. |
| **Consistency** | Pagination, filtering, and sorting follow the same conventions across all list endpoints. Learn the pattern once, apply it everywhere. |
| **Discoverability** | OpenAPI spec served at `/openapi.json`; interactive Scalar UI at `/docs`. Both available to any authenticated client. |
| **LLM grounding** | The engine publishes its own docs in the [llms-txt](https://llmstxt.org) format, unauthenticated, as `text/markdown`: `GET /llms.txt` (a robots.txt-style index) and `GET /llms-full.txt` (the full docs in one fetch). Point an MCP client or model at these to ground it on auth, error-code semantics, and conventions in prose the bare schema can't express. |

---

## MCP Integration

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) server is embedded in the sk engine and exposes the platform's capabilities to AI coding tools. Where the REST API targets direct programmatic use, the MCP server targets AI agents and AI-assisted development tools that reason about and invoke platform capabilities inside their own workflows.

**Supported clients.** Any MCP-compatible client — IDE assistants, coding agents, chat clients, custom MCP clients — connects with a single configuration line pointing at the engine's MCP endpoint.

**Three capability types** that match the MCP standard:

| MCP type | sk resource | What the client gets |
|---|---|---|
| **Callable entries** | Workflows as `wf.<slug>` functions | A workflow `payment-sync` becomes a callable entry: the client sees its input schema, calls it, receives the result. |
| **Resources** | Connectors as structured data access | A Stripe Connector surfaces as e.g. `stripe://customers` for the client to read available data shapes. |
| **Prompts** | Skills as curated context | On prompt request, sk injects the relevant Skill — best practices, integration patterns, known failure modes — into the AI's context. |

**Transport.** Streamable HTTP (the current MCP standard). Stdio is also supported via `sk mcp` for tools that expect a subprocess interface.

> **Behavior change (MCP elicitation).** Every `POST /mcp` response over the Streamable HTTP transport is now framed as an SSE stream (`text/event-stream`) rather than a single buffered JSON envelope — `enableJsonResponse` is `false`. This is required for MCP elicitation: a tool whose handler issues a server→client `elicitation/create` request mid-call (connector forms, OAuth authorization prompts) can only deliver that nested request and receive the reply while the originating POST holds an open stream. **MCP clients must accept `text/event-stream`-framed responses** — every spec-compliant Streamable HTTP client does (verified against current MCP clients across browser, IDE, and CLI surfaces). Note that `enableJsonResponse: false` also changes the `Content-Type` of the `initialize` response itself to `text/event-stream` — operators debugging an older client should expect that framing from the very first round-trip and not chase phantom 4xx errors caused by a client that hard-codes a `application/json` expectation. The stdio transport is unaffected.

> **Behavior change (MCP async Tasks — conversation tools).** The conversation cluster (`conversation_start`, `conversation_append`, `conversation_respond_elicitation`) no longer runs the authoring turn inside the `tools/call` handler. A real turn takes 68–160 s — well past the ~60 s MCP client timeout — so the handler now (1) inserts/validates the conversation row + persists the user message, (2) inserts an `mcp_tasks` index row and enqueues a `conversation.run-turn` background job, (3) returns immediately. The model loop runs in a pg-boss worker. Clients consume the result one of two ways:
>
> - **Tasks-capable clients** (SEP-1686) that send a task-augmented `tools/call` receive a `CreateTaskResult` and poll `tasks/get` / `tasks/result`; `tasks/cancel` aborts the running turn. The server advertises `capabilities.tasks = {list, cancel, requests:{tools:{call:{}}}}`.
> - **Non-Tasks clients** receive a fast plain `CallToolResult` — `{conversation_id, mcp_task_id, status:"working", poll_with:"conversation_get", poll_arg:{conversation_id}}` — and poll the new read-only `conversation_get({conversation_id})` tool until it reports `completed`, `failed`, or `input_required`.
>
> **Elicitation in a backgrounded turn.** A backgrounded turn has no live MCP session, so it cannot use the in-process `ElicitationBridge` (`elicitForm` / `elicitOob` need the open `tools/call` SSE stream). It always uses the DB-pause path: an `ask_user_*` / `authenticate_oauth` inserts a pending `conversation_elicitations` row, sets the conversation to `awaiting_input`, and the turn ends. The task then derives `input_required`; the client reads the pending form via `conversation_get` (or `tasks/get`) and resolves it with `conversation_respond_elicitation`, which enqueues the next turn. The `ElicitationBridge` is retained for any synchronous (non-conversation) tool that still runs inside its `tools/call`.

**Governance.** All MCP calls are subject to the same RBAC checks and Audit Log entries as direct API calls. There is no privileged back channel; identity and permissions are enforced identically regardless of which surface initiated the request.

**Destructive-action flow.** `tenant.*` writes (e.g. `tenant.delete_workflow`, `tenant.revoke_api_key`) follow the same `confirm_before_execution` policy as in-conversation authoring actions. The first call returns a structured pending envelope — `{pending: true, confirm_required: true, target: {...}, resume: "..." , tool_call_id: "..."}` — and an `approval.requested` audit row. The client relays the target to the operator, obtains consent, and re-issues the same call with `_meta.sk_confirm: true` (or `__policy_confirmed: true` inside the arguments). The second call emits `approval.approved` and executes the callable entry. This is two MCP round-trips and one human confirmation — no authoring conversation required for routine CRUD.

**Callable hints.** Every listed callable entry carries `_meta.subkit = {category, confirm_required, destructive}` so clients can render destructive warnings and skip self-authored pre-confirms. Clients that honour `confirm_required` from the listing avoid the two-elicitation trap.

**Workflow inputs.** Each `wf.<slug>` callable entry advertises an `inputSchema`. When the workflow declares `input_schema` on its DAG, that is passed through verbatim. When it doesn't, sk synthesises one by scanning the DAG for `${input.X}` placeholders in request steps and `input.input.X` references in JavaScript transforms, yielding `{type:"object", properties:{X:{type:"string"}}, additionalProperties: true}`.

**Non-fatal warnings.** When a workflow run hits a soft signal — for example a `loop.over` JSONata expression that resolved to a non-array because it referenced a step id not in scope — the MCP response wraps the output as `{output, warnings: [{code:"loop_over_unresolved", identifier, step_key, message}]}`. The run still reports `status: "succeeded"` but the client can surface the diagnostic so operators know why a payload looks partial.

**Read-only deployments.** For MCP deployments that expose only read callables (no write surface at all), set `SK_MCP_READ_ONLY=1`. Writes are visible by default and rely on the policy gate for safety.

**Resource update notifications.** When a client subscribes to a resource URI (`workflow://<id>`, `connector://<id>`, `knowledge://<id>`, `skill-candidate://<id>`), the engine emits `notifications/resources/updated` on every committed state change in that resource. The notification follows the MCP spec exactly: it carries only the URI — no event-type discriminator, no payload diff, no actor. Clients that need to distinguish a delete from a rename must re-fetch via `readResource`, or for workflows specifically observe the lifecycle audit row directly through `/v1/audit-log`. Delivery is at-most-once — a transient `sendResourceUpdated` failure is logged and dropped — so clients on critical paths should also poll. Subscriptions are subject to the same RBAC check as `readResource`: a portal token or custom role lacking `workflow:read` on the underlying resource receives no notifications, even if it knew the URI to subscribe.

### MCP OAuth 2.1 (ChatGPT / Claude.ai / Cursor)

The sk engine is a full OAuth 2.1 authorization server and resource server for `/mcp`. This lets OAuth-only clients — including the ChatGPT custom connector, Claude.ai, and Cursor — authenticate without a static API key.

**Prerequisites.** Set `server.public_base_url` to the engine's public `https://` URL in `subkit.config.json` (or via `sk settings set server.public_base_url '"https://your-engine.example.com"'`). The MCP OAuth feature is enabled by default (`auth.mcp_oauth.enabled = true`).

**Discovery endpoints.**

| Endpoint | Spec | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` | RFC 9728 | Points clients to the authorization server. |
| `GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` | RFC 8414 | Authorization server metadata (endpoints, scopes, PKCE). |

**OAuth flow.**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as MCP Client
    participant E as sk engine
    participant U as User browser

    C->>E: GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
    E-->>C: { authorization_server }
    C->>E: GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
    E-->>C: endpoints, scopes, PKCE required
    C->>E: POST /v1/oauth/register (DCR, RFC 7591)
    E-->>C: { client_id, client_secret? }
    C->>U: 302 to /v1/oauth/authorize?code_challenge=...
    U->>E: OIDC login + consent
    E-->>U: 302 to redirect_uri?code=...&state=...
    U-->>C: deliver code
    C->>E: POST /v1/oauth/token (code + verifier)
    E-->>C: { access_token: wf_mcp_*, refresh_token: wf_mcr_* }
    C->>E: POST /mcp (Authorization: Bearer wf_mcp_*)
    E-->>C: SSE stream
    Note over C,E: Refresh rotates the chain; replay revokes it.
```

1. Client fetches `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` to discover the authorization server.
2. Client fetches `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` to get all endpoints.
3. Client registers itself at `POST /v1/oauth/register` (dynamic client registration, RFC 7591). Returns `client_id` (and `client_secret` for confidential clients).
4. Client redirects the user to `GET /v1/oauth/authorize?client_id=...&redirect_uri=...&response_type=code&code_challenge=...&code_challenge_method=S256&scope=mcp:read&state=...`. PKCE S256 is mandatory; `plain` is rejected.
5. If not logged in, the engine redirects to `/v1/identity/login/start` (OIDC). After login the user returns to the authorize page.
6. The consent page shows the client name, tenant, and requested scopes. The user approves or denies.
7. On approval, the engine issues an authorization code and redirects to the client's `redirect_uri?code=...&state=...`.
8. Client exchanges the code at `POST /v1/oauth/token` (form-encoded, `grant_type=authorization_code`). Response: `{ access_token: "wf_mcp_...", refresh_token: "wf_mcr_...", token_type: "bearer", expires_in: 3600 }`.
9. Client uses `Authorization: Bearer wf_mcp_...` on subsequent `POST /mcp` calls.
10. Client refreshes at `POST /v1/oauth/token` (`grant_type=refresh_token`). Refresh tokens rotate on every use; replaying a rotated token revokes the whole chain.
11. Client revokes at `POST /v1/oauth/revoke`.

**Scopes.**

| Scope | MCP mode | What the token unlocks |
|---|---|---|
| `mcp:read` | product | Callable workflow entries and the `authenticate` tool only. |
| `mcp:authoring` | authoring | Adds `conversation.*` authoring tools. |
| `mcp:admin` | admin | Adds full `tenant.*` admin tools (subject to RBAC). |

The scope granted at consent is the intersection of what the client requested and what the consenting user's role permits. A token can never carry a scope its owner lacks.

**Connecting ChatGPT custom connector.**

1. In ChatGPT → Settings → Connectors → New connector, set the server URL to your engine's MCP endpoint (`https://your-engine.example.com/mcp`).
2. ChatGPT auto-discovers OAuth via `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`.
3. ChatGPT performs dynamic client registration and opens the sk login + consent flow.
4. After approval, ChatGPT stores the OAuth tokens and uses them on all future calls.

**Connecting Claude.ai.**

1. In Claude.ai → Settings → Integrations → Add integration, enter `https://your-engine.example.com/mcp`.
2. Claude.ai discovers OAuth metadata and performs DCR automatically.
3. Complete the login + consent flow in the browser.

**Connecting Cursor.**

Add to `.cursor/mcp.json`:
```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sk": {
      "url": "https://your-engine.example.com/mcp",
      "transport": "http"
    }
  }
}
```
Cursor discovers OAuth from the `WWW-Authenticate` header on the first unauthenticated request and opens the browser-based consent flow.

**Security notes.** Authorization codes are single-use with a 60-second TTL. `redirect_uri` is matched exactly against the registered URIs — no prefix or wildcard matching. Refresh tokens rotate on every use and replay of a rotated token revokes the full chain. Only SHA-256 hashes of tokens are persisted; the plaintext values are never stored. `mcp_oauth_clients` intentionally has no `tenant_id` because DCR (RFC 7591) registers the client before any tenant context exists; the tenant binds at consent time on the authorization-code row and on every token. This is a deliberate, documented exception to the "every row carries tenant_id" rule.

---

## Chat Systems (Slack, Teams, Google Chat)

Enterprise teams spend much of their day in chat. The sk chat integrations bring the Conversation authoring loop into the surfaces teams already use, so workflow authoring does not require context switching.

| Aspect | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **How it works** | Each platform has a dedicated adapter that normalises incoming messages — mentions, slash commands, interaction callbacks — into sk's Conversation model. The same AI authoring loop that runs in the sk CLI runs inside a Chat Session, rendered as native platform messages. A conversation started in Slack and continued the next day picks up exactly where it left off. |
| **Approval flow** | When a Draft or Patch Candidate needs approval, the platform surfaces an interactive card in the thread with native approve / reject buttons — no separate workflow call. The decision is recorded in the Audit Log with the chat platform as the request source. |
| **Identity linking** | A chat user's platform identity (Slack user ID, Teams user principal, Google Chat identity) is linked to their sk Tenant account through a user-initiated flow. Once linked, messages carry their full sk identity, role, and permissions. |
| **Notification routing** | Execution results, alerts, and approval requests route to specific channels or users via Notification Rules — by event, severity, and quiet-hour constraints. Chat is the primary notification channel in sk; email notifications are not supported. |

---

## Webhooks and Scheduled Triggers

Not every workflow starts with a human. Scheduled triggers and inbound webhooks let sk respond to time and to connector-boundary events without a person initiating anything.

| Trigger | Behavior | Audit source |
|---|---|---|
| **Inbound webhooks** | Each endpoint has a unique URL bound to one Workflow. When an external connector boundary — a payment processor, CI service, monitoring service — posts to it, sk verifies the signature via the Standard Webhooks specification, deduplicates replays, and triggers the bound Workflow. | `webhook` |
| **Outbound webhooks** | sk pushes events outward: operators configure Subscriptions that match internal platform events and fan them out to external connector boundaries as signed deliveries. Retries follow a defined cadence, failures go to a dead-letter queue, and repeated failures trip a per-subscriber circuit breaker. | — |
| **Scheduled triggers** | Cron expressions attach to any Workflow. The sk scheduler fires at the configured time with catch-up semantics — if the engine was offline when a run was due, it fires the missed run on return (subject to a configurable window). | `scheduler` |

**Triggering without a human.** Whether triggered by a webhook or a schedule, the resulting Execution is governed by exactly the same rules as a manual one: RBAC applies to the trigger, the Workflow runs deterministically as committed, and the full Execution record is written to the immutable log.

---

## Further reading

- [AI-assisted authoring](../authors/authoring-workflows.md) — how Conversations work, how the AI assembles Workflows, and how the approval gate turns a Draft into a committed, executable Workflow.
- [glossary](../concepts/glossary.md#group-6-surfaces) — definitions for sk CLI, MCP Server, Chat Adapter, Notification Rule, Service Metadata.

<!-- Source: docs/developers/quickstart.md -->

# Quickstart — Developer

Ship to sk with confidence: a green quality gate on every change keeps regressions out of production. From clone to a passing test suite and a live engine in about 10 minutes.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  clone[Clone] --> deps[Install deps]
  deps --> compose[compose:up · Postgres]
  compose --> tests[Quality gate green]
```

## Prerequisites

- [Bun](https://bun.sh) (`curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash`).
- Docker Desktop (or compatible) — required for Postgres.

## 1. Clone and install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/mikebild/subkit && cd subkit
bun install
```

## 2. Bring infra up

```bash
bun run compose:up          # Postgres only (engine runs on the host via `bun run dev`)
```

Local dev uses docker compose for postgres only (and optional MinIO under `--profile storage`); the engine runs on the host via `bun run dev` (step 4). For production, run the all-in-one Docker image — see [docs/developers/self-host.md](./self-host.md).

## 3. Run the quality gate

```bash
bun run lint                # biome
bun run typecheck           # tsc --noEmit
bun run test:unit           # fast inner loop (needs Postgres — see note below)
bun run test:integration    # db/queue/http/webhooks/credentials-oauth2
bun run test:e2e            # compiles sk and runs journeys
```

> **Note.** `test:unit` includes `execution/tests`, which uses a throwaway Postgres database. It's fast (seconds) because each file gets its own database, but you do need `compose:up` running.

`bun run verify` is the local release gate. It runs determinism lint,
unit tests, eval fixtures, integration tests, `build:sk`, and e2e coverage on top of lint and
typecheck. `bun run verify:ai` is the focused contract suite for prompt/context/authoring changes.

## 4. Develop

```bash
bun run dev                 # engine in watch mode
```

In another shell:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:3000/v1/health | jq
```

## 5. Where things live

- `apps/engine/src/` — the server. Subsystem-per-directory (43 in total). Start with [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md) for the map.
- `apps/sk/` — `sk` unified CLI. REPL for end-users; full admin surface for operators and admins.
- `packages/shared/` — cross-process types.
- `docs/` — eight concept docs. See [docs/README.md](../README.md) for the index.

## 6. Before you PR

- [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md) — non-negotiables: tenant isolation, audit coverage, Zod at boundaries, QuickJS sandbox, no auto-promote. Read this first.
- [docs/concepts/glossary.md](../concepts/glossary.md) — the domain model. Every term used in the codebase is defined here.

<!-- Source: docs/developers/self-host.md -->

# Quickstart — Zero to Running

**sk runs inside your own infrastructure — your data stays yours.** One container,
one stateful dependency (PostgreSQL), no SaaS lock-in and nothing leaving your
network except outbound LLM calls. Start from nothing and finish with a running
engine, an authenticated `sk` CLI, a working connector, a runnable workflow, and
an indexed knowledge article — all from the released Docker image.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Op["docker run"] --> Engine["engine container<br/>(bundled sk + PostgreSQL)"]
    Engine --> PG[("PostgreSQL<br/>your data, your volume")]
    Engine -. outbound only .-> LLM[("LLM provider")]
```

| What | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Time** | ~15 minutes |
| **You need** | Docker + one free [Anthropic API key](https://console.anthropic.com) |
| **Cost** | The weather API used here (open-meteo) is free and keyless |
| **Outcome** | A governed engine you own, end-to-end |

> **The primary interface is the conversational `sk` REPL.** You describe what you
> want in plain language; the AI proposes a connector or workflow, you review and
> approve. Declarative JSON and one-shot commands exist too — for scripting and CI —
> see [Scripting & CI](#scripting--ci-non-interactive). Every command and output
> below is real, run end-to-end against the released image.

---

## Concepts in 60 seconds

| Term | One line |
|---|---|
| **Tenant** | Your isolated workspace — every connector, workflow, and user lives in one tenant. |
| **Connector** | An authenticated link to an external API (here: open-meteo). |
| **Workflow** | A versioned sequence of steps (call an API, transform the result). |
| **Execution** | One immutable run of a workflow. |
| **Knowledge source** | A document (runbook, PDF) indexed for semantic search. |

Full glossary: [`docs/concepts/glossary.md`](../concepts/glossary.md).

---

## Step 1 — Run the engine

The all-in-one image bundles the engine, PostgreSQL, **and** the `sk` CLI.

```bash
docker run -d --name subkit -p 3000:3000 -v subkit-data:/data mikebild/subkit:latest
```

Wait a few seconds, then confirm it is healthy:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:3000/v1/health
# {"status":"ok","db_connected":true,"uptime_seconds":3}
```

The `subkit-data` volume holds **all** state — database, config, encryption key,
uploaded files — so restarts keep your data.

---

## Step 2 — First-run bootstrap (tenant + admin key + LLM)

A fresh engine has no tenants. Complete setup with `sk init` — on the all-in-one
image the bundled CLI **auto-detects the one-time bootstrap token** the engine
dropped on the `/data` volume, so you don't copy anything:

```bash
docker exec subkit sk init \
  --admin-email you@example.com \
  --tenant-name "My Org" \
  --llm-provider anthropic \
  --llm-api-key sk-ant-YOUR-KEY
# sk init: using bootstrap token from /data/config/bootstrap.token
# sk init: bootstrap complete — tenant 6c82c719-…
#   profile 'default' saved to /data/home/.sk/config.json
```

> **No API key handy?** Use `--llm-provider mock` to walk the mechanics with zero
> external accounts. Or pass `-e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-…` at `docker run` time
> and drop `--llm-api-key`.
>
> **Manual token (non-bundled deploys):** copy it from the logs and pass
> `--token` (valid 15 min; the engine reprints a fresh one on the next attempt):
> ```bash
> docker logs subkit 2>&1 | grep -oE 'sk init --token [a-f0-9]{64}' | tail -1
> ```

> **Authentication defaults to the local `subkit` provider** — people are added
> by admin invite and authenticate with engine-issued API keys; no external
> identity provider is involved (that's the [teammate flow](#add-a-teammate-multi-user)
> below). To switch the whole engine to SSO via Firebase, set the provider and
> restart:
> ```bash
> docker exec subkit sk settings set auth.provider '"firebase"' --force
> docker restart subkit
> ```

Verify:

```bash
docker exec subkit sk doctor
# ✔ profile / reachability / authn / setup / version_match … (exit 0)
docker exec subkit sk -p "Say only the word: pong" --output text
# pong            ← confirms the LLM is wired correctly
```

---

## Step 3 — Build by talking to it (the `sk` REPL) ★

This is the main way to use sk. Open the interactive REPL (it needs a terminal,
so add `-it`):

```bash
docker exec -it subkit sk
```

Now just say what you want. The AI proposes; **nothing is saved or run until you
`/approve`.** A real session — connector, then workflow, then a run — looks like:

```text
you ▸ create a keyless HTTP connector for the open-meteo forecast API
      (https://api.open-meteo.com, endpoint GET /v1/forecast), then probe it
 sk ▸ Created connector "open-meteo" (http, dev). Probe: GET /v1/forecast… → HTTP 200. ✓

you ▸ now a workflow that returns the current temperature in Berlin using it
 sk ▸ Proposed workflow "berlin-current-temperature":
        1. request   GET /v1/forecast?latitude=52.52&longitude=13.41&current=temperature_2m
        2. transform extract { city, time, temperature_c }
      Dry-run preview → { city: "Berlin", temperature_c: 23.7 }. Approve to save?
you ▸ /approve
 sk ▸ Saved "berlin-current-temperature" (v1).
you ▸ run it
 sk ▸ execution succeeded → { city: "Berlin", time: "…", temperature_c: 23.7 }
```

That's the whole loop: **describe → review the proposal + dry-run → `/approve` →
run.** You never hand-write JSON or look up an API shape.

### Slash commands (type `/` for the menu)

The ones you'll reach for, grouped by what they do (verified against the shipped
build):

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `/approve` · `/reject` | commit the AI's current proposal, or reject it (with a reason) |
| `/preview` · `/probe` | dry-run the workflow draft / test the connector draft now |
| `/draft` · `/connector` · `/workflow` | inspect the current authoring state |
| `/templates` | browse connector templates suggested for the draft |
| `/onboard` | guided wizard: pick a template, enter credentials, probe, save |
| `/versions` · `/restore <n>` | list committed workflow versions / roll back |
| `/skills` · `/knowledge` | list reusable context / knowledge sources in scope |
| `/clear` (`/new`) · `/compact` · `/resume` | new conversation · shrink history · reattach |
| `/setup` · `/status` · `/cost` · `/usage` | readiness · session+persona · token budget |
| `/config` · `/settings` | open the searchable settings UI (every engine setting) |
| `/model` · `/tenant` · `/login` · `/logout` | switch model · switch/list tenants · auth |
| `/attach` · `/upload` · `/files` | attach a file to the message · upload · list files |
| `/help` · `/exit` (`/quit`) | cheat sheet · leave |

Mentions: `@file:<id>` attaches an uploaded file; `@skill:<name>` pulls a Skill
into context. Full walkthrough: [`repl-tour.md`](../authors/repl-tour.md).

> **One-shot / scripted?** The exact same authoring loop runs non-interactively
> with `sk -p "<request>"` — see [Scripting & CI](#scripting--ci-non-interactive).

---

## Step 4 — Inspect what you built

Whether you authored in the REPL or via a script, the artifacts are normal,
versioned resources you can list and run:

```bash
docker exec subkit sk connectors list                 # name + slug + status
docker exec subkit sk connectors test <CONNECTOR_ID>  # re-probe connectivity
docker exec subkit sk workflows run berlin-current-temperature --follow
docker exec subkit sk executions list --limit 5
docker exec subkit sk executions result <EXECUTION_ID>  # the value it produced
```

---

## Step 5 — Add a knowledge article

In the REPL you can just say *“add this file as a knowledge source tagged
weather, runbook”*. The scriptable form:

```bash
docker cp note.md subkit:/tmp/note.md
docker exec subkit sk knowledge-sources create --file /tmp/note.md \
  --title "Weather Runbook" --tags "weather,runbook,open-meteo"
# ✓ Created knowledge source "Weather Runbook" · 4 chunks
docker exec subkit sk knowledge-sources list
docker exec subkit sk knowledge-sources search "open-meteo"   # semantic search; ranks by relevance
```

`--tags` you supply are authoritative (no AI auto-tagging); omit both `--tags`
and `--description` to let the engine generate them.

---

## Step 6 — Use it from Codex / any MCP client

The engine is an **MCP server**, so AI coding tools (Codex, Claude Desktop,
Cursor, …) can drive your governed workflows directly. Mint a Bearer key first
(see [from your own machine](#use-sk-from-your-own-machine-instead-of-docker-exec)).

**A. Streamable HTTP (recommended).** For **Codex** (`~/.codex/config.toml`, or
Settings → MCP Servers) — Codex auto-detects the transport from `url`, and
`bearer_token_env_var` names an env var so the key stays out of the file:

```toml
[mcp_servers.subkit]
url = "http://localhost:3000/mcp"
bearer_token_env_var = "SUBKIT_API_KEY"
```
```bash
export SUBKIT_API_KEY=wf_live_…   # the key from `engine --issue-admin-key`
```

Inline-header JSON shape (Claude Desktop / Cursor):

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "subkit": {
  "url": "http://localhost:3000/mcp",
  "transport": "streamable-http",
  "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer wf_live_…" }
} } }
```

**B. stdio (local).** After `sk login` on your machine, let the client spawn the
bundled proxy (reads `~/.sk/config.json`):

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "subkit": { "command": "sk", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

Once connected, the client sees your tenant's tools — author and run workflows
(`author_workflow`, `build_workflow`, `dry_run_workflow`), inspect connectors
(`test_connector`, `list_recipes`), and more. Destructive calls require a confirm
first. Verify the endpoint by hand:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:3000/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer wf_live_…" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"0"}}}'
# → 200 with an mcp-session-id response header
```

---

## Use `sk` from your own machine (instead of `docker exec`)

`docker exec subkit sk …` is the zero-install path. To run `sk` directly on your
host:

```bash
# 1. Install the CLI (also served by your engine at /install)
curl -fsSL http://localhost:3000/install | bash

# 2. Mint a full admin key — prints a ready-to-paste `sk login` line
docker exec subkit engine --issue-admin-key --tenant my-org
#   run this on your machine to log the host `sk` in:
#     sk login --engine-url http://localhost:3000 --api-key wf_live_…

# 3. Paste that line, then open the REPL on your machine
sk status
sk            # the same conversational REPL, now host-native
```

Host config lives at `~/.sk/config.json`.

---

## Add a teammate (multi-user)

With the local `subkit` provider, an admin provisions each teammate and the
teammate mints their **own** personal API key from a single-use invite — the
admin never sees that key. Three commands, in order:

```bash
# 1. Admin: create the user (roles: admin | member | enduser, default member)
docker exec subkit sk users create --email teammate@example.com --role member
# created user
#   id     <USER_ID>
#   email  teammate@example.com
#   role   member

# 2. Admin: issue a single-use invite — the wf_invite_ token is shown ONCE
docker exec subkit sk users invite <USER_ID>
# invite issued for user <USER_ID>
#   token    wf_invite_…
#   expires  …
# the invited user runs:
#   sk join --invite wf_invite_…
```

```bash
# 3. Teammate (on their own machine, no login required): redeem the token to
#    provision a personal API key into their ~/.sk profile
sk join --invite wf_invite_… --engine-url http://localhost:3000
# sk join: joined — profile 'default' saved to ~/.sk/config.json
#   personal api key prefix: wf_live_…
#   next: sk status
```

Hand the token over securely — it works only once. Admins can review or revoke
un-redeemed invites with `sk invites list` and `sk invites revoke <invite-id>`.

---

## Settings — one surface

Every runtime setting is managed with `sk settings` (the REPL's `/config` opens
the same thing):

```bash
docker exec subkit sk settings list                       # every leaf + value
docker exec subkit sk settings get llm.provider
docker exec subkit sk settings set llm.model '"claude-sonnet-4-6"'   # value is JSON
docker exec subkit sk settings configure                  # interactive UI
```

A few values are **not** `sk settings` on purpose: `MASTER_KEY`, `DATABASE_URL`,
and `ENGINE_LISTEN_HOST` are bootstrap env vars (needed before the engine/API
exist), and `engine --issue-admin-key` mints the *first* key (after that,
`sk apikeys create`). See [Operator configuration reference](#operator-configuration-reference) below.

---

## Scripting & CI (non-interactive)

The REPL is for humans; these are for automation. Same engine, same governance.

**Headless authoring** — the conversational loop without a TTY (no slash
commands; the AI completes autonomously up to `--max-turns`):

```bash
docker exec subkit sk -p "Create a keyless HTTP connector named open-meteo for \
https://api.open-meteo.com, endpoint GET /v1/forecast, then probe it." --output text
docker exec subkit sk -p "list my workflows" --output json
```

**Declarative workflow** — exact and repeatable; `create` runs
**validate → preview (real dry-run) → save**, so a green result proves the
connector works. Save `weather.json` (use your connector id from
`sk connectors list`):

```json
{
  "name": "Berlin Current Temperature",
  "slug": "berlin-current-temperature",
  "steps": [
    { "id": "fetch_weather", "kind": "request", "method": "GET", "path": "/v1/forecast",
      "query": { "latitude": "52.52", "longitude": "13.41", "current": "temperature_2m" },
      "on_error": "fail", "connector_id": "<CONNECTOR_ID>" },
    { "id": "extract_temperature", "kind": "transform", "language": "javascript", "on_error": "fail",
      "expression": "const c = input.scope.fetch_weather.data.current; return { city: 'Berlin', time: c.time, temperature_c: c.temperature_2m };" }
  ]
}
```
```bash
docker cp weather.json subkit:/tmp/weather.json
docker exec subkit sk workflows create --file /tmp/weather.json   # validate→preview→save
docker exec subkit sk workflows run berlin-current-temperature --follow
```

**Key-based connector, fully scripted** — create from a template, attach the
credential without a conversation:

```bash
docker exec subkit sk connectors create --template stripe --name stripe-prod --skip-checks
docker exec subkit sk credentials set <CONNECTOR_ID> --mode bearer --token sk_live_…
#   modes: bearer | header | query | basic | aws_sigv4 | none  (probes after, unless --skip-checks)
docker exec subkit sk credentials list <CONNECTOR_ID>
```

---

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause / fix |
|---|---|
| `llm_provider_misconfigured` on an AI command | Provider key missing/wrong: `sk settings set llm.providers.anthropic.api_key '"sk-ant-…"'` (or re-run `sk init`), then `sk -p "ping"`. |
| `bootstrap token expired` | Re-run `sk init` (it auto-detects a fresh token) or re-grep the logs (Step 2). |
| Connector `probe failed` | Wrong base URL / endpoint — tell the REPL the correct values and `/probe`. |
| `validation failed` on `workflows create` | Check the JSON against the Scripting section; `connector_id` must be a real id from `sk connectors list`. |
| Interactive prompt hangs under `docker exec` | Add `-it`: `docker exec -it subkit sk …`. |

---

## Production deployment

The quickstart above uses the all-in-one image — engine and PostgreSQL in one
container — ideal for trials, demos, and small single-node self-hosting. This
section covers what changes when you run sk for real.

### Deployment Topology

sk compiles to a single binary whose only stateful dependency is PostgreSQL. The
job queue, cron scheduler, and pub/sub event bus all run **inside** the engine
process, backed by PostgreSQL. No message broker, no distributed queue, no
coordination service — one dependency, and an entire class of distributed-systems
failure modes designed away.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Internet(("Internet"))
    Proxy["TLS reverse proxy / LB<br/>(your choice)"]
    Engine["engine container<br/>mikebild/subkit"]
    PG[("PostgreSQL")]
    LLM[("LLM Provider<br/>Anthropic / OpenAI / Google")]
    S3[("S3 (optional)<br/>step-result spillover")]

    Internet -- :443 --> Proxy
    Proxy -- :3000 --> Engine
    Engine --> PG
    Engine -. outbound .-> LLM
    Engine -. outbound .-> S3
```

| Concern | How sk handles it |
|---|---|
| **Queue / scheduler / events** | pg-boss + outbox in PostgreSQL — nothing extra to run |
| **Standard model** | one engine service + one PostgreSQL instance |
| **High availability** | run multiple engine containers behind a load balancer (no coordination overhead) |
| **Production database** | point at [external PostgreSQL](#external-database); engine auto-migrates on boot |
| **Local development** | `docker-compose.yml` brings up postgres only (MinIO under `--profile storage`); `bun run dev` runs the engine on the host |

### Installation

| Channel | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Binaries** | macOS (Intel + Apple Silicon), Linux (x64 + ARM64), Windows (x64) |
| **Primary binaries** | `sk` (CLI) and the engine — docs and examples use `sk` |
| **Install script** | one-liner for bash and PowerShell |
| **Container** | published image for Kubernetes / cloud-native deployments |
| **Auto-update** | binaries check on startup and update in place, gated by a signed `SHA256SUMS` — see [`../admins/credentials-and-keys.md`](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md) |

---

## Operator configuration reference

Every **runtime setting** is managed with `sk settings` (get / set / list / `configure`) — that is the one surface you need. The env vars below are deliberately *not* `sk settings`, and for a reason worth knowing:

- **`MASTER_KEY` / `DATABASE_URL` / `ENGINE_LISTEN_HOST` are bootstrap-only.** They're needed *before* the engine, its database, or its HTTP API exist — `MASTER_KEY` decrypts the credential vault, `DATABASE_URL` is *how* the engine reaches the database where settings are stored, and `ENGINE_LISTEN_HOST` is where the server binds. `sk settings` talks to a *running* engine, so it cannot set them (chicken-and-egg). `MASTER_KEY` isn't even a config leaf.
- **`engine --issue-admin-key` is the operator escape hatch for the *first* key.** `sk` authenticates with an API key, so it can't mint its own first one; that runs directly against the database on the `engine` binary. Once you have a key, `sk apikeys create` mints more through the API.
- **`SK_OVERRIDE_*` is the no-disk complement to `sk settings`** — ephemeral env overrides for CI / secret managers, re-applied each boot, never persisted.

Everything else lives in `subkit.config.json` on the volume. Full leaf reference: [`../admins/settings-reference.md`](../admins/settings-reference.md); the surrounding configuration model is [`../admins/configuration.md`](../admins/configuration.md).

| Env var | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `MASTER_KEY` | auto-generated + persisted to `/data/config/master.key` | 64-hex AES-256 key for at-rest credential encryption. **Set your own in production** — losing it makes stored credentials unrecoverable. |
| `DATABASE_URL` | embedded PostgreSQL | Set to use an external database (disables the embedded one). |
| `ENGINE_LISTEN_HOST` | `0.0.0.0` | Bind interface. The image defaults to all-interfaces so `-p` works; leave it. |
| `SK_OVERRIDE_*` | — | Override any config leaf at runtime (e.g. `SK_OVERRIDE_LLM_API_KEY`). |
| `NODE_ENV` | `production` | — |

### Bring your own MASTER_KEY

```bash
docker run -d --name subkit -p 3000:3000 -v subkit-data:/data \
  -e MASTER_KEY="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \
  mikebild/subkit:latest
```

Store it somewhere safe and pass the **same** value on every run — it must stay constant or previously encrypted credentials become unreadable. Rotation procedure: [`../admins/credentials-and-keys.md`](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md).

### External database

Skip the embedded PostgreSQL and connect to your own (managed RDS, a separate container, etc.). The engine still auto-migrates on boot:

```bash
docker run -d --name subkit -p 3000:3000 -v subkit-data:/data \
  -e DATABASE_URL="postgres://user:pass@db-host:5432/subkit" \
  -e MASTER_KEY="<your-64-hex-key>" \
  mikebild/subkit:latest
```

### Persistence & upgrades

State lives entirely in the `/data` volume. To upgrade, pull a newer tag and recreate the container against the same volume — migrations apply automatically on boot:

```bash
docker pull mikebild/subkit:latest
docker rm -f subkit
docker run -d --name subkit -p 3000:3000 -v subkit-data:/data mikebild/subkit:latest
```

### Notes & limits

- **Web-scraping connector**: Playwright browsers are not bundled (keeps the image lean). Scraping-dependent flows degrade gracefully; install browsers separately if you need them.
- **File scanning**: uploads are not virus-scanned by default — see [`../admins/production-hardening.md`](../admins/production-hardening.md) before accepting untrusted uploads.
- **Single-node only**: the embedded-database image is not built for horizontal scaling. Use an external `DATABASE_URL` (and run multiple engine containers) or the systemd path for production scale.

---

## Cleanup & next steps

```bash
docker rm -f subkit            # stop & remove the container
docker volume rm subkit-data   # also wipe all state (optional)
```

- [**Using the `sk` REPL**](../authors/repl-tour.md) — the primary interface, in depth.
- [`docs/concepts/connectors.md`](../concepts/connectors.md) — connectors, credentials, OAuth2.
- [`docs/concepts/workflows.md`](../concepts/workflows.md) — steps, versioning, scheduling.
- [`docs/authors/authoring-workflows.md`](../authors/authoring-workflows.md) — conversational authoring, skills, knowledge.
- Operator setup (TLS, external DB, settings): [Production deployment](#production-deployment) below.

<!-- Source: docs/developers/tool-palette.md -->

# Tool palette and dispatch

**Outcome:** every LLM action against sk is a *named, governed* tool — one
registry, one policy gate, one audit trail. No ad-hoc calls, no surface that
quietly skips a permission check. A write to prod gates the same whether it
arrives over chat or MCP.

> **Status:** authoritative. See
> [`apps/engine/src/tools/`](../../apps/engine/src/tools/) for the
> implementation and `AGENTS.md` lines 142–185 for the subsystem map.

## Why this exists

The engine speaks "LLM tool-calling" across two surfaces:

| Surface | Transport | Entry point |
|---|---|---|
| **Chat** | Anthropic-SDK tool calls in a conversation turn | `conversations/tools/sdk-wrap.ts` |
| **MCP** | `tools/list` + `tools/call` over Model Context Protocol | `apps/engine/src/mcp/` |

Before the unified palette, those two paths each owned their own dispatch,
schema, RBAC, audit, and policy. Two failure modes followed:

- **Literal duplication.** `test_connector` existed twice — as a
  `ConversationTool` (`conversations/tools/test-connector.ts`) *and* as an
  MCP-only file (`mcp/tools/test-connector.ts`) — both calling the same
  `probeConnector()` driver and `recordConnectorInvoked()` recorder.
- **Divergent gates.** Chat used `tool-policies.resolveToolMode()`; MCP used
  `mcp/capabilities/policy-gate.gateTenantToolCall()`. They disagreed on
  `tenant_read` escalation: a `probe_connector` POST against prod gated
  correctly on chat and **silently bypassed** on MCP.

One registry, one dispatcher, one policy gate, and one envelope shape close
both gaps. Per-surface adapters render that single envelope into MCP transport
or chat SDK shape — the only place surface differences live.

## Concepts

### ToolDescriptor

```ts
interface ToolDescriptor {
  name: string;
  description: string;
  category: "draft_write" | "tenant_read" | "tenant_write";
  inputSchema: unknown; // Zod for conversation tools; JSON Schema for static
  disabled?: { reason: string };
  requires_skill?: string;
}
```

| Field | Role |
|---|---|
| `category` | Drives the policy decision — see *Policy gate (unified)*. |
| `disabled` | Marks a tool `tools/call` rejects with a `not_available_on_surface` envelope pointing at `conversation_start`. |
| `requires_skill` | Gates the tool behind a granted skill. |

**Draft-write tools are HIDDEN from MCP `tools/list`, not badged.** Earlier
they were listed-with-`disabled` as an "honest signal" that the tool exists but
isn't headlessly callable. In practice external clients (e.g. claude.ai) ignore
the `_meta.subkit.disabled` badge, call the tool anyway, get rejected, and churn
instead of authoring — so the catalog `list()` now omits draft-write on MCP
entirely, steering the model to `conversation_start` (the only working authoring
entry point). `resolve()` deliberately still returns the disabled descriptor so
the call-time `not_available_on_surface` backstop stays intact for any client
that guesses the bare name. List and resolve intentionally disagree here, which
is safe because such a call can never execute on this surface.

### Surface

`"chat" | "mcp"` — drives visibility filtering and envelope rendering. No
surface-specific logic in the dispatcher itself; per-surface concerns live in
adapters.

### ToolEnvelope (status-discriminated)

```ts
type ToolEnvelope =
  | { status: "ok"; data: unknown; pause?; committed_workflow_id? }
  | { status: "error"; error_code; message; details?; next_best_actions? }
  | { status: "needs_confirm"; confirm: ConfirmEnvelope }
  | { status: "paused"; pause: ToolResultPause }
  | { status: "not_available_on_surface"; reason: string };
```

Replaces the legacy `ok: true | false` discriminated union from
`conversations/tools/index.ts:178`. The status discriminator makes the surface
adapters trivially total — each adapter has exactly one case per status.

### Provider, Registry, Dispatcher

Providers contribute descriptors + executors:

| Provider | Contributes |
|---|---|
| `StaticToolProvider` | MCP-unique handlers: `authenticate`, `list_recipes`, `self_healing.scan`. |
| `ConversationToolProvider` | everything in `conversations/tools/index.ts:listTools()`, filtered per `(surface, mcpMode, readOnly)`. |

`buildRegistry(providers)` enforces cross-provider name uniqueness at boot.
`registry.get(name, filter)` resolves an executor; `registry.list(filter)` gives
the visible catalog.

`dispatchTool(deps, invocation)` runs one pipeline for both surfaces:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Call["tool call (chat or MCP)"] --> Resolve{"registry.get(name)"}
    Resolve -->|miss| NotFound["tool_not_found"]
    Resolve -->|hit| Vis{"descriptor.disabled?"}
    Vis -->|yes| NAS["not_available_on_surface<br/>→ conversation_start"]
    Vis -->|no| Policy{"policyDecide(category)"}
    Policy -->|tenant_read · safe input| Proceed["proceed"]
    Policy -->|tenant_write · destructive input| Confirm["needs_confirm"]
    Policy -->|surface mismatch| NAS
    Confirm -->|operator approves| Proceed
    Confirm -->|operator declines| Reject["error: declined"]
    Proceed --> Audit["audit: APPROVAL_REQUESTED / APPROVED"]
    Audit --> Exec["execute executor"]
    Exec --> Norm["normalize → ToolEnvelope"]
    Norm --> Log["log: tool.dispatch.invoke"]
```

The seven stages in order: **resolve** → `tool_not_found` on miss · **visibility**
→ `not_available_on_surface` on `disabled` · **policy** → `proceed | needs_confirm
| not_available` · **audit** → `APPROVAL_*` rows · **execute** the resolved
executor · **normalize** into a `ToolEnvelope` · **log** one `tool.dispatch.invoke`
event per call.

### Policy gate (unified)

`policyDecide()` is a **pure synchronous function** that subsumes both
`resolveToolMode()` (chat) and `gateTenantToolCall()` (MCP). Audit is emitted by
the dispatcher, not the gate.

```ts
type PolicyDecision =
  | { kind: "proceed" }
  | { kind: "needs_confirm"; envelope: ConfirmEnvelope }
  | { kind: "not_available_on_surface"; reason: string };
```

| Category | Read / write | Default decision |
|---|---|---|
| `tenant_read` | reads tenant state | `proceed` (unless input predicates escalate it) |
| `tenant_write` | mutates tenant state | `needs_confirm` for destructive input |
| `draft_write` | authors a draft | MCP: `not_available_on_surface`; chat: in-loop |

**Key behavioral change vs. the legacy paths: no `tenant_read` shortcut.** The
legacy MCP gate (`policy-gate.ts:84`) returned `proceed` for every `tenant_read`
tool, ignoring `computeModeFromInput` predicates. The unified gate consults
`resolveToolMode` for every category, so `probe_connector` POST against prod
gates correctly on both surfaces.

## Adapters

The dispatcher is surface-agnostic; adapters translate the single `ToolEnvelope`
into each surface's wire shape.

### MCP adapter (`mcp/adapter.ts`)

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `listToolsViaRegistry(opts)` | `Tool[]` for `tools/list`. |
| `callToolViaDispatcher(opts)` | `{isError, content[], _meta}` for `tools/call`. |
| `buildMcpStubCtx(opts)` | minimal `ToolContext` so conversation tools run against an MCP caller without a real conversation session. |

Envelope rendering:

| ToolEnvelope.status        | MCP response                                                                                  |
|----------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `ok`                       | `{isError:false, content:[text(JSON.stringify(data))]}`                                       |
| `error`                    | `{isError:true,  content:[text({error_code, message, details, next_best_actions})]}`          |
| `needs_confirm`            | `{isError:false, content:[text(confirm)], _meta:{subkit:{confirm}}}`                          |
| `paused`                   | `{isError:false, content:[text(pause)],   _meta:{subkit:{paused}}}`                           |
| `not_available_on_surface` | `{isError:true,  content:[text({error_code:"not_available_on_surface", reason})], _meta:...}` |

### Chat adapter (`conversations/tools/dispatch-adapter.ts`)

- `invokeForSdk(opts)` — single entry point for the chat loop. **Not wired into
  `sdk-wrap.ts` yet** — the chat path stays on its existing inline wrapping
  (which owns rate-limiting, signal handling, event emission, and draft-state
  diff emission). The adapter exists so a future cutover lands in one focused
  change.
- `envelopeToToolResult(envelope)` — back-converts to the legacy `ToolResult`
  shape the conversation loop expects today. The `needs_confirm` case becomes an
  `ask_user_confirm` pause so the elicitation loop picks it up unchanged.

## Decisions and trade-offs

### Probe + test stay separate (no merge)

| Tool | Operation |
|---|---|
| `test_connector` | driver health check |
| `probe_connector` | caller-specified HTTP on a saved connector |
| `probe_connector_draft` | caller HTTP on a pre-creation envelope |

These are **three semantically distinct operations**. The early plan considered
merging probe+test under one tool with a `mode` arg; the audit found two RBAC
permissions, two audit shapes, and two rate-limit semantics — merging them hides
operational distinctions under one schema. We keep all three names; the MCP-side
duplicate of `test_connector` is the only thing deleted.

### `save_workflow_draft` and `dry_run_workflow` are MCP-hidden

Both are draft-write tools: OMITTED from MCP `tools/list`, and a direct
`tools/call` short-circuits to `not_available_on_surface` with a reason pointing
to `conversation_start`. They are driven by the engine's internal authoring loop
inside a conversation, never by the external client.

| Tool | Why it can't run standalone on MCP |
|---|---|
| `save_workflow_draft` | needs an MCP-side confirm protocol that doesn't exist standalone — the `ask_user_confirm` elicitation is conversation-shaped. |
| `dry_run_workflow` | needs a `def`/`draft_id` input extension — it only reads `ctx.getDraft()`. |

Listing them as callable — even badged disabled — only traps clients that ignore
the badge into calling and churning, so they are hidden outright.

### Status-discriminated envelope vs. flat `ok` boolean

The legacy `ToolResult` carried `pause` on both `ok:true` and `ok:false`
branches — an awkward shape because "paused but failed" is not a real state.
Status discrimination makes the four valid states explicit and totally
narrowable.

### No HTTP `/v1/tools/:name` surface (yet)

The dispatcher is surface-agnostic, but adding a third per-surface adapter
without a caller violates YAGNI. When an HTTP caller appears, the adapter is a
40-line file.

### Audit lives in the dispatcher

`policyDecide()` is pure. Audit emission (`APPROVAL_REQUESTED`,
`APPROVAL_APPROVED`) happens in the dispatcher around the policy decision. This
keeps the gate testable without DB and centralizes the audit semantics. Per-tool
audits (e.g. `recordConnectorInvoked` inside `test_connector`) continue to fire
from inside the tool's executor.

### Elicitation audit is a tri-state — transport ≠ approval

An elicitation resolve audit row carries up to three independent facts, and they
must not be conflated:

| Fact | Values | Records |
|---|---|---|
| `action` | `APPROVAL_APPROVED` · `APPROVAL_REJECTED` | the *governance decision* |
| `decision_reason` | `user_declined`, `oauth_timeout`, `elicitation_transport_failed`, … | machine code behind a cancel |
| `elicitation_transport` | `succeeded` · `failed` | whether a `protocol_native` bridge round-trip *delivered* — not whether it was approved |

Crucially, `elicitation_transport: "succeeded"` can coexist with a `cancelled`
resolution: a clean bridge round-trip whose operator declined, or did not
acknowledge an OAuth authorization, succeeded *as transport* but rejected *as a
decision*. An audit query for "successful elicitations" must therefore filter on
`action` / `decision_reason`, not on `elicitation_transport` — equating transport
success with approval double-counts every declined-but-delivered prompt.

## Layout

```
apps/engine/src/tools/
├── types.ts                    ToolDescriptor, ToolEnvelope, ToolInvocation, etc.
├── registry.ts                 ToolRegistry interface + buildRegistry()
├── policy.ts                   policyDecide() — pure unified policy gate
├── dispatcher.ts               dispatchTool() — the orchestrator
├── index.ts                    barrel
├── providers/
│   ├── static.ts               StaticToolProvider — MCP-unique handlers
│   └── conversation.ts         ConversationToolProvider — listTools() wrapper
└── tests/
    ├── registry.test.ts
    ├── dispatcher.test.ts
    ├── policy-decide.test.ts
    ├── result-shape-invariants.test.ts
    └── cross-surface-parity.test.ts

apps/engine/src/mcp/
├── adapter.ts                  listToolsViaRegistry / callToolViaDispatcher
└── tests/
    ├── tools-call-parity.test.ts
    ├── policy-gate-snapshot.test.ts
    ├── tools-list-disabled.test.ts
    ├── preview-attachment-flat-name.test.ts
    └── test-connector-dedupe.test.ts

apps/engine/src/conversations/tools/
├── dispatch-adapter.ts         invokeForSdk / envelopeToToolResult
└── tests/
    └── dispatcher-parity.test.ts
```

## Cross-refs

- [`docs/concepts/glossary.md`](../concepts/glossary.md) — vocabulary (workflow, connector, skill).
- [`docs/developers/input-surfaces.md`](./input-surfaces.md) — how chat/MCP/HTTP surfaces map to the conversation loop.

- `AGENTS.md` lines 142–185 — subsystem map (the row for `tools` lives here).

## Cutover plan

Tests-first: characterization tests in `mcp/tests/policy-gate-snapshot.test.ts`
and `mcp/tests/tools-call-parity.test.ts` pin current behavior. The new-behavior
tests in `apps/engine/src/tools/tests/` and the new MCP tests are `test.todo`
until their implementation commit lands.

The cutover in `mcp/capabilities/tools.ts` inserts a single early-return that
delegates to `mcp/adapter.callToolViaDispatcher()` for any tool the unified
registry recognizes; everything else falls through to the legacy prefix proxies
(`conversation.*`, `wf.<slug>`). The named-tool branches (authenticate,
list_recipes, test_connector, etc.) have all been deleted — the registry claims
those names exclusively.

The `tenant_*` prefix aliases have been **removed**. Every conversation tool
already surfaces under its bare name via the unified registry, so the aliases
were a pure duplicate that doubled the catalog and degraded tool-selection
accuracy on large clients. Bare names dispatch through the unified dispatcher,
which applies the same RBAC + policy gate the aliases did. Only `conversation.*`
session-management tools (`conversation_start`, `conversation_append`,
`conversation_commit`, `conversation_respond_elicitation`, `conversation_get`)
remain on the legacy path because they are MCP-specific session orchestration,
not LLM tool palette items.

The chat side keeps its existing `sdk-wrap.ts` inline path; the
`dispatch-adapter.invokeForSdk` entry exists for a future focused cutover but is
not invoked at runtime yet.
