# Admins — govern access

**Govern your tenants, identity, RBAC, secrets, and hardening — so a team moves fast while every run stays permission-checked, scoped, and audited.**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[quickstart.md] --> C[configuration.md]
    C --> S[settings-reference.md]
    Q --> R[rbac-and-roles.md]
    Q --> K[credentials-and-keys.md]
    C --> H[production-hardening.md]
    R --> H
    K --> H
```

Start at **quickstart.md** to wire configuration, roles, and keys in one pass. From there, **configuration.md** (with the generated **settings-reference.md**) governs the engine, **rbac-and-roles.md** governs who can do what, **credentials-and-keys.md** governs secrets, and **production-hardening.md** is the final checklist before you go live.

| Page | What it covers |
|---|---|
| [quickstart.md](quickstart.md) | Wire configuration, roles, and keys for a production tenant so every run is permission-checked and audited. |
| [configuration.md](configuration.md) | The `sk settings` model: one validated config or the engine refuses to boot — file, resolution order, bootstrap env. |
| [settings-reference.md](settings-reference.md) | Generated per-leaf reference: path, type, default, scope, sensitive, requiresRestart. |
| [rbac-and-roles.md](rbac-and-roles.md) | Identity (OIDC/SSO, API keys, portal tokens), RBAC/ABAC roles, and Before-Request Hooks. |
| [credentials-and-keys.md](credentials-and-keys.md) | The credential vault, master-key rotation, and release signing — secrets encrypted at rest and rotated on demand. |
| [production-hardening.md](production-hardening.md) | The readiness checklist plus backup and recovery to ship production-ready, audit-ready, and recoverable. |

<!-- Source: docs/admins/configuration.md -->

# Configuring the engine

**Outcome: one validated configuration, or the engine refuses to boot.**
There is no silent degraded mode. Every runtime setting lives in a single
JSON file, type-checked against a schema at startup — a misconfig fails fast
with the exact leaf path, so a broken deploy never reaches production traffic.

| You want | You run |
| --- | --- |
| Interactive form | `sk settings configure` |
| Scriptable access | `sk settings list / get / set` |
| Hand edit | `vim subkit.config.json`, then restart |

The per-leaf reference (type, default, scope, sensitivity, restart flag) is
auto-generated in
[`settings-reference.md`](./settings-reference.md). **This page covers the
model around it** — where the file lives, how a value resolves, what stays in
env, and how incident overrides work.

### How a value resolves

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    boot([Engine boot]) --> env{Bootstrap env\nMASTER_KEY, NODE_ENV,\nSUBKIT_CONFIG, DATABASE_URL}
    env --> load[Load subkit.config.json\nmissing file = schema defaults]
    load --> validate{Validate against\nZod schema}
    validate -- invalid --> fail[Exit non-zero\nwith exact leaf path]
    validate -- valid --> ready([Engine ready])

    read([Every settings read]) --> o{SK_OVERRIDE_KEY set?}
    o -- yes --> useo[Use override\nall tenants]
    o -- no --> t{Tenant overlay?}
    t -- yes --> uset[Use tenant value]
    t -- no --> g{Global value set?}
    g -- yes --> useg[Use global value]
    g -- no --> d[Use schema default]
```

Precedence, highest to lowest: **`SK_OVERRIDE_<KEY>` env → tenant overlay →
global value → schema default.**

---

## Bootstrap env (the only env vars the engine reads at startup)

| Variable | Required | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MASTER_KEY` | yes | 64-char hex AES-256-GCM key. Used to encrypt connector credentials at rest. Generate once with `openssl rand -hex 32`. Must be injected from a secret manager — keep it out of the config file. |
| `NODE_ENV` | no | `development` (default in dev) / `test` / `production`. Controls the `requiresRestart` guard and other defaults. |
| `SUBKIT_CONFIG` | no | Override the config-file path. Defaults to `./subkit.config.json` in dev or `/etc/subkit/subkit.config.json` under `NODE_ENV=production`. |
| `DATABASE_URL` | fallback | Consulted only when `database.url` is absent from the config file. Once the operator runs `sk settings set database.url '"…"'` the file value wins; if both are set and they differ the engine emits a warn line at boot and the **config-file value wins**. |

Every other historical env var (`LLM_PROVIDER`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`,
`OIDC_*`, `SLACK_*`, `LANGFUSE_*`, …) has moved to
`subkit.config.json`. Setting any of them at runtime emits a one-line
stderr warning at boot pointing at `sk settings configure`.

## The config file

`subkit.config.json` (or whatever `SUBKIT_CONFIG` points at). On a
fresh install the engine treats a missing file as "use schema
defaults" — the operator never has to hand-write the file.

- **Mode:** `0600`. Parent directory: `0700`. Both created
  automatically on first write.
- **Format:** JSON. Hand-edits are valid; the engine validates
  against the Zod schema at boot and exits non-zero with the
  precise leaf path when something is malformed.
- **Atomicity:** writes go through a same-directory temp file +
  `fsync(file)` + `fsync(parentDir)` + `rename`. A crashed write
  leaves the prior file intact.

### Sections

The schema groups leaves by section. Defaults live in the schema, so
the file only needs to carry overrides:

```jsonc
{
  "log":     { "level": "info", "format": "ndjson" },
  "server":  { "port": 3000, "public_base_url": "https://api.example.com" },
  "database":{ "url": "postgresql://..." },
  "llm":     { "provider": "anthropic",
               "api_key":  "…",                 // sensitive, masked everywhere
               "providers": { "anthropic": { "model": "claude-sonnet-4-6" } } },
  "auth":    { "oidc": { "issuer_url": "…" }, "session": { "secret": "auto-generated" } },
  "platform":      { "slack": { … }, "teams": { … }, "googlechat": { … } },
  "storage":       { "s3": { … }, "knowledge": { "backend": "local" } },
  "observability": { "langfuse": { "secret_key": "…" }, "otlp": { "endpoint": "…" } },
  "egress":        { "mode": "permissive", "provider_hosts_extra": [] },
  "mcp":     { "read_only": false },
  "errors":  { "ring_size": 100 },
  "spec":    { "allow_private_fetch": false },
  "queue":   { "concurrency": 8 },
  "tokens":  { "monthly_budget": 0 },

  "tenants": {
    "<tenant_id>": {
      // Only `scope: "tenant"` leaves are honored here. The schema
      // ships llm.* + queue.concurrency + tokens.monthly_budget as
      // tenant-overridable; everything else is global.
      "llm": { "api_key": "tenant-specific" }
    }
  }
}
```

### Resolution order (every read)

`SK_OVERRIDE_<KEY>` env var → tenant overlay → global value → schema
default (see the boot/read flowchart above).

| Layer | Scope | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SK_OVERRIDE_<KEY>` | All tenants (no per-tenant override env) | Incident-response env injection |
| Tenant overlay | One tenant, `scope: tenant` leaves only | `sk settings set … --tenant <id>` |
| Global value | All tenants | `sk settings set …` |
| Schema default | All tenants | Shipped in the schema |

## `sk settings configure` — interactive form

```bash
sk settings configure                      # open the form
sk settings configure --tab llm            # land on the llm section
sk settings configure --tenant <id>        # show only scope:tenant leaves
sk settings configure --non-interactive    # print JSON for piping / CI
```

The form is auto-detected as headless when stdin or stdout is not a
TTY, or when `--non-interactive` is passed; in that mode it prints
the `GET /v1/settings` response unchanged.

Keyboard model:

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Tab` / `Shift-Tab` | Next / previous section |
| `↑` / `↓` | Move row cursor |
| `Enter` | Edit the selected leaf |
| `/` | Filter by path or description |
| `Esc` (in search) | Clear the query and exit search |
| `Esc` / `q` | Exit the form |
| `Ctrl-R` (in editor) | Reveal a masked secret |
| `Y` / `N` | Restart-required prompt: retry with `force=true` / cancel |

Every successful write emits a `settings.changed` audit row carrying
the actor's principal, the target tenant (if any), and a masked
diff. Raw secrets never appear in audit rows.

## Headless: `sk settings list / get / set`

```bash
sk settings list                                    # tree + diagnostics
sk settings get llm.api_key                          # one leaf
sk settings set llm.api_key '"sk-…"'                 # JSON value
sk settings set server.port 3001 --force             # bypass the
                                                     # requiresRestart guard
sk settings set llm.api_key '"…"' --tenant <id>      # tenant overlay
```

`set` accepts JSON for the value (`'"abc"'`, `42`, `true`, `null`).
`--force` is required in production for any leaf marked
`requiresRestart: true` — the engine writes the value but tells you
to restart for the change to take full effect.

`log.level` and `log.format` are explicitly **hot-reloaded** at the
moment of write — `requiresRestart: false`. The setting.applied log
line documenting the change is emitted *before* the live logger is
reconfigured, so an operator who flips `log.level=error` still sees
the entry that flipped the threshold.

## SK_OVERRIDE_<KEY> — incident escape hatch

To rotate an LLM key under pressure without going through the
config file:

```bash
SK_OVERRIDE_LLM_API_KEY=sk-new-key engine
```

- Active overrides surface in `/v1/diagnostics/setup` and as
  `settings_override_active{key}` on `/metrics`.
- The override value never appears in `GET /v1/settings`, audit
  rows, or any other operator-readable surface — only the leaf
  path is visible.
- The override applies to **all** tenants. There is no per-tenant
  override env var.
- A boot warn line lists active overrides so they can't accumulate
  silently across container restarts.

## `engine_settings` table

The `engine_settings` table is internal-only — only the bootstrap
probe reads/writes it for sentinel state. Two keys:

| key | shape | purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bootstrap.completed` | `boolean` | Sentinel flipped after the first-run setup wizard succeeds. Prevents `sk init` from re-arming on a populated engine. |
| `bootstrap.token` | `{ token_sha256, expires_at_ms }` | Hashed one-time token + 15-minute TTL printed in the boot banner. Consumed by `POST /v1/setup`; deleted on success. |

## Quality gates wired into `bun run verify`

- `check:settings-doc-drift` — regenerates
  `docs/admins/settings-reference.md` and fails if it differs.
- `check:config-example-drift` — regenerates
  `subkit.config.example.json` and fails if it differs.
- The route's wire shape is locked down by the
  `apps/engine/src/http/routes/__tests__/settings.integration.test.ts`
  testcontainers test (audit identity, three response envelopes,
  scope rules).
- The Ink form's bridge is locked down by the schema-walk test in
  `apps/sk/src/settings-ui/__tests__/schema-walk.test.ts` — a new
  Zod kind in the schema fails the test until a corresponding
  `FormFieldKind` lands.

## Operational guarantees

- **Fail-fast boot.** Missing or invalid required settings exit non-zero with
  a descriptive, leaf-pathed error. No silent degraded mode.
- **Secrets stay out of the file.** Database passwords and API keys belong in a
  secrets manager, env injection (`MASTER_KEY`), or the masked, audited
  `sk settings` path — never in committed config.
- **OpenAI-compatible endpoints.** To point the `openai` provider at a
  self-hosted or third-party endpoint (custom `base_url`), see
  [AI-Assisted Authoring → OpenAI-compatible endpoints](../authors/authoring-workflows.md#openai-compatible-endpoints).
- **Resource-limit tunables** (timeouts, token budgets, ingestion/knowledge byte
  caps, circuit breakers) are kept cohesive in
  [Observability & Resource Limits](../operators/observability.md#resource-limits-and-operational-safety).

## See also

- [`settings-reference.md`](./settings-reference.md) — auto-generated
  per-leaf reference (path, type, default, scope, sensitive,
  requiresRestart).

<!-- Source: docs/admins/credentials-and-keys.md -->

# Credentials & Keys

**Every integration secret is encrypted at rest, rotated on demand, and never
logged, returned in an API response, or shown to the AI.** That property is what
lets a regulated tenant put Stripe keys, OAuth refresh tokens, and database
passwords behind sk without auditing each one by hand.

This is the admin home for the three primitives that enforce it:

| Primitive | What it protects | Rotates by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Credential vault** | Every integration secret (API keys, OAuth2 tokens, connection strings) | Re-issue per credential |
| **`MASTER_KEY`** | The AEAD key that encrypts the vault at rest | Redeploy + re-onboard (no envelope) |
| **Release-signing key** | Self-updates of the `engine` and `sk` binaries | Transitional signed release |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Vault["Credential vault — secrets at rest"]
        direction TB
        In["ask_user_form<br/>(masked, sensitive)"] --> Enc["AES-256-GCM encrypt<br/>AAD = tenant_id:cred_id"]
        Enc --> Row[("credentials row<br/>ciphertext + oauth2_refresh_ciphertext")]
    end

    MK["MASTER_KEY<br/>(env-only, never on disk)"] -. keys .-> Enc
    Row -- decrypt at use --> Drv["Driver / Connector"]
    Vault -. blocked .-x AI["AI context"]

    subgraph OAuth["OAuth2 auto-refresh"]
        direction TB
        Drv --> Exp{"access token<br/>expired?"}
        Exp -- no --> Call["call upstream"]
        Exp -- yes --> Refresh["refresh w/ stored token"]
        Refresh --> Reenc["re-encrypt rotated tokens"]
        Reenc --> Row
        Refresh --> Call
    end

    subgraph Rotate["MASTER_KEY rotation lifecycle"]
        direction TB
        Leak["key leaked / cadence / incident"] --> Freeze["freeze writes"]
        Freeze --> Snap["DB snapshot"]
        Snap --> NewKey["new key via secret manager"]
        NewKey --> Invalidate["invalidate ciphertext<br/>(truncate / blank)"]
        Invalidate --> Boot["boot on new key"]
        Boot --> Reissue["re-issue every credential"]
    end

    MK -. rotation invalidates .-> Rotate
    Reissue -. repopulates .-> Vault
```

---

## Rotating MASTER_KEY

> **Read first:** rotating `MASTER_KEY` invalidates every payload encrypted
> under it. The engine uses AES-256-GCM with no key-id envelope — there is
> no "old key" the engine can fall back to. This section describes what
> breaks, what to recover, and the operator-facing downtime window.

### When you must rotate

| Trigger | Rotate? |
| --- | --- |
| Key value leaked (committed to git, posted in chat, exfiltrated from backup) | **Yes** |
| Regulator / customer mandates a fixed cadence | **Yes** |
| Incident response demands it | **Yes** |
| Engine host compromised but key never on disk (injected at boot from a secret manager) | **No** — payloads at rest are useless without the key |

### Blast radius

`apps/engine/src/crypto/aes-gcm.ts` loads `env.MASTER_KEY` once at boot. Every
store below holds ciphertext keyed by that single key — rotation invalidates
every row in every one of them.

Each row is a Drizzle `pgTable` with at least one `bytea` column written through
`encryptSecret()` and read through `decryptSecret()`. The SQL name is the first
arg to `pgTable()`, verified against the schema file.

| SQL table | Encrypted column(s) | Schema definition | What's lost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `credentials` | `ciphertext` (NOT NULL), `oauth2_refresh_ciphertext` | `db/schema/connectors.ts:129` | Static secrets + OAuth access/refresh tokens for every connector instance. |
| `end_user_credentials` | `ciphertext` (NOT NULL) | `db/schema/connectors.ts:155` | Per-end-user OAuth secrets for portal flows. |
| `connector_template_credentials` | `ciphertext` (NOT NULL) | `db/schema/connector_template_credentials.ts` | Tenant-overridden template secrets. |
| `workflow_run_state` | `ciphertext` (NOT NULL) | `db/schema/workflow_run_state.ts` | Reverse-ETL watermarks and tenant-encrypted run state. |
| `webhooks_inbound` | `secret_ciphertext` (NOT NULL) | `db/schema/webhooks.ts:19` | Signing secrets for incoming webhooks (row also holds slug + verifier config). |
| `webhooks_outbound` | `secret_ciphertext` (NOT NULL), `rotating_secret_ciphertext` | `db/schema/webhooks.ts:75` | Signing secrets for outgoing webhooks (row also holds URL config). |
| `chat_workspaces` | `bot_ciphertext` (NOT NULL) | `db/schema/chat.ts:20` | Chat-platform bot tokens (row also holds workspace metadata). |
| `auth_provider_configs` | `config_ciphertext` (nullable) | `db/schema/identity.ts:208` | OIDC client secrets (issuer URL + client_id survive). |
| `tenant_llm_settings` | `llm_provider_credentials_ciphertext` (nullable) | `db/schema/llm.ts` | Tenant LLM provider API keys (model + provider config survive). |

Three invalidation classes drive the recovery SQL:

| Class | Tables | How to invalidate | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pure secret | `credentials`, `end_user_credentials`, `connector_template_credentials`, `workflow_run_state` | `TRUNCATE … CASCADE` | Row identity *is* the secret. |
| Secret + config, NOT NULL | `webhooks_inbound`, `webhooks_outbound`, `chat_workspaces` | `TRUNCATE … CASCADE`, re-create via API | Secret column can't be blanked in place; config rides along. |
| Nullable secret | `auth_provider_configs`, `tenant_llm_settings` | `SET … = NULL` | Config (issuer URL, client_id, model) survives; operator re-enters the leaf. |

Tenant-isolation is preserved by AAD binding (`aadFor(tenant_id, …)`), so a
leaked key still requires per-row knowledge to forge — but **legitimate decrypt
also fails after rotation**. There is no key-rotation envelope today.

### Recovery sequence

1. **Freeze writes.** Stop the engine on every host serving the tenant pool
   you're rotating. New encrypts under the old key during the transition are
   lost.
   ```sh
   docker stop subkit
   ```

2. **Take a database snapshot.** The only path back if rotation goes wrong.
   ```sh
   ssh ${HOST} 'pg_dump -Fc subkit > /opt/subkit/backups/pre-rotate-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).dump'
   ```

3. **Generate the new key + inject via your secret manager.**
   ```sh
   openssl rand -hex 32   # 64 hex chars; 32 bytes
   ```
   Update the secret store (Doppler / 1Password / DigitalOcean app-level env /
   `.env` for self-hosters) — never commit to git, never write to the config
   file. `MASTER_KEY` is the one bootstrap env that stays outside
   `subkit.config.json` (see [Configuration](configuration.md)).

4. **Invalidate every ciphertext keyed by the old `MASTER_KEY`.** Run as a
   single transaction so a partial failure doesn't leave half-rotated state.
   Verify each table name against your migration before running.
   ```sql
   BEGIN;

     -- Pure secret stores. The row identity is the secret; TRUNCATE drops
     -- the row entirely, then it gets re-issued in step 6.
     TRUNCATE
       credentials,
       end_user_credentials,
       connector_template_credentials,
       workflow_run_state
       CASCADE;

     -- Mixed secret-and-config rows: secret column is NOT NULL so it
     -- cannot be blanked in place. Drop the rows and re-create through
     -- the engine API in steps 6–7. CASCADE clears dependent
     -- subscriptions/deliveries/sessions rows.
     TRUNCATE
       webhooks_inbound,
       webhooks_outbound,
       chat_workspaces
       CASCADE;

     -- Nullable secret columns: blank in place; the row's config
     -- (issuer URL, client_id, model name, etc.) survives. Operators
     -- re-enter just the credential through the engine API.
     UPDATE auth_provider_configs SET config_ciphertext = NULL;
     UPDATE tenant_llm_settings   SET llm_provider_credentials_ciphertext = NULL;

   COMMIT;
   ```
   (If your migration names a column or table differently, correct it before
   running. The canonical column list is the Blast-radius table above.)

5. **Boot the engine on the new key.** Watch the boot log; the crypto layer
   asserts key length / hex shape at module load
   (`apps/engine/src/crypto/aes-gcm.ts:48-53`) and exits non-zero if the key is
   malformed.
   ```sh
   docker start subkit
   docker logs --since 1m subkit
   ```
   `/v1/health` should return `db_connected: true` within 30s.

6. **Re-issue every connector credential.** For each tenant × connector:
   - Regenerate static API keys at the upstream system (Stripe, GitHub, etc.)
     and re-add via `sk connectors credentials set`.
   - Re-run OAuth flows for OAuth-based connectors. The stored refresh tokens
     are gone — there is no silent re-auth path.

7. **Re-create every webhook subscription.** `webhooks_inbound` and
   `webhooks_outbound` were truncated, so the routing rows are also gone.
   - Inbound: re-create each subscription (slug + verifier + fresh secret) and
     update every upstream webhook configuration.
   - Outbound: re-create each subscription (URL + fresh signing secret) and
     update every consumer's verification config.

8. **Re-create every chat-platform workspace.** `chat_workspaces` was truncated
   — every Slack/Teams/Google Chat workspace must be re-installed and
   re-onboarded through the platform's add-app flow.

9. **Re-enter OIDC client secrets and tenant LLM API keys.** These tables
   (`auth_provider_configs`, `tenant_llm_settings`) kept their non-secret
   config; operators just re-enter the redacted credential leaf. CLI:
   `sk settings set auth.oidc.client_secret '"…"'` and per-tenant `llm.api_key`.

10. **Verify.** Hit `${ENGINE_URL}/v1/health` and run the tenant-scoped
    integration smoke; expect zero `decrypt_failed` `CryptoError` entries in the
    structured log.

### Downtime window

| Phase | Steps | Window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mandatory downtime** | 1 (freeze) → 5 (boot on new key) | ~5–15 min for a single host |
| **Re-onboarding** (engine running) | 6–9 | Runs in parallel; tenants see broken connectors, webhook signatures, chat integrations, OIDC sign-ins, and LLM calls until each is re-issued |

### Why there is no in-engine "rotate" command

The crypto layer is intentionally simple — one key, one algorithm, no key-id
envelope. Adding one is a real refactor: every encrypted column gains a
`key_version` field, the read path must dispatch on it, and the worker pool must
hold both keys during a window. Until that lands, rotation is a redeploy, not a
click.

If you need rotation without re-issuing every credential, that is the work to
commission — it is not a runbook task.

---

## The Credential Vault

All integration secrets — API keys, OAuth2 access and refresh tokens, database
passwords, connection strings — are stored in the credential vault, encrypted
with AES-256-GCM.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    User["User / Operator"]
    Form["ask_user_form<br/>(masked, sensitive: true)"]
    Vault[("Credential Vault<br/>AES-256-GCM<br/>AAD = credential:tenant_id:cred_id")]
    Conn["Connector"]
    Driver["Driver"]
    AI["AI context<br/>(never sees secret)"]

    User --> Form --> Vault
    Conn -- cred_id only --> Vault
    Vault -- decrypt at use --> Driver
    Vault -. blocked .-x AI
```

**Guarantees**

| Property | How it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Never logged / returned / shown to AI | Connectors reference credentials by identifier; the vault resolves to the secret only at the moment of use. Outside that moment the raw value exists in neither memory nor any logged context. |
| OAuth2 refresh is automatic | The engine owns the full lifecycle — access-token expiry, refresh-token rotation, re-authorization. Connectors never see an expired token. |
| End-user overrides | A user can supply their own credential for a connector (e.g. personal GitHub vs the org integration) with no operator involvement — same vault, same encryption. |

The conversational secret-handling defences that keep a credential out of LLM
tool arguments and transcripts live in
[Governance & Audit → Secret Hygiene](../concepts/governance-and-audit.md#secret-hygiene-at-the-conversational-surface).

---

## Self-update + release signing

The engine and `sk` binaries verify a signed `SHA256SUMS` (Ed25519) on every
`engine --self-update` / `sk update` before they will replace the running
binary. The release workflow signs `SHA256SUMS` with the `RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY`
GitHub secret; the matching public key is committed to
`packages/cli-core/src/release-public-key.ts` and embedded in every binary at
build time.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Trigger(["engine --self-update<br/>or sk update"])
    Fetch["Download new binary<br/>+ signed SHA256SUMS"]
    Verify{"Ed25519 verify<br/>against embedded public key"}
    Park["Park current → ~/.engine/versions/&lt;v&gt;/<br/>(keep last 3 with manifest.json)"]
    Swap["Atomic binary swap<br/>+ process restart"]
    Audit[("audit_log:<br/>engine.update.completed")]
    Fail[("audit_log:<br/>engine.update.failed")]
    Rollback(["engine --rollback"])

    Trigger --> Fetch --> Verify
    Verify -- ok --> Park --> Swap --> Audit
    Verify -- bad signature --> Fail
    Swap -- crash --> Fail
    Rollback -. re-hash retained binary .-> Swap
```

*Atomic swap; failure rolls back automatically; every transition lands in the
audit log under the system tenant. Losing the private key bricks future updates
for any binary that hasn't yet picked up a key rotation — treat it like the
database master key.*

### Audit trail

Every binary swap writes a pair of rows to `audit_log` under
`tenant_id = 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` (system tenant) with
`actor_type = system`, `actor_id = null` — the change is process-level, with no
`system_accounts` row backing it. `metadata.request_source` distinguishes
`self-update` from `rollback`.

| Action | Emitted when | `result` |
|---|---|---|
| `engine.update.initiated` | Before download / before retained-binary swap | `success` |
| `engine.update.completed` | `engine --self-update` succeeded | `success` |
| `engine.update.rolled_back` | `engine --rollback` succeeded | `success` |
| `engine.update.failed` | The swap threw at any point after INITIATED | `error` |

`metadata` carries `from_version`, `to_version`, `channel`, `sha256` (64-char
hex of the verified binary, or empty before verification), and
`request_source ∈ {self-update, rollback}`.

Both flags also emit a structured log entry under `module: "self-update"` and
bump `engine_update_total{result, channel}` (Prometheus). The `result` label is
one of `success`, `failed`, `rollback` — kept in lockstep with the audit-action
vocabulary so an SRE joining the metric to `audit_log` doesn't have to remember
an off-by-one.

### Risk-signal edges (`risk_signal_edges`)

`risk_signal_edges` (`db/schema/audit.ts`, used by `operator/risk-signals.ts`)
is the shared, cross-replica edge-state store that backs risk-signal raising.
Risk signals describe host-global infrastructure (one Postgres pool, one set of
DLQs, one engine RSS), so a standing critical must be audited exactly once per
`false→true` edge across the whole deployment — not once per digest read, per
reading tenant, or per replica. The signal builder runs on every MCP connect,
resource read, REPL start, and status call, so auditing inline would otherwise
flood `audit_log`. The risk-signal surface itself is documented in
[Observability](../operators/observability.md).

The table is keyed by signal `kind` (host-global, no `tenant_id`). Each replica
claims an edge through a microsecond-safe `INSERT … ON CONFLICT … WHERE` CAS
(`operator/risk-signals.ts` around lines 234–251) so exactly one replica wins
the `false→true` transition and the others observe no edge — two replicas cannot
double-raise the same edge. The winning replica audits `RISK_SIGNAL_RAISED`
(under the system tenant, since the signal is host-scoped). Recovery clears the
row, so a recovered-then-recurring signal re-fires exactly once on its next
occurrence.

### Rollback

The updater retains the last 3 signed binaries under
`~/.engine/versions/<version>/` together with a sidecar `manifest.json`
recording the SHA256 captured at retention time. `rollbackTo` re-hashes the
retained binary against the manifest and refuses to swap on hash drift.

```bash
engine --rollback              # restore the most recent retained binary
engine --rollback --to=7.0.0   # restore a specific retained version
```

`sk update --rollback` is the same path. The rolled-back binary is itself
parked, so re-rollback works.

### Key rotation procedure

The Ed25519 release-signing key is rotated through a transitional release that
contains the *new* public key signed by the *old* key. Any operator who
self-updates to that transitional release picks up the new public key; from the
next release onward the old private key is retired.

```bash
# 1. Generate a fresh keypair. Writes the new public key into the repo;
#    prints the matching private key once to stdout.
bun run scripts/generate-release-key.ts

# 2. Paste the printed private key into the GitHub secret.
gh secret set RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY --repo MikeBild/subkit

# 3. Commit the public-key change.
git add packages/cli-core/src/release-public-key.ts
git commit -m "chore: rotate release signing key"

# 4. Cut the transitional release on the BRANCH containing the new
#    public key, signed with the OLD private key (so existing binaries
#    still accept it). The release workflow signs with whatever the
#    secret holds at run time, so rotate the secret only AFTER cutting
#    the transitional release.
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "transitional release — new public key"
git push origin vX.Y.Z

# 5. Once the transitional release is in the wild, flip the secret to
#    the new private key. Subsequent releases sign with the new key,
#    and only binaries that picked up the transitional release will
#    accept them.
```

Losing the private key bricks future updates for any binary that hasn't yet
picked up a key rotation. Treat it like the database master key — back it up,
rotate after operator handover.

## See also

- `apps/engine/src/crypto/aes-gcm.ts` — the encrypt/decrypt primitives.
- `apps/engine/src/env.ts` — how `MASTER_KEY` is loaded and validated.
- `.env.example:18-21` — the warning operators see at first install.
- [Configuration](configuration.md) — why this stays in env, not config.

# Production hardening — known caveats & TODOs

**Outcome:** ship sk **production-ready, audit-ready, and recoverable.** Every
workflow run stays permission-checked, recorded, and replayable — and a clean
operator can rebuild the whole estate from a database backup alone.

This page lists the **deliberate defaults** the engine ships with. Each surfaces
as a loud `warn` line at boot — *not* a bug. For every item: what it is, the
risk, how to close it, and the future TODO.

## Hardening layers at a glance

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Edge["Edge"]
        proxy[Reverse proxy / TLS]
    end
    subgraph App["sk engine — stateless"]
        scan[File AV scan]
        store[Persistent file storage]
        key[MASTER_KEY + credential vault]
    end
    subgraph State["Durable state"]
        pg[(PostgreSQL)]
        ver[Workflow versions]
        audit[Audit log]
    end
    proxy --> scan --> store --> key
    key --> pg
    pg --> ver
    pg --> audit
    pg -. pg_dump / WAL .-> backup[(Backups)]
```

| Layer | Production-ready when | Section |
|---|---|---|
| File AV scan | a real scanner (clamd) answers under budget | [§1](#1-file-uploads-are-not-virus-scanned-scannernoop_in_production) |
| File storage | points at a persistent, backed-up path | [§2](#2-storage-directory-is-set-via-a-config-override-overrideactive) |
| Secrets | `MASTER_KEY` set + rotated | [credentials-and-keys.md](./credentials-and-keys.md) |
| Database | external managed PostgreSQL | [self-host.md](../developers/self-host.md) |
| Recovery | versioned workflows + PG backups | [Backup and Recovery](#backup-and-recovery) |

### Grep the boot warnings

The engine emits these at boot so you can grep for them:

```sh
# from the engine container logs
docker logs subkit 2>&1 | grep -E '"action":"(scanner.noop_in_production|override.active|ephemeral_dir_warning)"'
```

---

## 1. File uploads are NOT virus-scanned (`scanner.noop_in_production`)

### What it is

Every file uploaded into the engine (workflow attachments, inline uploads,
presigned uploads) passes through `getScanner().scan(stream, meta)` before the
file row flips to `status='ready'`. The **default scanner is a no-op**
(`NoopScanner`) — it returns `{ verdict: "clean", engine: "noop" }` for *every*
input without inspecting the bytes.

Boot log when `NODE_ENV=production`:

```
warn  files  scanner.noop_in_production
"FileScanner is NoopScanner in production. Every upload is reported as clean
 until a real scanner is wired. Replace getScanner() with a clamd-backed
 implementation before accepting tenant content."
```

### Risk

| Install shape | Risk | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Single trust boundary (you control every uploader) | **Low** | No untrusted bytes enter the system. |
| Untrusted / multi-tenant uploads | **Real** | A malicious file is accepted and stored unscanned; any later download/processing serves it as-is. Compliance/security hole (no AV gate). |

### Current behavior (by design)

- The upload pipeline calls the scanner **unconditionally** — wiring a real
  backend needs **no route changes**, only the resolver.
- Verdicts:

  | Verdict | File row | Side effect |
  |---|---|---|
  | `clean` | `ready` | — |
  | `infected` | `failed` | `FILE_SCAN_COMPLETED` audit event (verdict + signature) |
  | `timeout` (route wrapper only) | parked in `scanning` | reaped by the cleanup cron |

- Per-call ceiling: `SCANNER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 10` (in `files/scanner.ts`) — a
  real scanner must answer within this budget or the row is parked.

### How to close it (real fix — infra + a small code change)

1. **Provision ClamAV** on the host (or a sidecar):
   ```sh
   apt-get install -y clamav-daemon clamav-freshclam
   systemctl enable --now clamav-freshclam   # virus DB updates
   systemctl enable --now clamav-daemon       # clamd on /var/run/clamav/clamd.ctl or TCP 3310
   ```
2. **Implement a clamd-backed `FileScanner`** and return it from `getScanner()`
   in `apps/engine/src/files/scanner.ts`. The contract to satisfy:
   ```ts
   export interface FileScanner {
     scan(stream: AsyncIterable<Uint8Array>, meta: ScanMeta): Promise<ScanResult>;
   }
   // ScanResult = { verdict: "clean" | "infected" | "timeout"; engine: string; signature?: string }
   ```
   Stream the bytes to clamd (`INSTREAM`), map a clean result to
   `{ verdict: "clean", engine: "clamav/<dbver>" }` and a hit to
   `{ verdict: "infected", engine: "clamav/<dbver>", signature: <name> }`. Keep
   the scan under `SCANNER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`.
3. **Verify:** restart, confirm the boot warning is **gone**, then upload an
   [EICAR test file](https://www.eicar.org/download-anti-malware-testfile/) and
   confirm the file row flips to `failed` with a `FILE_SCAN_COMPLETED` audit row.

### TODO (future)

- [ ] Add `storage.scanner.*` config (backend = `noop | clamav`, host/port/socket,
      timeout) so the scanner is operator-configurable instead of code-swapped.
- [ ] Ship a clamd-backed `FileScanner` and have `getScanner()` construct it from
      that config.
- [ ] Document the AV DB-update cadence (`freshclam`) in `deploy.md`.
- [ ] Gate uploads (refuse, not warn) when `NODE_ENV=production` AND the scanner
      is `noop` AND a future `storage.scanner.require=true` is set.

> **Interim mitigation** if you do not need uploads: there is currently no
> config flag to disable the files surface — open an issue if you want one, or
> restrict the `/v1/files*` routes at the reverse proxy (Caddy) layer.

---

## 2. Storage directory is set via a config override (`override.active`)

### What it is

The engine resolves config from `subkit.config.json` plus **`SK_OVERRIDE_*`
environment overlays** (prefix `SK_OVERRIDE_`, see `config/loader.ts`). In
production, point file storage at a persistent path (e.g. the all-in-one
image's `/data` volume):

```
SK_OVERRIDE_STORAGE_FILES_DIR=/data/files
```

overrides `storage.files.dir`. Boot log:

```
warn  config  override.active   override_keys=["storage.files.dir"]
"SK_OVERRIDE_* active"
```

### Why this is correct (not a problem)

- `storage.files.dir` is **where uploaded files are written on disk**.
- If left **empty** with the `local` backend, `LocalDiskObjectStore` falls back
  to `os.tmpdir()/sk-files` and the engine emits a *different*, more serious
  warning — `ephemeral_dir_warning` — because **tmpdir is wiped on reboot and
  every customer file is lost**.
- Setting it to a **persistent path** (`/var/lib/subkit/files`) is exactly what
  you want: files survive reboots and redeploys. The `override.active` line is
  **pure transparency** — it tells an operator "this value didn't come from the
  default config."

### Action required

**None.** This is the intended production configuration. Keep the directory:

- on persistent storage (not tmpfs),
- backed up if uploads matter,
- owned/writable by the engine's system user.

### TODO (future, optional)

- [ ] Move `storage.files.dir` (and other stable prod values) from a
      `SK_OVERRIDE_*` env into the committed `subkit.config.json` so the
      `override.active` line stops appearing for settled config and overrides are
      reserved for secrets / per-host values.

---

## Quick production readiness checklist

| Item | Default | Production-ready? | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| File AV scan | `NoopScanner` (always clean) | ❌ wire clamd before untrusted uploads | `files/scanner.ts` |
| `storage.files.dir` | empty → ephemeral tmpdir | ✅ set to a persistent path (done via `SK_OVERRIDE_*`) | `config/loader.ts`, `index.ts` |
| `MASTER_KEY` | required | ✅ set; rotate per `credentials-and-keys.md` | `docs/admins/credentials-and-keys.md` |
| PostgreSQL | bundled in the all-in-one image | ✅ for scale, point at an external managed Postgres | `docs/developers/self-host.md` |

See also: [`self-host.md`](../developers/self-host.md) · [`configuration.md`](./configuration.md) ·
[`settings-reference.md`](./settings-reference.md) · [`credentials-and-keys.md`](./credentials-and-keys.md).

---

## Backup and Recovery

**Outcome:** any clean host can rebuild the entire estate from one backup —
workflows, connectors, credentials, executions, audit log, skills, and knowledge
sources all live in PostgreSQL.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Source["sk in production"]
        engine[Engine — stateless]
        pg[(PostgreSQL — single source of truth)]
    end
    engine -. durable queue .-> pg
    pg -->|pg_dump / WAL archive / managed backup| backup[(Backup store)]
    backup -->|restore| pg2[(PostgreSQL)]
    pg2 -->|start| engine2[New engine]
    engine2 -->|in-flight jobs resume| ready[Estate live]
    badversion[Bad deploy] -.->|roll back to version| ready
```

| Property | Guarantee |
|---|---|
| State of record | **PostgreSQL** — back it up and you have backed up sk. |
| Backup method | Standard `pg_dump`, WAL archiving, or managed cloud-database backup. |
| Engine state | **Stateless** — stop, replace, restart with no data loss. |
| In-flight jobs | Durably queued in PostgreSQL; resume automatically on restart. |
| In-memory state | None that must survive a restart. |
| App-level rollback | Every workflow change creates a new **immutable version**; roll back to a known-good version in a single command. History is always available. |

<!-- Source: docs/admins/quickstart.md -->

# Admin Quickstart

**Every workflow run is permission-checked, scoped, and audited — so a team can move fast without losing the governance trail compliance needs.** This page wires that in three steps on an already-running engine: **configuration**, **roles**, and **keys**.

> **Audience:** The admin standing up governance for a team.
> **Time:** ~10 minutes.
> **Prerequisite:** A running engine — see [Self-host](../developers/self-host.md) or the [Operator quickstart](../operators/quickstart.md).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Cfg["1. Configure<br/>(sk settings)"] --> Roles["2. Roles & users<br/>(RBAC)"]
    Roles --> Keys["3. Keys & credentials<br/>(vault + API keys)"]
```

---

## 1. Configure

Runtime configuration lives in a single JSON file managed through `sk settings` — never in scattered `.env` files. Set your LLM provider, database, and any platform integrations, then confirm:

```bash
sk settings configure          # interactive form
sk settings list               # every leaf + resolved value
sk settings get llm.provider
```

The full model — where the file lives, how values resolve, what stays in bootstrap env — is in [Configuration](./configuration.md), and the generated per-leaf table is [settings-reference.md](./settings-reference.md).

## 2. Roles & users

sk ships four built-in roles: **admin**, **member**, **end-user**, and **service account**. Provision teammates and assign roles; create custom roles and resource grants for finer control.

```bash
sk users create --email teammate@example.com --role member
sk users invite <USER_ID>      # single-use invite; the teammate mints their own key
sk roles list
```

The RBAC/ABAC model, identity providers (OIDC/SSO), and Before-Request Hooks are in [RBAC & Roles](./rbac-and-roles.md). The structural guarantees around it — multi-tenant isolation and the audit trail — are in [Governance & Audit](../concepts/governance-and-audit.md).

## 3. Keys & credentials

API keys are the standard programmatic credential — long-lived, revocable, scoped, hashed at rest, shown once. Connector secrets live in the encrypted Credential Vault.

```bash
sk apikeys create --name ci --role service
sk connectors credentials set <CONNECTOR_ID> --mode bearer --token sk_live_…
```

Set your own `MASTER_KEY` in production and learn the rotation procedure before you need it: [Credentials & Keys](./credentials-and-keys.md). Before accepting untrusted uploads or going live, walk [Production hardening](./production-hardening.md).

---

## Further reading

- [Configuration](./configuration.md) · [RBAC & Roles](./rbac-and-roles.md) · [Credentials & Keys](./credentials-and-keys.md) · [Production hardening](./production-hardening.md)
- [Governance & Audit](../concepts/governance-and-audit.md) — the model behind the controls you just wired.

<!-- Source: docs/admins/rbac-and-roles.md -->

# RBAC & Roles

> **Audience:** Security engineers, compliance reviewers, operators wiring access

**Least-privilege by default, every decision auditable.** No caller reaches a connector or a workflow without passing an explicit permission check, and every allow or deny lands in the immutable audit trail. This page covers the access surface: the pluggable identity chain, the built-in and custom roles, resource grants, and the dynamic policy layer added by Before-Request Hooks.

The structural guarantees around it — multi-tenant isolation, the audit trail, the compliance posture — live in [Governance & Audit](../concepts/governance-and-audit.md).

## At a glance

| Layer | Question it answers | Fails to |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | Who is calling? | Reject (401) |
| Role | What class of action may they take? | Deny + audit |
| Grant | Which specific resources, until when? | Deny + audit |
| Before-Request Hook | Is this request allowed *right now*? | Deny + audit (fail-closed) |
| Driver | Execute against the connector | — |

---

## Identity and Authentication

sk authenticates callers through a pluggable chain. Organisations pick the methods that fit their posture; each request resolves to exactly one principal.

| Method | Lifetime | Scope | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OIDC** | Session | Tenant account from token claims | Enterprise SSO (Azure AD, Okta, Google Workspace, any OIDC provider) |
| **API Key** | Long-lived, revocable | Tenant + permission set | Programmatic and CI access |
| **Portal Token** | Short-lived, auto-expiring | Single workflow/conversation | Customer-facing, controlled end-user flows |

**OIDC** provisions tenant accounts from the identity token's claims, so provisioning and deprovisioning stay with the organisation's IdP — users sign in with the credential they already use everywhere.

**API Keys** are hashed before storage; the raw key is shown exactly once at creation and can never be retrieved afterward. Lose one and you mint a replacement and revoke the old. Overlap-window rotation lets a new key go live before the old expires, so access is never interrupted.

**Portal Tokens** carry only the permissions their flow requires — nothing more — and expire automatically. They are the right credential when an end user must touch a specific workflow without becoming a full tenant member.

---

## Role-Based and Attribute-Based Access Control

Every API route, MCP call, and workflow trigger is permission-checked **before** any resource is read or any action is taken. There is no path through the platform that bypasses authorization.

### Persona and permission hierarchy

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Identity["Identity (one principal per request)"]
        OIDC["OIDC session"]
        Key["API key"]
        Portal["Portal token"]
    end

    subgraph Roles["Built-in roles"]
        Admin["admin<br/>full platform control"]
        Member["member<br/>author + trigger"]
        EndUser["end-user<br/>trigger + view"]
        Svc["service account<br/>programmatic, no UI"]
    end

    Custom["Custom roles<br/>(granular permission sets)"]
    Grant["Resource grants<br/>(per-resource, expiring)"]

    OIDC --> Admin & Member & EndUser
    Key --> Svc & Custom
    Portal -. allow-list only .-> Grant

    Admin --> Grant
    Member --> Grant
    EndUser --> Grant
    Custom --> Grant
    Svc --> Grant
```

| Role | Can do | Cannot do |
|---|---|---|
| **admin** | Full platform control: roles, keys, connectors, workflows | — |
| **member** | Author and trigger workflows | Manage tenant identity/keys |
| **end-user** | Trigger and view workflows | Modify any definition |
| **service account** | Programmatic access | Reach any interactive surface |

Beyond the built-ins, operators define **custom roles** for finer control, attach **resource grants** scoped to a single resource with an expiry, and group users for assignment.

### Before-Request Hooks

A Before-Request Hook is a sandboxed script that runs immediately before a connector request executes, adding a dynamic policy layer on top of static RBAC. It receives the full request context — caller identity, target connector, operation type, request parameters — and enforces rules that roles cannot express.

| Property | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Sandbox | Isolated QuickJS-WASM, strict CPU budget |
| Access | No network, no file system, no database |
| Error / timeout | **Fails closed** — request denied |
| Auditing | Every execution recorded in the audit log |

Typical hooks: block writes during a maintenance window, require extra approval for specific production connectors, enforce data-residency constraints, or log requests matching a pattern. The operator how-to for authoring and wiring a hook is in [Scheduling & Hooks](../operators/scheduling-and-hooks.md).

### Policy evaluation order

Evaluation is sequential and short-circuits on the first denial.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Req(["Inbound request<br/>(any surface)"])
    RBAC{{"RBAC<br/>can(actor, action, resource)?"}}
    Hook{{"Before-Request Hook<br/>(sandboxed, fail-closed)"}}
    Driver[/Connector driver/]
    Deny["Deny + audit row<br/>(policy.denied)"]

    Req --> RBAC
    RBAC -- deny --> Deny
    RBAC -- allow --> Hook
    Hook -- abort --> Deny
    Hook -- proceed --> Driver
```

1. **RBAC first.** No permission for the action → denied before the hook is ever consulted.
2. **Hook second.** RBAC passed → the Before-Request Hook runs. If it aborts, the request is denied with the hook's reason.
3. **Driver last.** Only when both pass does the request reach the connector.

### `stats:read` is operator-tier

`stats:read` exposes process-scoped operational signals — grant it only to operator/admin principals on a shared deployment.

The operator health digest (`GET /v1/operator/health-digest`, the `subkit://operator/health-digest` MCP resource, and the on-connect MCP `instructions` summary) is gated on `stats:read`. Its **failing-runs** and **pending-patch** sections are tenant-scoped, but its predictive-maintenance **risk signals** (Postgres-pool saturation, dead-letter-queue growth, transient-DB-retry rate, connector-health mix, LLM-fallback fraction, RSS high-water) read *engine-wide* gauges — the pool, the DLQs, and the host RSS are shared infrastructure, not per-tenant. A principal with `stats:read` on a multi-tenant deployment can therefore infer host-level load that other tenants contribute to.

This is intentional: `stats:read` is the operator-tier permission, and "your runs are fine but the host is about to OOM" is exactly the warning the per-tenant lagging signals cannot give in time.

| Guard | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Portal-token-class principals | **Structurally barred** from `stats:read` regardless of role. The RBAC evaluator short-circuits every identity path (resource grant, group, role) for a `portal_token` provider and admits only the workflow/conversation allow-list (`apps/engine/src/rbac/evaluator.ts:256-306`). A portal token can never resolve `stats:read`, even if a tenant admin mints a custom role carrying it. |
| Audit attribution | Risk values are written to the audit trail under the **system** tenant (`operator.risk_signal_raised` / `operator.risk_signal_cleared`), not the reading tenant's — so the SIEM trail attributes a host condition once rather than per reader. |

---

## Further reading

- [Governance & Audit](../concepts/governance-and-audit.md) — multi-tenancy, the immutable audit trail, the compliance posture, and conversational secret hygiene.
- [Credentials & Keys](./credentials-and-keys.md) — the credential vault, master-key rotation, and release signing.
- [Scheduling & Hooks](../operators/scheduling-and-hooks.md) — the operator how-to for Before-Request Hooks.
- [glossary — governance terms](../concepts/glossary.md#group-5-governance) — Audit Log, RBAC, Before-Request Hook, Self-Healing, Patch Candidate.

# subkit runtime settings

Every value below lives in `subkit.config.json` and is editable via
`sk settings configure` or `sk settings set <path> <value>`. Per-tenant
overrides go into the file's `tenants` section and only honor leaves
tagged `scope=tenant`.

Path resolution: `SK_OVERRIDE_<UPPERCASE_PATH>` env → tenant overlay →
global value → schema default. Overrides apply across all tenants.

Observability

| path | type | default | scope | sensitive | requiresRestart | description |

| `observability.analytics.endpoint` | string | `""` | global | no | no | Self-hostable analytics ingest endpoint. Empty disables emission even when enabled=true. |
| `observability.analytics.project` | string | `""` | global | no | no | Project or workspace identifier on the analytics platform. |
| `observability.field_truncation_chars` | number | `2048` | global | no | no | Per-field cap (in characters / UTF-16 code units, not bytes) applied to structured log fields after redaction. |
| `observability.langfuse.host` | string | `""` | global | no | no |  |
| `observability.langfuse.public_key` | string | `""` | global | no | no |  |

| `observability.otlp.service_name` | string | `"subkit"` | global | no | no |  |
| `observability.predictive.connector_unhealthy_pct` | number | `80` | global | no | no | Percent of recent connector calls returning a non-ok health verdict above which connector drift is flagged. |
| `observability.predictive.dlq_critical_depth` | number | `5` | global | no | no | Standing dead-letter-queue depth at or above which DLQ accumulation is flagged critical (a worker-failure backlog, not a per-window delta). |
| `observability.predictive.llm_fallback_pct` | number | `80` | global | no | no | Percent of LLM calls falling back to the secondary provider above which primary-provider degradation is flagged. |
| `observability.predictive.memory_cap_fraction` | number | `0.9` | global | no | no | Fraction of the host memory cap the RSS high-water may reach before an OOM-risk warning. |
| `observability.predictive.pool_saturation_pct` | number | `80` | global | no | no | Percent of the Postgres pool in use (or any waiting clients) above which saturation is flagged. |
| `observability.predictive.transient_retry_rate` | number | `1` | global | no | no | Transient-DB-retries-per-minute above which a flapping Postgres is flagged. |

## sandbox
QuickJS JS sandbox limits

| path | type | default | scope | sensitive | requiresRestart | description |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ----- | --------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `sandbox.memory_bytes` | number | `134217728` | global | no | no | Hard WASM heap cap for a JS sandbox run, in bytes. Default 128 MB. |
| `sandbox.stack_bytes` | number | `2097152` | global | no | no | Max stack size for a JS sandbox run, in bytes. Default 2 MB. |
| `sandbox.tick_budget` | number | `10000000` | global | no | no | Interrupt-tick budget (coarse runaway backstop, not an opcode count). |
| `sandbox.transform_wall_ms` | number | `60000` | global | no | no | Wall-clock cap for transform steps, in ms (overridable per step via timeout_ms). Long synchronous transforms block the worker — chunk via for_each instead of raising. Default 60 s. |
| `sandbox.wall_ms` | number | `30000` | global | no | no | Default wall-clock cap for a JS sandbox run, in ms. Default 30 s. |

## connectors
Per-connector tunables. Each sub-section is owned by one connector template.

| path | type | default | scope | sensitive | requiresRestart | description |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ----- | --------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `connectors.http.max_response_bytes` | number | `104857600` | tenant | no | no | Max bytes read from a single HTTP/GraphQL connector response before it is rejected as response_too_large. OOM guard; generous default (100 MB). |
| `connectors.web_scraper.authoring.extract_too_large_yellow_pct` | number | `30` | tenant | no | no | Past-run extract_too_large ratio (over last 20 runs) above which the gate Yellows. |
| `connectors.web_scraper.authoring.red_sitemap_threshold` | number | `100000` | tenant | no | no | Sitemap entry count above which analyze_scrape_target refuses (Red). |
| `connectors.web_scraper.authoring.yellow_sitemap_threshold` | number | `10000` | tenant | no | no | Sitemap entry count above which analyze_scrape_target returns Yellow. |
| `connectors.web_scraper.optimization.min_runs_before_proposing` | number | `3` | tenant | no | no | Minimum recent runs before any candidate is emitted. |
| `connectors.web_scraper.optimization.sample_size` | number | `10` | tenant | no | no | Number of recent runs the analyzer reads per recipe. |
| `connectors.web_scraper.optimization.scan_cron` | string | `"0 3 * * *"` | global | no | no | Crontab for the per-tenant optimization scan (default daily 03:00). |
| `connectors.web_scraper.optimization.trivial_markdown_bytes` | number | `512` | tenant | no | no | Pages whose MarkdownOutput.bytes is below this count as trivial. |
| `connectors.web_scraper.robots_cache.max_entries` | number | `2000` | global | no | no | LRU ceiling shared across tenants (keyed by tenant_id + origin). |
| `connectors.web_scraper.robots_cache.ttl_ms` | number | `3600000` | global | no | no | TTL for the per-tenant robots.txt LRU. |
| `connectors.web_scraper.runtime.default_wait_ms` | number | `0` | tenant | no | no | Floor for between-page wait inside the crawl loop. Raised if robots.txt declares a higher Crawl-delay. |
| `connectors.web_scraper.runtime.max_chars_markdown` | number | `100000` | tenant | no | no | Per-page markdown output cap (extract_too_large). |
| `connectors.web_scraper.runtime.max_chars_readability` | number | `100000` | tenant | no | no | Per-page input cap into Readability (extract_too_large). |
| `connectors.web_scraper.runtime.max_pages` | number | `1000` | tenant | no | no | Per-run crawl cap. Hard ceiling 10 000 (crawl_max_pages_exceeded). |
| `connectors.web_scraper.runtime.respect_robots` | boolean | `true` | tenant | no | no | Skip URLs that robots.txt disallows for the configured User-Agent. |
| `connectors.web_scraper.runtime.user_agent` | string | `"sk-web-scraper/1.0 (+https://subkit.io/bot)"` | tenant | no | no | User-Agent header on every fetch; passed to robots-parser matching. |
